Beards, braids and babies: Meet the Christchurch Dads Stroller Club

New Zealand Herald October 31, 2026

Club founder Mattai Meafou with his children, Arthur, 3, and Nimaya, 1, during one of the group’s stroller walks. Photo / Rafaella Melo Fathers and their children during a walk organised by the Christchurch Dads Stroller Club. Photo / Rafaella Melo Club founder Mattai Meafou with his children, Arthur, 3, and Nimaya, 1, during one of the group’s stroller walks. Photo / Rafaella Melo Dads push their prams through Christchurch’s CBD during one of the club’s regular walks. Photo / Rafaella Melo

It’s an evening out in Christchurch, and about 35 men have gathered in the CBD.

But instead of beers, the tables are covered with hair gel, brushes and spray bottles.

It’s not quite what you would expect. They are fathers learning how to style their children’s hair.

And it’s not a one-off.

From stroller walks and coffee catch-ups to hair tutorials, yoga classes and conversations about mental health, the Christchurch Dads Stroller Club is giving fathers a chance to connect with other dads.

The club has 465 members in its private Facebook group, and about 25 fathers regularly turn up for its walks, often with little ones in tow, drawing smiles from passersby as dozens of dads push their prams through the CBD.

Behind it all is Burnside father-of-two Mattai Meafou, who came up with the idea after becoming a parent.

When his son Arthur was born three years ago, Meafou noticed there were plenty of opportunities for mothers to meet other mums, but not quite as many for fathers.

He wanted somewhere he could talk about the joys, challenges and occasional chaos of raising children with men who were going through the same thing.

With the help of his wife Brittany, he decided to create it.

The club launched in March last year, drawing about 60 fathers and their children to its first gathering.

“I was like ‘Oh, no one is going to come for this’, but the evidence shows over the last year and a half that actually dads do really want this,” Meafou said.

What began with monthly stroller walks has grown into something bigger, including hair-styling workshops, mental health events, and plans for a “pints and periods” session on puberty and supporting children through it.

Members also use the club’s platforms to organise their own meetups, including hikes and coffee outings, and to support one another through shared advice.

“We’ve got dads on the Facebook page asking about what’s the best way to transition their kids from a balance bike to a bike with training wheels,” Meafou said.

“Also, dads asking about tips and tricks because they’re about to go onto the plane for the first time with their kids, and what’s the best way to keep them occupied.

“And there’s some deeper things, like ‘I’m a new dad struggling with this at the moment’, and there’s a lot of encouragement and a lot of community to get behind those kinds of things as well.”

Meafou has also found himself benefiting from the support he set out to create.

When his daughter Nimaya, now 1, was born, he worried about giving her “the exact same kind of love” he had given his first child.

During one of the walks, a father of three shared advice that helped him.

“Everything he had said to me just felt very raw and honest ... it hit me in the right way.”

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

For 28-year-old Fong Kittiputarapol, becoming a dad meant finding himself at a different stage of life from many people his age.

While his workmates in hospitality were often going out drinking after work, he was navigating fatherhood and sometimes feeling “lonely”.

He joined the club after discovering it on social media, and although work commitments mean he cannot attend every event, he has found a community he didn’t know he needed.

“When I got to the club, I just felt like I was a part of something ... I feel like there’s a place where all dads belong.”

Kittiputarapol, whose son Ari is 18 months old, recalled hearing another father admit he felt unsure whether he was doing things right.

It struck a chord as he had felt much the same when Ari was born.

Hearing other dads share similar struggles has helped him feel more confident as a father and partner, he said.

“I can read so many books, which I do, but it’s different when you talk to another dad who lives around the same area, and they’re going through the same thing, or they went through the same thing,” Kittiputarapol said.

“Every dad deserves to know about this.”

Brett McGlashan, a father of two daughters, Amelia, 3, and Eleanor, 1, said the club has brought new friendships – and some hairstyling skills.

He joined the club about eight months ago, with his first event being a hair-tutorial workshop.

“It was bloody awesome,” he said.

Having barely styled his daughters’ hair before, McGlashan now does it often before work.

“It helped me gain the confidence to do it.”

The Dads Strollers club is free to join, most activities cost nothing, and there’s no strict age limit for children.

Expectant fathers were also welcomed.

Rafaella Melo is a multimedia journalist with more than 10 years’ experience in Brazil. She spent two years reporting for Hawke’s Bay Today before joining the NZ Herald’s Christchurch team in 2026.

Don’t take the privilege of voting for granted – Editorial

New Zealand Herald October 31, 2026

Voting papers being printed in Petone, Wellington weeks ahead of the election. Photo / Samuel Rilestone, RNZ

Whatever your political leaning, one thing everyone should agree on is that every eligible Kiwi ought to get out and vote this week.

Our geographic isolation can mean at times it is easy to take what we have for granted.

One can think the rest of the world lives in relative peace and prosperity like we do.

However, it only takes a short time away to realise how special New Zealand is.

The world is in a state of upheaval and uncertainty.

Technology is advancing at a rapid pace, there is global economic turmoil, social unrest plagues European societies, and significant wars continue to rage and kill thousands on multiple continents.

In times like these, having a stable, reliable and functioning democracy is as valuable as it has been in decades.

What is encouraging is New Zealanders appear to have got the message early.

The number of early votes cast soared over the half a million mark on Friday, hitting 593,953, according to figures published by the Electoral Commission.

That compares with 449,706 advance votes being cast at a similar point in the 2023 election.

Large numbers of advance votes have been a feature of this election so far and will likely climb higher over the weekend, when many people are expected to vote.

Early voting was higher in 2020 but voting opened earlier that year, and people voted early on account of the pandemic.

When you read the next edition of this newspaper in a week’s time there will be much to discuss, debate and dissect. The initial results will be in, and the polls suggest it is going to be a tight race to determine the make-up of our next government.

There was much talk about the earlier deadline to enrol to vote for this election, but that date has now come and gone. What is left for every eligible voter to do is get out, exercise their right, cast their votes and have their voice heard.

Let’s show the world how much we value our small democracy at the bottom of the globe.

Don’t take the privilege for granted.

It’s tipped to be one of the best matches of the Rugby League World Cup tournament, as Tonga and Samoa face each other in the ultimate Pacific showdown.

Excitement has been building for weeks ahead of tonight’s sold-out game at CommBank Stadium in Sydney, which kicks off at 10.05pm NZT.

In Auckland, the biggest Polynesian city in the world, spontaneous parades and celebrations have popped up all around over the past few weeks since the tournament started.

Samoan and Tongan flags have been particularly prominent this week as the communities show their pride and support for their respective teams.

On Ōtāhuhu’s main shopping strip, on Great South Rd, blue and red shirts have pride of place in front of several stores, with Samoan and Tongan flags waving wildly in the Auckland wind that day.

Gary Wang, owner of the Bargain House store, is busy hanging up Tonga and Samoa-branded rugby league jerseys and shirts when the Herald arrives.

“Very busy,” he says.

There are flags of all sizes at the store – small, medium, large and mega large, that are sometimes seen on the sides of trucks or flying outside houses. There are also tiny flags for desks – the Samoan flags have sold out in that size.

“Over the last two weeks, we’ve sold probably nearly 1000 flags. Tonga is most popular,” Wang says with a smile.

Mele Finau is easily spotted in her bright red shirt, complete with the word “TONGA” on the front.

The 27-year-old from Parnell said she had been showing off her Tongan pride by wearing red and white this week. Seeing all the excitement among both Tongan and Samoan communities had been wonderful.

“I think it’s a great way for us to show our pride in our country, especially living away from the islands. It’s our way to connect back to our motherland.”

Proud Samoan Chris Paea’s car has two mega-sized Samoan flags flying from it. There is another huge one outside his house just around the corner, he says.

Speaking in Samoan, he shared a message to the Toa Samoa players: “We are supporting you, brothers. We’re praying for a good game and a good result.”

He lets out a sudden “cheehoo” – making several passersby jump.

There is no doubt who Penisimani Latu is backing to win tonight, with the entire bonnet of his vehicle covered in the distinctive red and white flag.

“You’ve got to be proud of where you come from. But it doesn’t matter if you’re Tongan or Samoan – at the end of the day, we all come from the islands.

“If Tonga goes down this weekend, then we will turn around and support Samoa.”

Police and community leaders are backing both teams, but calling on members of the public to stay safe and be mindful of the whole community.

Officers will be out and about to ensure celebrations are safe and respectful.

Superintendent Riki Whiu said celebrations should not put anyone in danger or disrupt other people’s evenings.

“Keep celebrations away from open roads and intersections. Flags can fly freely outside your vehicle, but all passengers must remain safely inside.”

Over the past few weeks, authorities have received noise complaints in relation to loud music, horn tooting and celebrations going into the early hours of the morning.

“Be mindful of neighbours and residential areas. Keep the music down and your hands on the steering wheel, not the horn,” Whiu said.

Manukau ward councillor Alf Filipaina said it was an exciting time for many rugby league fans around the world; but especially for Samoan and Tongan fans this weekend.

“It’s always been exciting when you get two Pacific nations playing against each other. And we know with the Rugby League World Cup, we’ve got Samoa and Tonga.

“But my plea to the supporters is, please, safety is number one – safety is first. Whether you’re driving around with your flags, be wary.”

Filipaina spoke about an incident during Rugby League World Cup celebrations in 2022, when a woman was seriously injured at a parade in Māngere.

Police said she had been sitting on the bonnet of a moving vehicle when she fell and was then run over by a car.

“That’s what’s so important – the safety,” Filipaina said.

“Don’t sit outside the window. You want to make sure you end up watching the game too – and watch more games.”

Asked whether he had any country flags on his car, Filipaina laughed, saying that although he did not have any, he was backing Samoa because of his father’s side of the aiga.

He is also a supporter of the Kiwis, he said, as an ode to his Māori roots on his mother’s side. His brother is also Kiwis rugby league legend, the late Olsen Filipaina.

Vaimoana Mase is the Pasifika editor for the Herald’s Talanoa section, sharing stories from the Pacific community. She won junior reporter of the year at the then Qantas Media Awards in 2010 and won the best opinion writing award at the 2023 Voyager Media Awards.

Sydney Morning Herald November 01, 2026

The Lotus Nail Studio in Tregear in Sydney’s west was winding down just after 6pm one Saturday late last month when the three hooded figures walked in, demanding cash and brandishing a hammer.

Closed-circuit television shows one of the figures lunging with the hammer at the salon’s sole worker, a terrified 55-year-old woman who asked not to be named.

The most disturbing aspect of the alleged crime was that the would-be attackers were aged just 11 and 12.

1:49

Boy, 13, arrested after bottle shop rampage

A 13-year-old boy has been arrested and accused of stealing and assaulting staff after allegedly storming a bottle shop in Sydney’s south-west.

Across the city in Narellan Vale earlier that month, a group of teens and pre-teens allegedly swarmed a bottle shop, fighting staff and stealing cases of drinks. Five boys, aged between 12 and 15, were charged.

“I couldn’t believe that was happening here, and they are so young,” said Santiago Wu, whose mother owns the store.

The two incidents are tiny pieces in a mosaic of youth crime that police and experts say is seeing younger and younger children sucked from the fringes of the criminal world into violent criminal acts.

Youth crime rates across the state are mostly either stable or trending down – with the exception of murder and some forms of assault.

Widespread use of encrypted phone apps and social media has allowed children to transition from misdemeanours into more serious violent criminal activity very swiftly, in some cases within weeks, experts say.

The Australian Federal Police warned a federal parliamentary committee last month that “Australia is at the crossroads of a tsunami of youth crime” as online platforms and tools become more secret, sophisticated and popular.

“It has certainly lowered the barrier to entry into organised crime,” says Detective acting Superintendent Jason Smith, acting head of Taskforce Falcon, the NSW Police squad charged with combating gang warfare and organised crime.

Of the 530 people arrested by Taskforce Falcon so far this year, almost 50 have been children, the youngest being 14. Most are being paid peanuts.

“Call it market forces or whatever you like, but the saturation of the market with young people willing to take on these roles has resulted in a drop in the amount of money being paid,” Smith says.

“We’ve got young people essentially throwing their life away for $500.

“The problem is that there is a never-ending supply of young people who are willing to become involved. These people are being exploited by organised crime figures living overseas because they’re cheap, and they’re expendable.”

Data collected by the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (BOCSAR) shows fewer young people are becoming entangled in the justice system than in recent decades.

“Young people today are much less likely to commit crimes,” Jackie Fitzgerald, executive director of BOCSAR, says.

It’s not accurate to speak in terms of a youth crime wave, despite the involvement of children in high-profile gangland hits, she says.

The latest figures, which cover up to June this year, paint a nuanced picture of youth crime across the state.

Central and inner south Sydney have the state’s highest youth crime rate, while the eastern suburbs have a higher youth crime rate per person than areas such as south-west Sydney and Blacktown.

This is because the city and the east are often entertainment or social destinations for young people and accessible by public transport, and the influx of young people – a tiny proportion of whom commit crimes – skews the numbers, BOCSAR says.

“The trend is steady, and if there is a tsunami of youth crime it hasn’t shown up in the numbers yet,” Alex Simpson, an associate professor of criminology at Macquarie University, says.

Fitzgerald says average youth crime rates in western and northern NSW are higher than almost all parts of Sydney.

“Sydney gets a lot of focus, but there are communities outside Sydney that are dealing with levels of victimisation and offending [that] are much higher,” she says.

“Many people in these communities have safety concerns that people in Sydney cannot relate to.”

The apparent uptick in the number of violent crimes, including murder and assault, which appeared to begin just before the COVID-19 pandemic, follows a decade of relatively few violent crimes being committed by young people.

“Over the last five years we’ve seen roughly 10 young people charged with murder, and that’s higher than we were seeing a decade ago,” Fitzgerald says. “But if we expand our view, we can see that 20 years ago, there were many more kids being charged with murder.”

The numbers of murders for which children are charged are small, usually fewer than a dozen a year, and therefore are barely visible in the overall crime statistics.

But the recent spike is concerning criminologists who are unsure whether the spate of violent crimes by children is an anomaly before a return to lower levels of violence, or something new.

“It is a post-COVID phenomena,” Associate Professor Garner Clancey, a criminologist at the University of Sydney, says.

“On the back of the pandemic we’ve got a whole new landscape that’s been affected by the ‘manosphere’, kids spending more time online, kids being de-schooled, the rise of the ‘crimfluencers’. Their exposure to anti-government commentary, pornography, deep fakes is much higher. Our prevention strategies need to be recalibrated.

“So it’s an interesting time and there are some novel aspects. There’s a general world on social media [of] ‘crimfluencers’ and people who are generating content built around a gangster lifestyle online.”

Clancey describes a globalised world of organised crime that has become wearily familiar to police over the past two years.

The model features the big bosses who remain offshore, outside the reach of Australian law enforcement. They co-ordinate crimes such as arson, theft and public-place shootings from encrypted apps, using a series of middlemen who are not connected to each other, before orders for crime jobs filter down to young people in NSW, who have no idea who they are working for.

In subsets of online culture, “posting and boasting” about relatively minor crimes on social media can act as a “calling card” for adult criminals to recruit them, he says.

“It is a bit like online grooming, but unlike with sex offending, there’s a sense of volition. The evidence suggests they go in with their eyes somewhat open.

“With the ‘posting and boasting’, it shows a willingness to do certain things, and shows they have certain skills. These acts require a degree of thinking and planning and executing, and you have to know how to do things, like steal a car or burn a tobacco shop.”

The grooming process can be alarmingly swift, Clancey says.

“From what we know, it’s definitely not years, more likely weeks or months. Sometimes quicker if there’s a bit of cash.”

Smith agrees, but says officers in Taskforce Falcon mostly encounter a “hybrid model” where calling card-style recruitment is accompanied by in-person approaches by criminals, or links via family members.

A caseworker who works with young people involved in gangland crimes in Sydney says family connections are probably the strongest indicator of involvement.

“In most cases with young offenders there is the cousin, or a parent, or sometimes a long-standing friendship network that provides the entree,” says the caseworker, who asked not be named because they are not permitted to speak publicly about their work.

“Apps are a tool but behaviours can be seeded, often quite early, by social life, family life and background.”

A BOCSAR report, published in December, sought to isolate which factors were most likely to bring children in NSW into contact with the justice system.

It used information from seven government departmental data sets, including the police, juvenile justice, health and education departments, and examined the anonymised records of all people born in NSW in 1998, 1999 and 2000.

Gender and Aboriginality were the biggest factors in whether pre-teens came into contact with the justice system, but as children grew into teenagers, school attendance became by far the strongest predictor of whether a young person would be involved in crime.

“By the age of 15, we see that the model is essentially only making predictions using school suspension data, indicating that observable behavioural indicators become increasingly influential in later adolescence.”

The most recent survey of young people in custody by government agency Youth Justice NSW found the majority of children who participated in the research had had one or both parents incarcerated.

New NSW bail laws have had a big impact on the number of young people being locked up in youth detention centres with a 34 per cent jump since April last year when the rules came into force. The laws removed some of the discretion from judges to grant bail for 14- to 17-year-olds if they had a previous property or car theft charge. Most of the young people detained by the state are on remand, not serving sentences.

“There are large numbers of young people churning through the system, but there is strong evidence that this does not actually reduce crime,” says Mindy Sotiri, the executive director of the Justice Reform Initiative, a research group at the University of NSW.

Sotiri cites examples of overseas reforms that focus on keeping young people out of detention, where they are liable to be influenced by other offenders, leading to reductions in youth crime.

In Scotland, the prison population of children is zero after reforms in 2024 shifted the focus from punishment to child welfare, and youth crime rates appear to be falling, though it is too early to assess the long-term effects.

“There absolutely has to be consequences [for youth offending] and there is a role for detention,” Sotiri says. “But the common thread running through success stories in this space is a recognition that punishing children is not how you reduce crime.”

Hamish Blake is useless. And he’d like you to hire him for your next job

Sydney Morning Herald November 01, 2026

Having made a fortune from being a regular guy, Hamish Blake has decided it’s time to get some real skills. You have been warned.

Hamish Blake is a bit useless. To be clear, that’s not my view, it’s his own. “I’m well into my forties and after essentially just talking for a living, I’ve got to this point in my life and realised I don’t really have any other skills,” he says in the intro to his new series, Unskilled Adult. “I look around everywhere and see people who can do actual useful stuff, and I guess I’m a bit jealous. So I wondered, could that be me.”

The reality series is essentially Blake’s effort to learn by doing. He sets up a business – UA (for unskilled adult) Enterprises – ropes in a couple of similarly useless mates, typically from the world of comedy, and sets about completing actual tasks for actual people for actual money. If they think he’s done a good job, they pay him in full. If not, they pay him what they think it’s worth.

At the end of it all, they get the job done, and he gets to be, well, a little less useless. Well, that’s the theory anyway.

Let’s start with the basics, Hamish. Do you really think you’re an unskilled adult?

“I think it is a fair description of me, and people who feel like me, usually from the entertainment industry,” he says. “If you don’t get taught those skills [building, sewing, cooking] as a kid or in your teenage years, I guess you can just grow up without them. So this was my attempt to force myself to learn things.”

Given enough time and resources, most people could probably learn to do most of the things Blake and co set about undertaking in the series – in the first four episodes, that includes basic carpentry, welding, panel beating and catering. But UA Enterprises appears to have a predisposition for the tight turnaround – jobs typically land on a Wednesday and need to be finished by close of business on Friday – though the budget for tools, gear and lunch is seemingly unlimited.

Making the task that little bit harder is that Blake and his guest workers tend to spend most of the first day gasbagging, eating and shopping; day two is typically long, and day three is where the poop really hits the oscillating wind-blowing machine.

“It does a strange thing to your head when you know you have to do it, you know it’s on you,” he says, attempting to explain the procrastination. “When you don’t know how to do something, it’s just human nature that your first port of call is to do a lot of things that aren’t the thing, to make you feel like you’re getting somewhere. So a lot of planning, a lot of wild ideas – you’re on with really funny people, so everyone’s having lots of ideas – but then it does slowly dawn on you that the people who have to do all these ideas are still us.”

The customers know what they’re signing up for, of course – on the off-chance they don’t recognise Blake or any of his guests (including long-time collaborator and mate Andy Lee, Flight of the Conchords’ Bret McKenzie, Spelling Bee host Guy Montgomery, comedian Becky Lucas and the ubiquitous Sophie Monk), the camera crew is a dead giveaway. But Blake insists that the job at hand is real, there’s no safety blanket – stuff up that car repair and there isn’t a new car waiting for you – and the exchange of cash is genuinely based on how they assess the work.

“It was important for us to keep it real because it is central to the idea of biting off more than you can chew, and genuinely having to figure your way out of it, and not being allowed to give up. And I think if you combine those elements that creates a great adventure.”

Blake describes himself as someone who talks for a living. In reality, he’s parlayed being a regular bloke – good-looking, affable, a bit of a doofus, always willing to poke fun at himself – into a very significant media career (radio, podcasts, TV, the occasional movie role) and a considerable fortune. “I’ve talked to good effect,” he concedes. “But I haven’t really done anything that you would hang your hat on as a skill.”

Has doing this show changed that at all – have you actually acquired any real skills?

“Shamefully not as much as I was hoping,” he says.

He tells me that before they set out on this adventure, he and his co-creator and director Tim Bartley wondered if there was any risk that he might become too capable, and thus kill the gag. “I was like, ‘I guess we’ll cross that bridge when we come to it’,” Blake says. “And we have not come to that bridge.”

He did, however, become passably good at “some wood stuff”, he boasts.

I think they call it carpentry, I note.

“Yeah. I think if I had to go and be an apprentice in any field, I’d be a chippy. If they’d take [me].”

So since doing this, have you done anything in your own actual life, like maybe put up a shelf at home?

“I did something the other day, and the family was cheering,” he says. “My kids were like, ‘He’s done it! He’s done it! He’s not unskilled’.”

For a moment, he struggles to recall what it was. And then it comes to him. “We live a couple of blocks from the beach in Sydney, and I’d left a jacket in the garage and the zip had rusted. I put WD40 on it, and I used pliers. ‘Look at that everyone, come gather round. Dad’s going to do something’.”

And that’s something you wouldn’t have been able to do before this show?

“How would I know what to do?”

As much as he talks up his incompetence, in the episodes I’ve seen Blake and co actually manage to do a passable job of mastering the basics. I mean, you might not hire them to build your next house, but you might entrust them with a planter box.

Given the enormous following he has with tradies, is there a risk that he might inadvertently be giving the impression that being a carpenter, a bricklayer, a chef, a welder is a breeze, that two days is all anyone needs to master it? To put it bluntly, might some people think their favourite multimillionaire is being just a bit disrespectful?

“Look, I did actually kind of wonder the same thing,” he says. “This is certainly not us going, ‘Wow, these trades are easy. Being a chef is easy. Being a carpenter is easy. Anyone can do it.’ It’s certainly not that. I know it takes years and years to acquire mastery of these skills. But what could you get done in a few days? Can you just learn anything?

“I suppose it’s just learning the bare, bare, bare basics. There’s no risk of any bricklayers looking at it and going, ‘Well, I can’t fault them. They’re the best bricklayers I’ve ever seen.’ It’s more that thrill – and I really enjoy this in life – of being a beginner. I think anyone who has any level of proficiency in any of these things would look at [our efforts] and go, ‘That’s about what I thought people with one day of experience would be able to achieve’.”

Blake has shown some of the show to an electrician mate, whose response gave him confidence that no one is going to mistakenly conclude he is passing himself off as the real deal.

“He was laughing at stuff I didn’t even know was funny, where we’re telling the client, ‘All right, we’ll see you at 10’,” he says. “He spat out his coffee, he was like, ‘That’s hilarious’.”

After 23 years as one of the most affable personalities in Australian showbiz, Blake has a huge network of friends and colleagues he could tap to be part of this exercise in comedic upskilling. But one person who doesn’t turn up as a guest labourer is his wife, Zoe Foster Blake.

The beauty entrepreneur and author is plenty busy with her career, but that’s not why she’s not on Unskilled Adult.

“I floated it with her,” he says. “I was like, ‘Hey, if you wanted to be on the show, that would be funny.’ And she was like, ‘That is my hell. It’s my absolute hell.’ She was just like, ‘No f---ing way, mate’.”

Why?

“I think what it comes down to is we have a real different relationship with uncertainty and with chaos,” Blake says. “I feel quite comfortable in uncertainty. I’m really bad with a script, the times I’ve had to learn something word-perfect, I’m the worst. I like just being a bit loosey-goosey. But Zoe would prefer to know what’s going on. So I don’t know if it’d be great for our marriage if I had her as one of my workers on the show.”

That sounds like a very wise decision there from the adult in your relationship.

“The best skill I have is keeping my marriage.”

Unskilled Adult premieres on Sunday, November 1, on Stan, with new episodes dropping weekly.

‘They wanted our WhatsApps’: Staff claim culture of fear at Florey

Sydney Morning Herald November 01, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

No gift articles left

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Article gifting is here

Give anyone free access to subscriber-only stories when you subscribe.

In December 2024, researchers at the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health were called into a meeting with senior leadership.

Recollections differ about the tone of the meeting, but the message was clear.

Taxpayer-funded research grants are the lifeblood of independent research institutes – and the Florey was not winning nearly enough.

“At a time when most researchers were devastated at finding they were unsuccessful after spending months preparing applications,” one said, leadership “got up in front of everyone and berated us for not doing good enough”.

“After that meeting, everyone was walking around chatting to colleagues saying ‘can you believe it? I can’t believe that happened’.”

Yesterday, an investigation by this masthead revealed the venerable institute – which the Rockefeller Foundation helped establish and was named after penicillin pioneer and Nobel Laureate Howard Florey – had become embroiled in chaos as it faced financial strife and an exodus of top research talent.

Today, the investigation focuses on the scientific fallout from that turmoil – numerous complaints about the culture inside the Florey and the string of court cases in which it is now embroiled.

This masthead has spoken to 22 former or current Florey staff – very few willing to be identified publicly for fear of retribution – to build a picture of a once-great institution under extreme financial pressure and facing accusations of building an unhealthy atmosphere for a workforce trying to solve dementia, Alzheimer’s, epilepsy, MND and mental health conditions.

“They’ve created this culture: the scientists are the ones to blame for the problem they are in. A pure toxic culture has developed,” said a current researcher, speaking under condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal.

“They have taken the option to go completely corporate. You can’t do that with a research institute because you’re just going to end up getting rid of most people – and the rest are going to want to leave.”

A Florey spokeswoman said falls in grant income “reflect[ed] a tightening national funding environment” and “notably, funding for dementia reduced by 48% over the same time period” according to the National Health and Medical Research Council, website and annual disease funding statistics.

They denied anyone had been “berated” about grant success rates, and said the meeting discussed “low national success rates”.

“This was a constructive discussion that identified other grant schemes that our researchers could apply to.”

But a confidential Florey presentation from February 2025 lamented “limited grant success in 2024 funding round, below expectations, partly due to inconsistent and inefficient grant support”.

“Every funding round was just a constant disappointment,” said a former staff member.

In response to poor success rates, the institute proposed implementing an internal vetting system before grants could be submitted.

“The result is less grants being submitted in order to artificially inflate the apparent success rate, a metric which has absolutely no impact on researchers,” said a former researcher.

A spokeswoman for the Florey said it was “committed to attracting and retaining the brightest minds in medical research, while supporting professional development and opportunities across the medical research sector”. The institute does not prevent researchers from submitting grant applications, she said.

Three current and two former researchers said the turmoil, staff losses and cost-cutting at the institute made it hard to do quality science.

“It’s so sad. Seeing the good these scientists want to do and can do, but at the top there’s this group that is so focused on money, nothing else really matters,” said a former staff member.

“And that’s the most disappointing thing. There was this obsession with monetising anything they could – the science got lost, it really got lost.”

Yesterday, this masthead’s investigation into the Florey revealed it had been running multimillion-dollar deficits since 2022, while commercial revenues – crucial to the Florey business model – have nearly halved since 2022.

“We need to continue to look at all measures that can help The Florey’s ongoing financial sustainability,” a confidential presentation from February 2025 reads.

In an effort to cut costs, “they are nickel-and-diming everything”, said a current researcher. “Every penny gets fought over.”

In early 2024, Florey scientists were told they would be asked to pay “bench fees”: thousands of dollars per researcher for using the Florey’s laboratory benches to do science.

Staff have been limited from accessing machines and ordering chemicals essential to basic experiments, two current researchers said.

“They have brought in lots of different costs. They are charging extra things, and making it almost impossible to do research,” said a current Florey scientist, speaking anonymously due to fear of retribution.

“Can you tell me any organisation in research that’s able to work on a cost-recovery basis? That’s not how it works.”

Following complaints from staff, leadership did not end up imposing the new “bench fees”; a spokeswoman said it did not operate a full cost-recovery model.

But the incident is emblematic of a new, corporate culture focused on cost cuts at the venerable institute, staff say.

The Florey receives a federal government grant to fund free testing for patients who may have prion disease, a lethal neurodegenerative condition. In February, the funding agreement was varied allowing the Florey to charge for the service.

The institute has been trying to cut down on conference travel and catering. A staff member recalled being scolded after handing out a $12 parking voucher.

“Most scientists are fed up with Florey’s lack of support and they mostly had to deal with the political atmosphere created by the senior executives, who were mostly from [the] corporate world and who are trying to corporatise the Florey,” said a former researcher.

“To do good research you need a good environment to attract and – most importantly – keep good researchers, which is not the case in recent years,” said a current researcher.

Four current and seven former staff said the workplace had become “toxic”, with senior management increasingly paranoid.

“They want to instigate a little bit of fear. Because that’s a very good tool to keep people’s head down, not to go to the union, not to know their rights,” said a former researcher.

A current researcher described being treated “like criminals”, and watching another team being surveilled.

“They took their phones and laptops. They cut their access to the building. They asked someone to export all their WhatsApp chats,” they said.

Another researcher confirmed the institute had tried to search WhatsApp chats.

“No one feels safe. Even when I leave my laptop on the desk, people say, take it – they don’t know if [management is] going to take it.”

Another current researcher described “a culture of paranoia”, where employees are worried the institute is using microphones on laptops to spy on them. “Every one of us now has second email accounts because we know the emails are being monitored.”

The Florey said it “rejects this characterisation of the culture of the institute”, and “does not search personal phones”.

The Florey faces another strain on its budget: a remarkable pattern of lawsuits involving current and former staff.

This masthead can reveal the institute has been embroiled in at least 10 court cases since 2024, some involving its biggest names.

“For an organisation of that size, it is a lot,” said a former staff member with direct knowledge of the legal actions.

Three former or current Florey scientists, including star researcher Bradley Turner, have appeared before the Fair Work Commission since May, according to court listings.

Its former chief operating officer took the Florey to the Fair Work Commission in December 2023; the outcome of his case was not disclosed, and he did not return requests for comment.

An institute spokeswoman said it did not comment on legal cases. The number of cases before the Fair Work Commission was “not disproportionate with other organisations of our size, in an environment where funding is tough”. No fair work rulings have been made against the Florey.

Staff members Susan Cox and Soniya Survase applied to the commission in March 2025 after their employment at the Florey ended; both were on repeatedly renewed one-year contracts, with Cox having been there for 14 years.

The commission ruled they were not fixed-term employees, and therefore rejected their claim for redundancy payments.

“There are so many cases in Fair Work,” said one former senior staff member. “They are inundated with the number of lawsuits or other legal cases,” said a current staff member.

The most critical lawsuit involves former Florey business development manager James Tran.

The Florey last year alleged, in a suit filed in Victoria’s Supreme Court, Tran stole thousands of documents, and entered the Florey late at night to delete other files.

Tran denies the allegation. He is now pursuing a separate workplace relations claim against the Florey in the Federal Circuit Court.

He told the court in September he had raised concerns at the Florey and then was accused of misconduct, threatened with termination, and placed under “sustained pressure” to resign.

The Florey’s legal representative described Tran’s remarks as “a form of tirade against a former employer”.

It is not the first time the Florey has faced allegations it forced out staff who raised concerns.

In March 2024, Hannah Hellwich, an animal technician, was sacked by the Florey following an internal investigation.

According to Fair Work Commission documents, Hellwich was then told her termination could be reclassified as a resignation, and she would get six weeks’ pay if she signed a “deed of release” – an agreement typically used to close off any future legal claims against an employer.

As part of an unfair dismissal application later that year, Hellwich told the commission she “felt pressured to sign the deed, and that she believed that the Florey wanted her to do so in order to ‘shut her up’.”

She told the commission the Florey “just wanted to get rid of her” after she made “serious allegations against another employee” – something the Florey “rejected”.

The commission found Hellwich submitted her unfair dismissal application a day late, and rejected the application.

“There are plenty of people who have received allegations and have been basically forced to resign. There are plenty,” said a former researcher. “They definitely looked at certain researchers and decided they have to go, so we’ll be mean to them so they have to leave,” said another.

Two former researchers said they were accused of misconduct as a pretext for terminating them. Other former staff allege they were given poor performance reviews to allow the Florey to terminate them.

“They overwhelm you, and tell you ‘you are shit’, until you leave,” said one.

In response to detailed questions about staffing and culture, a spokeswoman for the Florey said it “does not have a strategy to ‘push out’ particular staff members”.

“Reductions in staff numbers is a sector-wide occurrence associated with intense funding pressures,” she said.

Man in Belfast charged with possessing explosives and firearms

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 20:21:08 GMT

The 35-year-old was charged after police searched properties in Shankill Road and Edwina Street areas

A man has been charged under the Explosives Act and Firearms Order after police searched properties in Belfast.

The 35-year-old was charged with offences including two counts of possessing explosives under suspicious circumstances, and possession of a prohibited weapon (discharge of electricity or noxious gas).

He is due to appear before Belfast magistrates court on Monday, the Police Service of Northern Ireland said.

The charges follow searches at properties in the Shankill Road and Edwina Street areas of north Belfast on Friday and Saturday.

DCI McCallum said: “Following these searches a number of suspicious devices, along with other items, were located and seized by officers for forensic examination.

“Local residents who were evacuated as a precaution have now been allowed to return home following the public safety operation conducted alongside ammunition technical officers.

“All cordons have now been lifted from the area, and we thank local residents for their patience as inquiries were conducted yesterday and into today.”

McCallum added: “As we continue to investigate the circumstances surrounding this incident, we would appeal to anyone who may have information that could assist with inquiries to contact us on 101, quoting reference number 261 30/10/26.”

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 20:06:46 GMT

Bayern Munich held to 2-2 draw after Silva equaliser

Atlético Madrid go top of La Liga after win over Levante

The Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane missed a penalty and hit the post for ⁠Bayern Munich as Borussia Dortmund snatched a last-gasp equaliser through Fabio Silva for a 2-2 draw ⁠in Der Klassiker on ⁠Saturday ​that kept the teams level on points at the top.

Kane, who collected his prize in a ceremony ⁠in London on Monday, was an unused substitute in the 6-1 German Cup second-round demolition of Magdeburg on Wednesday ⁠but returned to the starting lineup on Saturday, missing from the spot with Bayern 1-0 up. He also hit ​the post, one of four ‌times Bayern struck ‌the woodwork.

Silva snatched the equaliser in the 89th minute to leave both ‌teams on 18 points, with Bayern top on goal difference.

In a rollercoaster first half Bayern hit the post through Michael Olise and Ismael Saibari missed a golden chance before the visitors had a goal ruled out by VAR.

Bayern, ‌also hit by injuries to Serge Gnabry and Olise, struck in the 38th minute thanks to Konrad Laimer’s goal on ​the rebound, after his first effort was blocked by Dortmund’s Gregor Kobel.

With the Bayern head coach, Vincent Kompany, recovering after his collapse last week, Bayern’s full-back Laimer was more threatening than Kane, who sent his 56th ⁠minute spot-kick against the crossbar.

Dortmund scored through Serhou Guirassy on ​the hour but parity lasted only ​six minutes as Dayot Upamecano tapped in from a Kane ​assist from close ‌range.

Kane’s low shot ​bounced off ​the post before Silva scored the equaliser. Bayern’s Lennart Karl still had time to see his shot in stoppage time bounce off the crossbar and cap a frustrating day for the champions.

Elsewhere in the Bundesliga, last season’s Europa League finalist Freiburg beat Augsburg 2-1 thanks to Cyriaque Irie’s 85th-minute goal to stay third. RB Leipzig are close behind in fourth after beating Schalke 2-0. The league top scorer, Niclas Füllkrug, added his ninth goal as Werder Bremen beat Hoffenheim 2-0 to move up to fifth.

Bayer Leverkusen’s strong early form hit another setback in a 4-2 loss at home to Stuttgart for back-to-back defeats. Borussia Mönchengladbach and Paderborn drew 0-0.

Atlético Madrid went to the top of La Liga – for a few hours, at least – after beating Levante 2-0.

Mitchell injury blow adds to England’s woes as Northampton sink Gloucester

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 20:05:25 GMT

Northampton 28-14 Gloucester

Alex Mitchell limps off with suspected hamstring pull

England’s injury headaches are mounting before next Sunday’s autumn opener against Australia with the scrum-half Alex Mitchell a major doubt after limping out of Northampton’s hard-fought victory over Gloucester with another hamstring problem.

It is to the credit of Northampton that they weathered that setback, withheld Gloucester’s early onslaught to score 28 unanswered points and see off the early-season pace-setters. Northampton’s last league outing here ended with 119 points scored but this was a victory founded on their defensive resilience with Tom Pearson, back in the England picture this autumn, outstanding throughout.

If Pearson’s performance will have pleased Borthwick, Mitchell’s withdrawal will not. He is already sweating on the fitness of the Northampton fly-half Fin Smith, who sat in the stands with an injured calf here, and now has concerns over his half-back partner Mitchell. England begin a crucial autumn series against the Wallabies and Borthwick now has significant concerns in two key positions. Mitchell’s injury is all the more of a worry with Archie McParland, his Northampton team-mate and fellow scrum-half, omitted from the matchday squad against Gloucester due to a calf injury sustained earlier in the week at England’s training camp.

It would be rough on Mitchell should he miss out considering it is a fourth hamstring injury of the year and his body language when leaving the field does not bode well. He suffered similar injuries during the Six Nations, at an England camp in May – recovering to take his place in the Northampton squad for the Prem final win over Exeter – and during the summer Test against Fiji. Jack van Poortvliet was England’s starting scrum-half for the summer given Mitchell’s lack of game time but when fit and firing the Northampton Saint is England’s first-choice No 9.

Joe Shaw praised Saracens’ character as they saw off a highly competitive and scrapping Newcastle side at the StoneX Stadium. The head coach saw his team overturn a 17-7 half-time deficit to run out 39-31 bonus-point winners for their third Prem victory of the season and move up to third.

Noah Caluori came on after the break to lift what had been a lacklustre home performance by racing over for a score as Sarries ran in five second-half tries to finally get the better of visitors who had threatened an upset.

Shaw said: “It’s probably best to forget about that first half because it wasn’t a pretty watch and was unexpected … Fortunately, the guys improved a lot with their execution after the break and we created several fine tries.”

Johann van Graan was upbeat after seeing Bath returned to winning ways with a comfortable 36-28 bonus-point victory over Sale at the Rec. After three consecutive defeats, the home side were greatly improved, playing with far more speed and efficiency than in recent weeks to entertain the sell-out crowd with a number of well-created tries. Joe Cokanasiga (pictured) scored two of them, Henry Arundell, Tom de Glanville and Louie Hennessey the others, with Finn Russell converting four and adding a penalty.

Nathan Jibulu, Tom O’Flaherty, Luke Cowan-Dickie and Elia Canakaivata scored Sale’s tries, all of which George Ford converted.

Van Graan, Bath's director of rugby, said: “Last week we didn’t take our opportunities, but we were much more clinical today. We had a good balance to our game, with Finn expertly using the space out wide against a big physical side. We were really positive throughout and closed the game out well."

Harlequins' head coach, Jason Gilmore, said a big improvement in his side’s discipline paved the way for their 31-28 victory at Exeter. Quins led 14-0 after 11 minutes but then allowed the Chiefs back into the contest by giving away nine penalties and it was 14-14 at the break.

Gilmore said: “We went eight or nine penalties on the bounce against us, which was poor, and a yellow card, and we gave Exeter good field position … I said to the boys at half-time: 'If we can stop giving penalties away and get our hands back on the ball, we will be all right,' and I don’t think we gave away a penalty again until the last minute of the game.” Press Association

“Fin and Archie are both calf, Fin probably not as bad as Archie but it remains to be seen,” said Northampton’s director of rugby, Phil Dowson. “Mitchell has hurt his hamstring but I don’t know how bad. We have to be super careful with Alex and he knows his own body.”

This was always likely to be an anxious watch for Borthwick given 10 of the players on show were included in England’s mini-training camp earlier in the week. If he finds himself without both Northampton scrum-halves for the Wallabies Test, Ben Spencer would come into the frame with Harry Randall another option. Borthwick also has problems at hooker with Theo Dan going off early in Saracens’ win over Newcastle amid fitness concerns over Bath youngster Kepu Tuipulotu. Guy Pepper and Benhard van Rensburg have already been ruled out of England’s autumn campaign.

Mitchell’s withdrawal here came midway through the first half after he was caught by a Gloucester chaser when covering back to gather a loose ball. Northampton were under the pump by this stage – George Skivington’s side beginning in a manner which befitted their lofty league position.

They struck first with a well-worked move after eight minutes. Gloucester’s driving maul has been a lethal weapon this season but while Northampton withstood the drive, they had no answer to the visitors’ quick hands. The captain Seb Atkinson, who this week signed a new contract until 2029, put the excellent George Barton through a gap and he offloaded to Max Llewellyn to score. Will Joseph was next over, showing his acceleration to dash under the posts after a clever pass out the back by Atkinson, who impressed throughout. The form of those two is at least solace for Borthwick, all the more so because Atkinson has just recovered from a knee problem.

Northampton had not really got going but managed to find parity at the half-time interval. Both tries came from driving mauls, finished by Pearson and Curtis Langdon. Not exactly the type of scores for which Saints are associated but evidently their canny group of coaches had done their homework.

Midway through the second half Northampton turned down a straightforward penalty at goal to kick to the corner. It felt a risk given the scrappy nature of this contest but it ultimately paid off with George Hendy eventually splashing over on the left. With a spring in their step, Saints chalked up the bonus-point score after some nifty footwork from the replacement Rory Hutchinson to move into third in the table, sitting pretty as the league now takes a break until December.

If Mikel Arteta’s dossier is part of a deliberate strategy, it is a dangerous one for Arsenal

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 20:00:01 GMT

The manager is not yet in Alex Ferguson and José Mourinho’s league, but his conspiracy theories have reached new levels

English football loves the word “dossier”. It doesn’t love dossiers themselves, of course; they’re for nerds – unless, that is, they’re a “secret dossier”, which have a thrilling redolence of spy dramas, invisible ink and dead drops. Non-secret dossiers, though, are inherently risible: call something a “dossier” in English football and you’re immediately signalling: this is absurd poindextering. Dossiers were preposterous when Don Revie was – imagine the pretension! – drawing up scouting reports on opposing players, and they are preposterous today as Mikel Arteta collates images of rival managers stepping outside their technical area.

Arteta, it should be said, did not use the word “dossier”; rather it was swiftly applied to what he had called “a massive storage of images”. During Arsenal’s 2-0 win against Everton last Saturday, he received his second booking of the season for leaving his technical area. This, it turns out, is another part of the vast conspiracy against Arsenal. Yes, Arteta accepted, he left his technical area (44 times before being booked, according to the former referee Graham Scott), but other managers do it too. “There are managers who have the record in the league, 36 times in 10 minutes [they] leave the touchline – no yellows,” he said. “I am clipping all of that … so if somebody comes to me I can say: ‘I am not in the record yet.’ Somebody else has the record so let’s see. Then it’s 36 yellow cards in 10 minutes for the managers.”

There are two ways of looking at this. Perhaps it’s genuine. Perhaps Arteta really is a ludicrous Pooterish figure, counting the misdemeanours of others, the worst kind of neighbourhood watch curtain-twitcher who happens also to have been cursed with a persecution complex: “I got a fine because my parking permit was partially obscured, but Mr Emery at No 17 has been six inches out of his bay on at least three occasions this month and … nothing.” Or perhaps he really is an inveterate snitch, glorying in telling on his peers: “Please, Miss! Miss, Daniel’s been chewing gum again, Miss.”

Or, perhaps awed by the misguided defiance of Manchester City fans after their club was found to have perpetrated the greatest act of cheating in English sporting history, he is trying to persuade his base that everybody is against Arsenal to generate a siege mentality. Declan Rice mystifyingly got away with kicking Malick Yalcouyé off the ball against Brighton, but it’s important to remember that Arsenal remain the real victims here.

The history of mind games in football is long and storied. Before the 1939 FA Cup final, for instance, Major Frank Buckley, the flamboyant manager of Wolves, claimed to have injected his players with “animal secretions”. A French surgeon, Serge Voronoff, had begun transplanting tissue from monkey testicles on to human testicles as an anti-ageing treatment, and it was widely believed that it was this monkey gland treatment that Buckley was employing. In fact, he almost certainly gave his players nothing stronger than vitamins but the idea was that Wolves’ morale would be boosted, while their opponents in the final, Portsmouth, would be intimidated by the prospect of taking on players juiced up on simian fluids. It didn’t work, Portsmouth winning 4-1 despite finishing 15 places below Wolves in the table, but the logic is familiar.

The monkey glands were relatively benign, little more than a publicity stunt, but it’s easy for attempts at psychological manipulation to take on a darker aspect. Before Inter played Liverpool in the second leg of the 1965 European Cup semi-final, for instance, their manager, Helenio Herrera, had 100,000 leaflets distributed claiming that at the end of the first leg at Anfield, Liverpool fans had sung “Go home, Italians” to the tune of “Santa Lucia” which supposedly was intended “to deride us and make us feel we are just a race of cheap mandolin players”. Suitably enraged, Inter fans ensured San Siro seethed with fury, which perhaps encouraged some questionable refereeing decisions (although it probably wasn’t the only factor) as Liverpool lost 3-0 and went out 4-3 on aggregate.

Alex Ferguson was a master of the art, while José Mourinho openly acknowledged that the next game begins in the post-match press conference for the previous one. Mourinho, in particular, often crossed the line of professional decency. Arteta, clearly, is not at that level, at least not yet, but if his dossier is part of a deliberate strategy it is a dangerous one.

Arteta’s conspiracy theory is likely to find fertile ground among certain online Arsenal fans, who remain convinced that referees have been machinating against them for years. Even on Tuesday there were those who leaped to the defence of Max Dowman after he had been sent off for thrusting a knee towards Harrison Neal’s chest, even though Arteta himself appeared furious with the 16-year-old’s petulance. Why, ran the argument, had Cole Palmer not been shown a straight red for retaliating against Mateus Fernandes in Chelsea’s defeat by Tottenham on Saturday? Dowman went with his knee and Palmer with his belly, which is perhaps enough to explain the discrepancy, but even if it isn’t, so what? If you don’t want to be punished, don’t go thrusting knees or bellies or anything at opponents, no matter how bad a foul they’ve just committed.

It’s not only that football is groaning under the weight of the paranoia of various fan groups, each adamant that Pro Ref is acting with the rosicrucians, the Masons, the mob, Opus Dei and the Cubans to deny their club a spot in the Europa League, a distraction that deflects from the game’s true crisis: its descent from an endeavour in which sporting merit and integrity are paramount into a grimly capitalistic vehicle to make very rich and powerful people even richer and more powerful.

It’s also dangerous because a mood of insecurity, of being convinced everything is against you, is not conducive to winning league titles – as Arsenal know. In 2024-25, their title bid was undermined by their early-season ill discipline, each red card greeted not with the resilience of champions but with bleating about how it wasn’t really their fault and everybody was picking on them, including the injury gods.

Abdicating responsibility rarely helps, snitches seldom prosper and, in English football, dossiers are always a bad idea.

Fortune is not favouring Pierre Sage. Just when the Crystal Palace manager needed a positive result, Jean-Philippe Mateta’s early red card condemned his side to a third straight defeat in the league, leaving their manager’s position hanging by a thread.

Goals from Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke ensured that Tottenham recorded a third successive victory for the first time in 616 days as they moved into the top half of the table. To put that into context, Spurs have had three full-time managers since then, so it was no wonder that Roberto De Zerbi looked so pleased at full-time.

By contrast, Sage’s future is in doubt, given that there was an expectation he could be sacked if they lost this game. While Mateta’s reckless red card did him no favours and Palace managed to stay in the game until Van Hecke’s innovative finish 17 minutes from full time, they now find themselves in the bottom three. Only the chair, Steve Parish, will decide his fate with Liverpool up next at home before the international break. Sean Dyche and Thomas Frank are waiting in the wings.

“I told the players I want to be the first on pitch on Monday. I will do the best session I can. Now I have the rage to train more, because the game I saw this evening is not in line with my conviction,” said a defiant Sage. “It’s not me to decide this thing, but if I have one hour, I will give my best during one hour, and if I have 10 years, I will give my best during 10 years. I am responsible for the situation, and I am the guy who will find the solution for the situation.”

Having only won twice at home in the league all year, Tottenham’s supporters had reason to be optimistic after successive victories over Coventry and Chelsea. But while De Zerbi used his programme notes to urge his players not to get complacent, there is no mistaking the signs of momentum, and the Italian singled out the performance of his compatriot - £100m summer signing Sandro Tonali - in midfield. “We played with two players more,” said De Zerbi. “We can’t forget where we were before the last international break. But now we are playing as a team.”

Tottenham’s cause was certainly aided when Mateta was sent off after only 13 minutes. The France striker was never going to get to the ball before Micky van de Ven as he passed it back to Antonin Kinsky, and Mateta’s studs caught the Tottenham defender on the back of his heel. The referee, Michael Oliver, initially showed a yellow card but the outcome was inevitable when the VAR directed him upstairs. Some of the home supporters gasped when they saw a slow-motion replay on the giant screens, although that made it look much worse.

Sage shook his head as Mateta trudged down the tunnel. Not for the first time this season, after Axel Disasi’s red card against Ipswich last month, Palace found themselves down to 10 men with most of the game still to play. They kept Tottenham at bay for a while but played a part in their own downfall again. No one was picking up Gray - who scored his first Spurs goal against Palace in a rare win under Thomas Frank last year - at the back post from a deep Mohammed Kudus corner, and he headed in unopposed. The television cameras cut to Parish in the stand looking less than impressed.

Oleshky evacuees reunite with families after truce allows crossing back into Ukraine

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 19:17:22 GMT

Residents of nearby villages line highway waving flags to greet the evacuees’ convoy from the Russian-occupied city

Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky have been reunited with their families after crossing into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday.

The major rescue operation began on Friday and was carried out under the most significant truce since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago.

Evacuees wrapped in Ukrainian flags stepped off buses at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border to be reunited with family members. Volunteers with hand-drawn welcome signs handed coffee to the weary people who had travelled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus. Residents of nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and torches to greet the convoy.

Tetiana Leonidivna, 71, thanked the Ukrainian soldiers who helped her to flee. “We love them, we love them,” she said through tears. “We know that they are protecting us. And a deep bow to them, and a deep bow to their parents, for having such children. I am proud, I am simply proud.”

The ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region began early on Tuesday and was expected to continue through Sunday evening. The White House said the first lady Melania Trump helped broker the localised deal, while Pope Leo XIV pressed Russia and Ukraine to allow aid deliveries and evacuations.

Relatives and volunteers with the Red Cross, Médecins Sans Frontières and World Central Kitchen welcomed the evacuees as they arrived at the border, ready to provide aid and food, including for their pets.

Holding a cigarette between shaking fingers, 48-year-old Ivan Yevhenovych described his last months in Oleshky. “It was very difficult. There were a lot of drones. It was hard to move around the streets,” he said. “Since spring, there hasn’t really been any staple food left. People had a little bit of their own reserves. We are thrifty people.”

He said landmines or drone strikes were killing residents every day.

An estimated 2,000 people remained in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of being evacuated to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.

“Many people stayed behind and didn’t want to leave,” Yevhenovych said. “Some for their houses, some for their animals.”

Ukrainian authorities, seeking to protect those who remained and safeguard future humanitarian missions, have not said how many residents evacuated Oleshky and have restricted details of their route. Melania Trump posted on social media on Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.

Liza Paliy, 19, waited at the border for her father, whom she last saw more than two and a half years earlier when she fled the occupied city with her mother and sister. “We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately two years have already passed,” she said.

Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, hailed the humanitarian mission as a win.

“This is an extremely important moment. Behind us are difficult negotiations, agreements, preparations, and an enormous amount of work. But most importantly, the people who waited so long to be rescued are finally safe,” he said in an online post.

Lubinets said evacuees ranged in age from just over one year old to 94, and they brought pets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon. He said he hoped the Oleshky truce could be replicated elsewhere, saying it “could form the basis of a new mechanism for responding to the most difficult humanitarian crises”.

Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner, said both sides have agreed to conduct regular humanitarian missions in and around Oleshky. Lubinets did not mention this development.

“The mission has concluded, but, unfortunately, living conditions in Oleshky remain extremely difficult,” she said. “We will make every effort to support those residents who have made the decision to stay.”

Some Oleshky evacuees who chose to move to Russian-occupied territory were taken to a temporary shelter in Simferopol, Lantratova said. The city is in Ukraine’s Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.

“After everything they have endured and a long journey, it is essential for these people to rest, recover and feel cared for. However, support should not be limited to just a roof over their heads and a hot meal,” she said in a social media post.

A Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia’s western Bryansk region, the local governor, Yegor Kovalchuk, said on Saturday. Five others were wounded, he said.

Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region’s capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.

The Russian defence ministry said on Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.

The moment I knew: He loved to travel, I had a fear of flying. I expected him to skol his beer and wish me well

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 19:00:50 GMT

On Danni Smith’s first date with Kev, she made a few disclosures and expected him to skol his beer and wish her well – but his response surprised her

Find more stories from the moment I knew series

In September 2023 I’d been divorced for about a year. At 59 I thought to myself, “surely there’s got to be a little bit more love that I could give in my life”. But I was also keenly aware that not many people find romance organically these days.

I gave Bumble a go, had some pretty average dates and thought it wasn’t for me, but I decided to give it one last shot. It was Kev’s smile and his eyes that caught my attention. His profile said travel was really important to him, which gave me a bit of a laugh because I have huge anxiety issues around holidaying of any sort. We exchanged a few texts and decided to arrange a date. It was nothing fancy, just a few drinks at a bar in a bayside suburb of Melbourne.

It was all very easy between us, so about half an hour in, not wanting to waste our time, I thought I should make a few disclosures. Firstly I told him that as a divorcee twice over, I obviously wasn’t very good at relationships. He surprised me by saying we were on par there. Then I went on to explain my pathological fear of flying, and that I wouldn’t be a great travel buddy.

I fully expected him to skol his beer and wish me well but instead he asked lots of questions about my anxiety and listened intently before saying: “Well, you don’t need to get on a plane to experience Australia!” I thought that was so nice of him and a little spark lit up in me – if he’s willing to compromise on something so important to him, maybe this could go somewhere.

We caught up the next week, and then he returned home to Newcastle. We stayed in touch and I started to realise you really can learn a lot about a person over the phone. He had a great sense of humour and we were getting along so well, but about six weeks later he told me he didn’t think a long-distance relationship could work. I was sad but wished him all the best and left the door open for him to reach out if he was ever back in Melbourne.

It felt brazen, but a few weeks later, I sent him a text. He replied immediately and said he would love to catch up while visiting family for Christmas. When he arrived at my door on Boxing Day, his smile had me swooning. We talked and laughed and the chemistry was palpable. We met again the next day and, thinking it would be the last I’d see of him. I wrote him a card thanking him for giving me hope and saying had circumstances been different, I would have given a relationship between us 100%.

By New Year’s Eve he’d messaged to say he missed me. A few weeks later he came back to Melbourne, where we both now live, and we went on our first road trip together.

Three and a half years later Kev has never put pressure on me to fly. Instead he’s helped me, by letting me be and warming me up for bigger and bigger jaunts. It’s all still totally anxiety-inducing for me, but it gets a little bit easier every time because he’s there encouraging me. I’m sure he thinks I’m completely neurotic, but he never lets on. Instead he makes considerations for the most problematic triggers, like elevators or staying up high in hotels, while helping me extend myself and see places I never would have without him. We’ve just returned from Jervis Bay, and a trip to Canberra.

I’ve never been in a relationship with anyone who could help me through my anxiety. I’ve always felt very alone in those experiences, but Kev’s way of dealing with it is a balm. Not only does it show me that he’s willing to accept me as I am, but he shows such compassion and patience that it reduces the anxiety itself.

I don’t think I’ll ever get on a plane, but Kev’s gentle, flexible attitude to my anxieties has helped me spread my wings. We plan to set off to central Australia in 2027.

Almost 140 arrested at protest against Palestine Action ban outside US embassy in London

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 18:28:30 GMT

Met alleges demonstrators ‘meeting to purposefully commit a crime’ in largest such gathering under Burnham

Almost 140 people have been arrested at the largest mass demonstrations under Andy Burnham’s premiership opposing the proscription of Palestine Action.

Hundreds of people gathered outside the US embassy in Battersea, south London, holding signs that read: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.” Demonstrators also held a vigil in support of the group outside the US consulate in Edinburgh.

Before the London gathering, the Metropolitan police warned those taking part “that they face arrest as part of a robust policing operation” and that anyone “playing a key role in organising the event, giving instructions to others and/or providing logistical support” would probably be committing an offence.

In a statement on X, the Metropolitan police said: “139 people have now been arrested. Officers remain on scene and are continuing to make arrests.”

Commander Adam Slonecki, who is leading the policing operation, said: “All those intending on coming to this event know that supporting a proscribed organisation is unlawful – they are essentially meeting to purposefully commit a crime.

Defend Our Juries, the group behind the demonstrations, said the Met was “terrified of facilitating US embarrassment” and estimated that “around 400 people” gathered to take part.

More than 4,000 arrests have been made for supporting Palestine Action since the ban came into effect, Defend Our Juries said, representing the vast majority of terror arrests since last July.

Among those sitting outside the US embassy, holding a sign that appeared to express support for Palestine Action, was Sue Morhall. “The USA is complicit in most of the wars that are going on. I just feel the leaders of this world, including Trump, need to know that people are so against what’s happening in Gaza,” said the 79-year-old retiree.

Morhall believes there is a chance Burnham could rescind the proscription. “I think it’s early days. I’m hopeful, though pigs might fly,” she said. “I think he’s going to perhaps wait until the midterm elections in America. It’s a terrible shame that people who are trying to stop a genocide are being arrested.”

She has been arrested “five or six” times at previous demonstrations and feels “OK” about being hauled into a police van again. “It’s the principle, and this is one that I feel very strongly about,” she said.

The Rev Bill White, 72, who also held a sign that read: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action,” said: “I’m appalled that Britain is helping facilitate the genocide that is happening in Palestine. We supply weapons that are being used on Palestinians.”

He said he had “hoped for better” from Burnham and resigned from the Labour party after Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist group.

As a faith leader, he said there was “no choice” other than to take part in the demonstration. “This is the right thing to do. There’s a bad law and it is wrong to criminalise people that are trying to prevent genocide,” he said. “How can I not be here?”

A Defend Our Juries spokesperson said: “The Met police overzealous response outside the US embassy today only serves to further expose how far authorities in the UK will go to appease American interests. Israel’s war crimes that have caused death and injury to thousands could not happen without the US’s approval.”

The protests come before an appeal at the UK supreme court against Palestine Action’s designation as a terror group on 4 November.

Last month, more than 160 people were arrested or reported for summons at a similar demonstration in support of Palestine Action staged outside the Labour party conference in Liverpool.

The new government has come under pressure to rescind the ban, though Shabana Mahmood, who has stood firm in favour of the group’s proscription, remained in post as home secretary.

The journalist and author Sarah Helm, the wife of the prime minister’s national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, was accused of supporting Palestine Action after posting on X: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.” Her post came in response to news that the Irish author Sally Rooney can no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for the group.

During the Labour party conference, two activists confronted the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, during a meal at Pizza Express in the city centre where he was challenged about the arrests. Video of the incident showed one of the protesters urging Miliband to declare a genocide in Gaza and de-proscribe Palestine Action.

Miliband said he was happy to discuss the issue but at another time, before the protesters were ushered out.

One woman, who held a sign that, bar swapping the word “authors” to “retirees”, replicated the X post by Sarah Helm, was among those arrested in London, despite the Met ultimately assessing that Helm’s post “did not meet the criminal threshold”.
