Police clash with masked rioters after largely peaceful protests across France

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 18:23:56 GMT

Demonstrations also taking place in Germany, where officers fire teargas to disperse crowds as evening falls

Clashes have erupted in Paris, Marseille and other cities after tens of thousands of demonstrators, some in Halloween fancy dress, marched across France in a third wave of protests over the cost of living and deteriorating public services.

The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said about 150 planned demonstrations around the country had passed off peacefully, but police had encountered an “extraordinary” level of violence from some rioters as the rallies ended.

One riot police officer had been hit by a Molotov cocktail in Paris, he said, describing the incident as an “attempted murder” and adding that the night was not yet over. “We are fully prepared for those looking for confrontation tonight,” he said.

About 320,000 people – down from an estimated 410,000 last weekend – took part in rallies around the country, the interior ministry said, including 70,000 in Paris who marched along boulevards on the south-eastern outskirts, avoiding the city centre.

As evening approached and the largely peaceful demonstrations came to an end, police in several cities fired teargas and stun grenades to disperse crowds joined – as on the previous Saturday – by groups of masked rioters. Police carried out 511 arrests.

Nuñez said earlier this week that 70,000 police and gendarmes, including elite units, would be deployed in an effort to quell violence on the protests’ sidelines, warning that Saturday looked like “a very high risk” day.

The Paris protesters set off peacefully from the Porte de Bagnolet near the ring road, holding placards with slogans including “No need for teargas to make our future look bleak” and “Disguised as an angry citizen for Halloween”, as a helicopter flew overhead

On and around its destination, the Porte de Charenton, dozens of masked people dressed in black used hammers to pry up paving stones and hurl them at police, and at least one incendiary device was thrown at security forces.

Police responded with teargas and baton charges. “A hardcore of several hundred rioters” had attacked police with projectiles, the Paris police prefecture said. Officers had “manoeuvred to restore public order”, it added.

In Lyon protesters threw projectiles at police, prompting officers to fire teargas, and in Toulouse police used water cannon against an unauthorised protest that drew several thousand people, mostly young demonstrators.

The marches brought together school students, who have been calling for better conditions for a month, trade unions and gilets jaune (yellow vests) protesters united in anger at the cost of living, widening inequalities and Emmanuel Macron’s ⁠government.

“The French economy is doing badly no matter what happens, because today we’re being run by a group of incompetents who juggle billions while families are struggling with a few cents,” said one protester on the Paris march, Jérôme Rodrigues. “That’s why we’re here, to keep shouting our demands louder and ‌louder.”

A protester in Nantes, Camille Guérin, said: “We say no to the cost of living, no to the far right, yes to high school students’ demands, yes to giving citizens a voice.”

Saturday’s rallies came two weeks after widespread street violence and looting rocked numerous French cities during a first wave of mass protest on 17 October that became one of the worst days of civil unrest in the country’s recent history.

Student protesters vowed to stage new high school and university blockades on Tuesday and Thursday. “Then we will join the 5 November demonstration called by workers and trade unions,” said Sabrine Kharbach of the Union Étudiante, a student organisation.

Protests also took place elsewhere in Europe. In Germany, police fired water cannon to disperse protesters who hurled firework and other projectiles at the end of youth-led protests organised by a group called “Gen Z regelt!” (Gen Z will sort this).

Thousands of police were deployed across the country, with tensions rising as evening fell after mostly peaceful demonstrations for “for education, health, the climate and an affordable life” in dozens of cities.

In the western city of Cologne, police fired water cannon to disperse a crowd after saying protesters had targeted officers with fireworks, and a march was also temporarily halted in Frankfurt after protesters set off fireworks.

In Berlin, protesters hurled bottles and eggs while protesters set barricades ablaze in Hamburg, and police were using pepper spray on demonstrators in some places, the newspaper Bild reported.

Police were also on alert in Barcelona after an anonymous TikTok network called Blocus urged new gatherings, and in Italy after recent clashes with protesters in Milan, Turin and Bologna.

Ayari on target as Brighton stun Manchester City to close gap on leaders

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 16:59:12 GMT

Manchester City have lost two consecutive league games, but no alarm should be sounded. Enzo Maresca’s fast-passing team were defeated on Saturday because Yasin Ayari took one of Brighton’s rare chances, the 11th-minute winner deriving from what appeared a wrongly awarded free-kick for Elliot Anderson’s foul on Ayari.

Brighton can be proud of victory here – and of being third. They are worth the lofty position and who would bet against Champions League qualification? They protected their lead admirably because City kept coming at them: City’s problem was the final touch or finish and not creating enough for the lethal Erling Haaland.

When Nico O’Reilly, a second-half substitute, zipped the ball across goal towards the end, Iliman Ndiaye sprayed wide – a fair summation of what cost City.

Ndiaye and Josko Gvardiol were replaced after this by Phil Foden and Allan Elias as Maresca tried to salvage a point or better. It did not occur, but his stewardship continues to impress, three months in.

City were slick throughout, as when Ayyoub Bouaddi’s quick feet found Enzo Fernández and he poked the ball out to the left with a no-look pass that found the menacing Jérémy Doku.

But they were made to look chumps when Ayari scored despite the move emanating from the free-kick given against Anderson. Maresca said he had not seen the incident back.

Lewis Dunk swept the dead ball right to Diego Gómez and from this point City slumbered. When Gómez crossed, Matheus Nunes missed his clearance, the ball came back in via Maxim De Cuyper, and Ayari scored into an empty goal, with Gianluigi Donnarumma stranded.

As in City’s Carabao Cup penalty shootout win over Brighton here on Wednesday, the visitors pummelled the hosts – for a period. City required a spark, so Anderson stepped up, his snake-hips along the right creating space for a pinpoint ball that Ndiaye should have headed home, not wide.

The Senegal international next wowed with a throwback slaloming run that took him from the right and near halfway into Brighton’s area. Suddenly, the target gaped and if he had driven beyond Bart Verbruggen and not into the goalkeeper’s gloves it would have been a goal of the season contender.

It was the centrepiece of a swashbuckling response from City, as a Doku raid wreaked havoc along Brighton’s right and Haaland, Gvardiol and Fernández all might have scored an equaliser.

• Brighton have beaten Manchester City away from home in any competition for the very first time, at the 18th attempt (D5 L12).

• Manchester City have failed to score at home in the Premier League for the first time in 23 games, since a 2-0 defeat to Spurs in August 2025.

• Brighton have won five of their last six Premier League matches, keeping a clean sheet in all five victories, indeed they have the most clean sheets (6) in the competition this season.

• Manchester City have lost consecutive Premier League games for the first time since August 2025, which included a 2-1 victory for Brighton.

• Manchester City had 21 shots against Brighton, their most attempts without scoring in a Premier League home game since November 2024 (23 against Spurs).

• This was the first Saturday 3pm Premier League game between two sides in the top three since October 2019, when Liverpool, as leaders, beat third-place Leicester 2-1 at Anfield. Opta

If this thrust and cut recalled Pep Guardiola’s finer City vintages, there was an added element of the pace that is Maresca’s particular special sauce. A 50-yard diagonal speared from Anderson to the galloping Doku was another moment of high quality. As half-time neared, Haaland was the recipient after more of Anderson’s scheming; the Norwegian adjusted his feet and unloaded but was thwarted.

There was a loud City cry for a penalty when Luka Vuskovic handled the ball but no infringement was the ruling; it was the same when Ndiaye’s cross seemed to be parried by Dunk’s arm.

Maresca kept his word about City (currently) being “Gio plus 10” as Donnarumma started, though there were two changes from the loss at Aston Villa as Marc Guéhi and Rayan Cherki were dropped, Matheus Nunes and Bouaddi selected.

For the second half the Italian could retain his XI as City promised they might score soon. This was if the ascendancy of the opening period continued. But Brighton dominated for a passage, as they did during the initial exchanges.

De Cuyper blasted over a fine chance before Ndiaye’s radar was better, another blazing run along the right this time ending with a blistering shot that Verbruggen tipped on to the bar.

This was end-to-end fare. Pascal Gross tipped the ball in and De Cuyper headed it, Donnarumma diving right to fend it away from goal.

On 55 minutes, Maresca brought on Cherki for Bouaddi and the Frenchman’s contribution was to thread Nunes in, but the right-back’s fierce effort was saved. Jack Hinshelwood, introduced on 72 minutes, spurned a chance, as the end of normal time neared, to double Brighton’s lead, missing with a lob.

It did not matter as they moved to 19 points, two behind City; expect both to remain high up throughout.

Pakistan win tri-series final as Fakhar Zaman century denies Sri Lanka in thrilling chase

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 16:46:30 GMT

Opener scores 127 from 99 balls in Lahore

Kamindu Mendis’s 131 proves in vain for Sri Lanka

This mini-tournament has been a welcome change of pace, carrying more meaning than your bog-standard three-match white-ball slog between two teams. And then there’s the gift of a final. This was a fitting conclusion under the lights in a packed-out Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore, settled in the penultimate over as Pakistan beat Sri Lanka by three wickets to win the tri-series.

Fakhar Zaman, Pakistan’s hero from the 2017 Champions Trophy final, crashed his way to 127 in a chase of 326. But plenty of work remained after his dismissal, and the new boys needed to stay calm. Arafat Minhas, 21, and Hasan Nawaz, 24, played like old-timers, their partnership of 94 securing the game. Minhas and Faheem Ashraf fell with two runs still required, but Shaheen Afridi finished the evening with a wallop over the ropes.

Minhas was particularly brutal, middling four sixes on his way to 61 off 31 balls. Pakistan have got something special brewing, Minhas having decimated England with a six-wicket haul at the start of the tri-series. His left-arm spin was expensive here, but he made up for it.

With Sri Lanka setting a target for the first time in the series, Kamindu Mendis was the lead pulveriser in the first half, his 131 ultimately in vain. The left-hander had a Bradmanesque Test average a couple of years ago after hitting five hundreds in his first eight matches, but he’s been waiting for a breakthrough knock in white-ball cricket. Seven years on from his ODI debut, he finally has a hundred, more than doubling his previous career-best. He was helped by in-form colleagues, with Avishka Fernando building an opening stand of 87 and the irrepressible Pavan Rathnayake joining Kamindu for a partnership of 146 inside 20 overs.

Rathnayake has had a cracking couple of weeks, and his half-century took him to 427 runs in the tri-series at 106.75, two tons against England to go with a healthy strike rate. His 77 left Pakistan looking lost on another flat one, and they relied on Salman Agha’s part-time off-breaks for their first two wickets. With Rathnayake and Kamindu pushing Sri Lanka to 255 after 41 overs, Dasun Shanaka, unrelenting in his side’s remarkable chase of 430 against England, was waiting for the final bash.

Yet Shaheen brought his side back, stopping Sri Lanka from going stratospheric. The left-armer went full to dismiss Kamindu and Shanaka; Haris Rauf went short for his two late wickets as Pakistan took six in the last nine overs. “We had to score another 30 runs,” lamented Sri Lanka’s captain, Kusal Mendis. This was a target well within reach, even for a batting lineup bowled out for 110 by Sri Lanka four days earlier.

The chase called for a Babar Azam special at his home ground but Pakistan’s most accomplished batter is struggling for runs, now nine innings without a half-century. There was no unconverted start this time, just a thick edge to a wide slip without a run to his name. Rathnayake juggled before desperately holding on.

Maaz Sadaqat had already fallen to Dilshan Madushanka after an errant drive, bringing together Fakhar and Saad Baig on 14 for two. Both are freewheeling left-handers at vastly different junctures, one making his way, the other nearing the end. Both clattered the ball at a similar rate, and Baig, hours before his 20th birthday, advanced to his first international half-century off 52 balls. While Baig perished on 74 with a return catch to Maheesh Theekshana, the Sri Lanka spinner dropped Fakhar on 69 and 106.

The left-armers kept Sri Lanka alive. Madushanka’s pace snuck past Fakhar’s swinging bat with 106 still required, and Dunith Wellalage’s spin beat Agha’s sweep. With 46 needed from 30 balls, a 15-run over off Shanaka turned the game completely Pakistan’s way, Minhas’ power delighting the stands before Shaheen applied the perfect finish.

A-listers and AI stylists: how high-street brands are staging a fashion comeback

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 16:00:47 GMT

Gap, M&S, Topshop and more are taking a leaf from luxury label playbooks to satisfy savvier generation of shoppers

High street brands that boomed in the noughties before the squeeze of both sustainably minded consumers and the rise of ultra-cheap online labels are staging a comeback.

This time, rather than focusing solely on trend-led affordable designs, the names familiar to any shopper are courting luxury fashion, A-list collaborations and enhanced services in an attempt to engage consumers.

Think Gap’s new collection with Victoria Beckham. Or Marks & Spencer showcasing a covetable catwalk collection at London fashion week with celebrities including Joan Collins and assorted gen Z Gallaghers in attendance, then making it available to buy immediately, with half of the pieces under £50. Topshop relaunched last year and now has concessions in 30 John Lewis stores, as well as the luxury retailer Liberty.

Lisa Illis, the head of design at M&S, describes their recent catwalk show as “making the buzz of London fashion week accessible to everyone”. She says “more fashion-informed seasonal collections” have seen the number of under-35s shopping at the retailer increase 16% year on year.

The Hollywood stylist Law Roach, whose clients include Zendaya, has been appointed stylist-in-residence at Asos, where his influence will be felt not just in advertising campaigns, but also through his suggestions on different items from across the site to wear together.

“In research, we found that 68% of consumers say what they need to know is how to wear something,” says Vanessa Spence, Asos’s executive vice-president of brand.

The online retailer has added AI stylists, virtual try-on tools and a Buy the Look option, which allows consumers to buy an outfit in one go, a feature that Spence says is very popular. “We’re helping customers find pieces that they want to wear. Then they can get more from every purchase and extend the life of their product.”

Ella Baynes, insight manager at retail consultants Savvy Marketing, says the shift shows brands are adapting to the more sophisticated ways consumers are approaching fashion, particularly online. “Instead of competing directly, [these retailers] are borrowing some of luxury fashion’s cultural cues,” she says. “You’re meeting both that shopper aspiration, but also the shopper reality [with the price].”

Asos’s extensive adaptive collection for disabled customers also shows this broader way of thinking. The company worked with disabled consultancy Tilting the Lens on the range. “There is an ability to develop, even for yourself, a capsule collection,” says founder and disability advocate Sinéad Burke, who has achondroplasia, the most common form of restricted growth. “It’s not just one suit, it’s not just one skirt, you can customise the pieces. You can wear the magnetic waistcoat with the pants. We hope what we’re giving people is greater choice.”

Crucially, these items are affordable – nothing is more than £65 – which is particularly important for disabled people, 46% of whom are not in work in the UK. “Whenever we’re looking at shopper attitude, cost is absolutely king,” confirms Baynes.

For Asos in particular, which registered a sharp decline in sales post-Covid and new competition from ultra-cheap brands like Shein, an overhaul was needed. Sales were down 12% last August. A cost-cutting drive, including charging for returns, helped the site turn a corner, and they announced a 50% growth of profits this March, although the impact of a cyber-attack at the beginning of October is yet to become clear.

Andrea Cheong, fashion commentator and author of Why Don’t I Have Anything to Wear?, regularly posts Instagram videos reviewing different items from affordable brands, in order to assess how well made they are. She has noticed that brands are not signposting their environmental credentials as much as they once did – due to a combination of criticism from campaigners, cost and the rise of conservatism. “It wasn’t something that was very lucrative once the economy was in decline, and then bring politics into it, that has a huge impact,” she says.

At M&S, which first launched its eco-commitments in 2007, value and sustainability are not competing priorities. “By designing pieces with longevity in mind, from everyday wardrobe staples to more fashion-led seasonal collections, we’re helping customers build wardrobes they’ll wear and love for longer,” says Illis.

But regardless of making more enduring styles, retailers are always up against changeable consumer behaviour – and damning statistics like the estimate that a garment is on average worn seven times before it is thrown away.

Even if brands are borrowing from the luxury playbook, the reality may not always match up, argues Cheong. “However much they try to elevate what it is, it is not the same [fabric] that they use at, for example, Dior.” The use of human-made fibres in ranges like the M&S catwalk collection and Asos Adaptive is just one example of the difference between high fashion and high street.

Cheong says a lot of gen Z and millennial customers are also shopping secondhand, with resale app Vinted now the third biggest retailer in the UK. “I would say 70% or 80% of my audience are 25 to 35 and they are really jaded. They are a lot more savvy than brands seem to think.”

Sustainability aside, perhaps this new shift shows that brands are realising consumers are more cynical now – and that they need to do more to reach their radar.

Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 16:00:46 GMT

We need policies that stop treating property as a store of wealth and that allow people to move home cheaply

John Healey’s critics on the right and left accused him of dodging the big questions in his first budget. The chancellor failed to announce reforms that might tackle some of Britain’s chronic problems, they say.

Healey’s scatter-gun budget, as the Resolution Foundation called it, was more about politics than economics, and unapologetically so.

Housing was one area of policy that took up a considerable chunk of his speech. And yet the measures amounted to very little, if a test of his policy changes was to ask how different will the UK be at the next election. Or, as that date is only two and a half years away, 10 years from now.

Housing is more than a single element of a complex economy. It is both its driving force and a disease eating its way through the body, from the inside out.

More than 80% of global investment is in property and the vast majority of that is in residential. Countries that once had a more communitarian approach, such as France and Germany, with a highly regulated mix of social, private rented and home ownership, have succumbed to building wealth through property.

It doesn’t seem to matter that Japan was ruined in the 1990s by a vicious property price crash. And China is still suffering domestically after Beijing allowed a property Ponzi scheme to develop that enriched the already super-wealthy and left tens of millions of middle-income earners in negative equity.

Nowhere is the situation worse than in the UK, where property prices have cooled somewhat, but remain at levels that deny younger generations the chance to find a home at a reasonable price and some financial security.

UK property has also become the method by which Gen Xers pay for social care for their parents and release housing deposits for their offspring. Then there is the debilitating leasehold/freehold split that is both a source of angry disputes and stymies investment in solar panels and insulation (who should pay?).

The lack of regulation and ill-thought-out subsidies affecting new private housing means developers are incentivised to enter an arm-twisting contest with local authorities. Without robust planning guidelines, developers champion building on flood plains or erecting tower blocks that are later dubbed ovens for their lack of ventilation in hot summers.

And all the while the tax system is working to make the situation worse.

The Oxford academic John Muellbauer has spent almost 40 years researching the UK’s housing system. He calls it “one of the most dysfunctional in the world”.

In an academic article published in September by the British Academy, he says: “Many of the UK’s current economic and social problems, including its housing affordability crisis, can be traced to decades of land and housing policy failures. The role of land markets is strongly dependent on institutions, including land use regulation, financial regulation and property taxation.”

The Treasury and Angela Rayner’s Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government have considered proposals from Muellbauer and others that remodel council tax, turning it into a fairer annual levy on households and using the reform to abolish stamp duty on transactions, which has calcified the housing market.

Rachel Reeves’s mansion tax is a good start. It is only a start though, because the former chancellor was persuaded to keep the council tax banding system when she should have applied a percentage to the 150,000-odd homes valued above £2m that will be captured by the new policy.

after newsletter promotion

There was the potential for a database of homes valued above £2m to be the beginning of a revaluation process, carrying on until all homes were logged. With a percentage tax of, say, 0.5%, applied to all homes, a £150,000 property would pay an annual tax rate of £750 while a £3m home would pay £15,000.

Of course, the real problem is not the £3m homeowner for whom policymakers will have little sympathy – it’s the professionals occupying £1.5m homes in London, the south-east and affluent suburbs around other big cities, who will see council tax rates more than double to £7,500.

The professional classes will be the worst affected in the short term. Yet there will only be progress when this powerful lobby group of owner-occupiers – working and retired – are prepared to accept the trade-off with stamp duty, which would disappear for those who sell.

There are plenty of people in government who understand the need to resolve housing market issues in a more fundamental fashion. The Treasury minister Torsten Bell is one. His book, Great Britain?: How We Get Our Future Back, talks about “our housing omnishambles”.

However, they have had little influence on policy in this area so far. In his first budget Healey revamped a much-discredited help-to-buy scheme for new-build homes, which will only boost prices and line the pockets of developers. He also gave some more money towards council housebuilding, slapped an extra tax on landlords (that will probably push up rents) and promised to tackle homelessness.

Healey and Andy Burnham put all their revolutionary zeal into a long, and possibly tortuous, process of devolution from London to the regions to kickstart growth.

However, it is tax incentives that are causing the problems, not whether policy decisions are made locally or centrally. Bad policy decisions can be made locally just as much as centrally. What makes the difference is a permanently reformed tax landscape that discourages treating housing as a store of wealth, allows people to move home cheaply – especially older homeowners who want to downsize – and supports the building of more truly affordable homes to buy and rent.

UK charity shop profits plummet amid shift in secondhand clothes market

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 15:10:52 GMT

British Heart Foundation describes ‘exceptionally challenging’ trading after Oxfam’s retail profit reportedly fell 23% amid rise of platforms such as Vinted

Profits at some of the UK’s best-known charity shops have plummeted as they face a number of pressures, including from online secondhand clothes platforms, prompting claims that a key part of the sector’s fundraising model could be under threat.

According to unpublished accounts seen by the Financial Times, Oxfam’s retail profit fell 23% to £4.9m in the last financial year, compared with £6.4m in the previous year.

The British Heart Foundation (BHF), which has the biggest high street presence of any charity in the country, has announced plans to close 150 stores after they made a £3.3m loss in the last financial year. Cancer Research UK and Scope have also closed, or are closing, some of their shops.

But these losses come despite UK spending on secondhand clothing having quadrupled over the past decade, rising to £8.8bn a year, according to GlobalData.

The shift has come alongside the rise of websites such as Vinted and Depop, suggesting that people who might previously have donated clothes to charity shops are instead selling them directly to other consumers and profiting themselves.

Alongside this change, Chinese companies are selling more clothes in developing countries, particularly in Africa, which has long been a major market for unwanted secondhand clothing.

“It has been challenging … and it is going to be painful for the sector,” Lorna Fallon, the head of Oxfam’s retail operation, told the Financial Times.

Oxfam’s latest filings reveal that for every £100 people spend in its shops, just £6 now goes towards the charity’s work on alleviating global poverty. As recently as 2022, the figure was £22, the FT reports. However, the organisation’s focus on books and music means it has no plans to reduce its number of shops.

In June, BHF carried out a major review of its retail arm, which employs almost 3,700 staff, after profits from its shops plunged from £18.8m in 2024 to £3.6m in the year to 31 March 2025.

The charity cited “an exceptionally challenging trading environment”, and said it was aiming to close 90 stores by the end of March 2027 and another 60 by the following March.

The rapid change in fortunes for charity shops also highlights their limitations in the face of greater competition. Whereas Vinted and Depop directly connect sellers with buyers, charity shops remain at the mercy of high street and warehouse rents and other associated costs and inefficiencies, including collecting, sorting, pricing and storing clothes.

Another issue hampering high street charity shops is that the clothes being donated are increasingly substandard. Speaking to the Guardian earlier this month, Tansy Hoskins, the author of Charity Shop World, described the sector as dealing with “avalanches” of poor-quality clothes across the country, as people use charity shops as convenient dumping grounds for unwanted purchases.

“Quality is the big change marker – it’s gone through the floor. You’re just fighting against the waste,” Hoskins said.

Robin Osterley, the chief executive of the Charity Retail Association, said: “Fast fashion has had an impact on donations quality, there’s no question about that.”

But he added: “We don’t see Vinted or any of the other online platforms as an issue at all. It might be having a little bit of an effect – where people have one bag for charity shop donations and one for Vinted – but we believe these effects are significantly mitigated by two things.

“The first is that Vinted and other platforms are having a very positive effect on people’s attitudes towards secondhand shopping, and creating an environment where it’s much more normalised. A rising tide floats all ships.

“The second factor is that there are a lot of people who buy things from charity shops to sell on the online platforms. Our members get a significant income from them.”

Osterley instead suggested the November 2024 budget had had a much larger impact on bricks and mortar charity shops, in which national insurance increases and the lowering of the national insurance threshold – affecting more part-time staff – has had a “really significant” effect on the costs charity shops face, as well as inflationary pressures across the economy.

Richard Hawkes, Oxfam GB’s chief executive, said: “Whilst there is no getting away from the fact that the charity retail sector has been impacted by the cost-of-living crisis, like the rest of the high street, there is still much to be hopeful and positive about for the future.

“The growth of secondhand presents real opportunities for the whole sector, but it also means we need to think differently about the traditional charity retail model.

He added: “Our shops also offer much more than just an income. They give us a presence in communities where we might not otherwise be, while providing opportunities to engage with more than 20,000 volunteers. This wider role remains a vital part of what makes charity retail so valuable.”

A world-first focus on long-term outcomes could transform UK government – or create new spending fights

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 15:00:46 GMT

Tucked away in John Healey’s budget is decision to ringfence preventative projects where future savings outweigh initial cost

It merited the briefest of mentions in John Healey’s speech and just one paragraph in the 166-page budget document, but some believe it could revolutionise not just public spending but the very process of government itself: a new focus on long-term outcomes.

The idea in the broad sense is very simple. Any spending deemed to be “preventative” – that is, the initial outlay will be more than made up for by future savings – will from now on be ringfenced, meaning it cannot be raided for more immediate needs.

This might sound uncontroversial, but it follows many years of long-term spending being pillaged to plug day-to-day gaps, particularly so during and after the austerity measures of the 2010 coalition government, which slashed numerous prevention-based services, not least the Sure Start programme for families with young children.

But now, starting from the upcoming spending review, which kicks off next year, projects that can be shown to bring down costs in the future will be protected via a new piece of jargon – a preventative departmental expenditure limit, or PDEL.

“It could end up being quite a major change in how the government runs spending reviews, and the entire spending framework,” said Stuart Hoddinott, at the Institute for Government thinktank, which had called for such a system to be implemented. Officials in the Treasury agree, with one calling it an “important reform”.

That is, however, about as straightforward as it gets. The budget document uses Andy Burnham’s new spending to prevent rough sleeping as an example of the sort of thing that would qualify. A few other areas would seem likely: for example, public health programmes to prevent future illness, and Sure Start-type early years schemes.

But beyond that, no one really knows what might or might not qualify for PDEL status. Departments say they are waiting for Treasury guidance, which has not yet been drawn up. “A lot depends on the definition,” Hoddinott said. “While it sounds simple, it becomes quite difficult when you think about how it will work in practice, as you could make any argument that almost all types of spending are preventative.”

Government officials agree, with one making the point that, in theory, the Ministry of Defence could argue all its spending is preventive, given the very obvious costs to the country of fighting a war, let alone losing one.

There is therefore the potential for a new variant of the endless spending-review tussles between departments and the Treasury, as ministers try to protect their pet projects from future plunder.

But what is perhaps just as important is the symbolism. Some other governments around the world protect specific preventative budgets – public health, for example – but this is believed to be the first time one has introduced this as a blanket policy.

Government officials are billing the decision as part of a wider focus under Burnham to try to deal with knotty and neglected issues that have longer-term costs and repercussions, including rough sleeping and adult social care.

One said: “Too often government departments have ended up raiding these types of budgets to fund short-term measures. This is an attempt to combat that as part of a wider push to transform the way the state operates.”

Those whose work revolves around trying to generate long-term benefits to the public are cautiously delighted.

“This does feel like a really good thing,” said Greg Fell, Sheffield city council’s director of public health and the president of the Association of Directors of Public Health.

“There are a lot of questions about how it will work. Is it about preventing future acute demand, or creating the conditions for communities to thrive? Those are different things and they require a different mindset and way of operating. And with some spending, it might take decades to realise the benefits.

“But as a country we have never been very good at this sort of thing, so it’s up to all of us to make sure it works.”

Ads accusing Republican candidates of protecting Epstein fill airwaves in final midterm push

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 15:00:45 GMT

But select Democrats, too, are being accused of having ties to the late sex offender as country prepares to vote

In races across the country, Democratic candidates or groups that support them have released ads accusing Republicans of protecting pedophiles by voting against legislation to release files related to Jeffrey Epstein.

The ads appear intended to evoke an emotional response by accusing candidates of “protecting” Epstein, a notorious pedophile accused of running a sex-trafficking ring involving minors.

An analysis from CNN found that candidates and outside groups have spent more than $35m on Epstein-related ads. Another from the Washington Post found that Democrats spent more than $40m on Epstein-related ads across six key Senate races.

In Colorado, ads targeting Republican Jeff Crank note that the lawmaker voted against releasing the Epstein files. In one, the family members of Virginia Giuffre, a woman who survived abuse at the hands of Epstein and died by suicide last year, claim Crank “covered up Epstein’s crimes to protect Donald Trump”.

Ashley Hinson, a Senate candidate in Iowa, was accused of voting to “protect her donors” by refusing to vote to release the Epstein files.

“This week I had to explain to my boys, ‘No, Mom does not protect pedophiles,’” Hinson said in a campaign ad responding to attacks over the Epstein files.

An ad targeting Mike Collins, the Republican running for a Georgia Senate seat, says “Mike Collins voted against releasing the Epstein files even after he knew Epstein’s sex-trafficking operation exploited 14-year-old girls for sex”.

Florida Republican Jimmy Patronis faced an attack from his Democratic opponent, claiming he called investigating Epstein “a waste of his time”.

A spokesperson for Crank’s campaign accused the Epstein-related ad of being “intentionally vague”, in a statement to the Washington Post, because his position was that he would vote against the file’s release until he could be confident that victim information was properly redacted. The campaign also said it was “unfortunate” that his opponent, Jessica Killin, was “preying on a grieving family with the help of the Washington Democrats”.

Crank’s staff invited and met with Giuffre’s family, though Crank himself did not meet with them in person, the New York Times reported. Crank’s campaign also said it offered to meet with Epstein victims before the vote on the legislation.

Last year, Democrats and a select few House Republicans tried to force a vote on the Epstein files through a discharge petition – a procedure used in Congress to bypass the traditional steps of legislation and force a vote on the House floor.

Donald Trump, who knew Epstein in the 1990s and early 2000s, opposed the discharge petition for the files, reversing his campaign promise to increase government transparency. House Republicans largely aligned themselves with him, prompting anger from high-profile Trump voters.

Eventually, under pressure from allies, Trump supported the legislation, giving Republican lawmakers the go-ahead to vote for it. All but one House Republican voted for the Epstein Files Transparency Act.

Many of the ads omit the fact that nearly every House Republican voted to release the Epstein files when the Epstein Files Transparency Act came to the floor, although at that point Trump had agreed to sign the legislation and release the files. Instead, the ads refer to Republicans opposing early attempts to force the legislation to the floor.

Republicans have pointed to this fact when disputing the attack ads.

“Of course I voted to release the Epstein files,” Hinson said in a direct-to-camera ad, accusing her opponent, Josh Turek, of lying. While Hinson voted for the final Epstein Files Transparency Act, she did not sign on to the discharge petition.

Patronis, meanwhile, never called the investigation a “waste of time”, but told a local radio station that while he had “no problem getting everything all released”, the issue was a “massive energy and time suck at the end of the day”.

Melissa Stone, a spokesperson for Patronis’s campaign, highlighted his work with Trump to obtain disaster funding after Hurricane Isaias and said his opponent, Gay Valimont, was “still talking about a dead pedophile in a sad web video than helping the people of [the first congressional district] recover.”

Some Republicans and groups supporting the GOP have sought to flip the script, accusing Democrats of taking money from donors who had ties to Epstein.

During a Georgia Senate debate, Collins accused his opponent, Jon Ossoff, of accepting campaign donations from Reid Hoffman, a tech billionaire who had ties to Epstein. Hoffman has said he only knew Epstein through fundraising relationships and regrets it.

“You can claim to fight against the Epstein class, but I’m going to tell you, this call is coming from inside the house and the Epstein class is on stage right now and it’s you,” Collins said.

In New Mexico’s gubernatorial race, an outside group released an ad accusing Democratic candidate Deb Haaland of accepting a ride on Epstein’s private jet and taking “tens of thousands of dollars from Epstein businesses” and then “asking for more”.

Haaland did not fly on Epstein’s jet, but did take a flight booked by one of Epstein’s companies in 2014. Haaland has said she was unaware the chartered flight was owned by an Epstein-owned company.

Manchester United crisis deepens with Chelsea defeat and Martínez red card

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 14:42:36 GMT

Get ready for another week of agonising over the sorry state of Manchester United. The legends of old will rage on podcasts, clips of a fuming Gary Neville will fly around social media and by the time United play again there is every chance a new manager will be in the dugout.

There were echoes of Erik ten Hag’s final game in charge as the walls closed in on Michael Carrick here on Saturday. United missed chances at 0-0, just as they did when Ten Hag lost to West Ham a day before his sacking two years ago, and Chelsea exacted punishment after initially delivering a performance so bad it had you worrying for the nascent Xabi Alonso project.

Chelsea were appalling during the first half, so it was just as well their opponents were in a giving mood. United had opportunities to make their decision to give Carrick a stay of execution look like a wise move rather than the consequence of executive-level confusion, but the finishing was awful and the defending was worse. Morgan Rogers cantered past five players to make it 1-0 and a seventh defeat in 13 games was confirmed when Lisandro Martínez’s faux hard man act led to him being sent off after conceding the penalty that allowed Cole Palmer to seal Chelsea’s rise into fourth place.

Here was a moment to symbolise United’s decline under the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. Martínez has had a lot to say about those above him recently, but this is a player who should have been sold along. United have too many in that category and it is hard to see a change of manager alone fixing the problem.

Carrick could limp on until the international break. He is symptom rather than cause, although perhaps a different voice is required. United host Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday, but they will be playing in the Championship if this persists.

They are winless in nine games, their worst run since 1988, and are drifting into a relegation battle. The ending was similar to last week’s defeat to Bournemouth, the away end serenading Carrick before booing United’s players, and there was plenty of hate to go around. Chants criticising Jason Wilcox’s work as director of football and urging the Glazers to sell up captured the sense of mutiny.

The first half had been encouraging from United, but with Benjamin Sesko absent until the new year the lack of a finisher proved costly. Bruno Fernandes, restored after clear the air talks with Carrick, fired an early chance over, Amad Diallo and Bryan Mbeumo produced glaring misses and the returning Matheus Cunha had a goal ruled out for offside at 0-0.

The spotlight was also on Alonso, defeats to Tottenham in the league and Liverpool in the Carabao Cup sparking criticism over team selections, and he lifted Chelsea by handing Estêvão Willian his first start in the league this season.

Estêvão was dangerous on the right flank as Alonso adjusted without João Pedro up front. Pedro Neto rather than Danny Welbeck led the line in a 4-2-3-1 system, but it was United who threatened first. Diogo Dalot combined with Cunha before Andrey Santos, who left Chelsea for United in the summer, swept a shot just wide.

Both sides were vulnerable. Chelsea had a long list of absentees – illness ruled Jordan Henderson out in midfield – and their defence wobbled without Maxence Lacroix. United, though not exactly secure whenever Chelsea punched through on the counterattack, felt optimistic at first.

The visitors had an escape when Senne Lammens spilled a Neto shot and an offside Estêvão tapped home. Diallo ran at Marco Palestra and Fernandes shimmered in a floating role from the left.

• Chelsea won a Premier League home game without conceding for the first time in 13 matches, since a 2-0 victory against Brentford in January.

Chelsea, enjoying neither possession nor control against Santos and Carlos Baleba, were forced back. Levi Colwill intervened when Cunha broke through and Wesley Fofana, a £75m accident waiting to happen, took flak from the home fans after a couple of trademark brain fades.

United could not take advantage. There were a couple of flashes from Chelsea as half-time approached; Moisés Caicedo diverted a Fofana header against the woodwork and Neto shot wide after a stumble from Harry Maguire.

Chelsea were more assertive at the start of the second half and it was easy to predict United’s unravelling. They were punished when Mbeumo turned into trouble. Caicedo blocked his path, Roméo Lavia nicked the ball past Baleba and Rogers sauntering through the middle placed United’s failure to strengthen in defence into sharp focus.

It was brilliant from Rogers, but a bit like a goal you see at the end of a five-a-side between a group of dads playing for the first time since 2019. Maguire barely lifted a leg, Martínez gawped and Rogers dinked over Lammens for 1-0.

United had to dig in. Good luck with that. Lavia was running the midfield for Chelsea. United’s response to falling behind was to crumble. Martínez was on a booking when he elbowed Fofana at a corner. Peter Bankes reviewed the incident and showed the centre-back a second yellow before Palmer made it 2-0 from the spot.

Chelsea relaxed. Estêvão had a scorching strike ruled out. Baleba, still unable to complete 90 minutes, made way for Kobbie Mainoo and the home fans jeered when Mason Mount came on. Mount has toiled since leaving Chelsea for United in 2023. Old Trafford is the place where talent goes to die. Carrick will merely be the latest victim.

‘Was I not enough?’: care worker barred from meeting home secretary

The meeting with Shabana Mahmood had already been rescheduled twice. When the third date fell during a holiday, he cut his trip short to travel to London. But hours before the meeting was due to take place, it was cancelled after Mahmood declined to allow him to attend.

The rejection left him in tears. “It was a feeling of humiliation,” Kolade said. “I cried because I felt like someone saw me less to be in the same room with her.

“Was I not enough to be in the same room with the home secretary? It’s not right to have treated anybody that way.”

The meeting, scheduled for 21 October, was to be the first between Mahmood and the general secretary of Unison, Andrea Egan, since she took office. Egan planned to attend alongside a union policy officer and Kolade, who had been selected by fellow migrant workers to represent them.

Two hours before the meeting, the home secretary’s office informed Unison that Kolade would not be permitted to attend because Mahmood considered his presence “inappropriate”, according to the union.

Egan said ministers should welcome opportunities to hear directly from workers about their experiences. “Kolade is a dedicated care worker and an inspirational campaigner. In other words, he’s a true representative of our migrant workers,” she said.

“The government should be celebrating these brilliant people who give everything to care for our loved ones and keep us healthy. Not demonising, attacking and leaving them vulnerable to exploitation and abuse.”

A spokesperson said the government was considering more than 200,000 responses to its consultation on earned settlement, including submissions from more than 145,000 people directly affected by the proposals. “It would not have been appropriate to prioritise the views of a single individual while the responses to this are being considered,” the spokesperson added.

“The home secretary hoped that the meeting could go ahead regardless. However, Unison’s general secretary cancelled.”

The dispute comes amid pressure on Mahmood to abandon proposals that would force migrant care workers to wait 15 years before qualifying for indefinite leave to remain, rather than the five years they had expected.

Under the proposed “earned settlement” system, the standard qualifying period would double from five to 10 years, with workers in lower-paid occupations, including social care, facing a 15-year wait.

For Kolade, the row encapsulates what he believes is missing from the immigration debate: the voices of those whose lives could be upended by its policies. He has watched politicians dismiss care work as low-skilled and portray migrant workers as a burden on the British economy.

“I was just going to tell her that is not correct,” he said. “We are not a burden to the British state. We are also contributing as much as we can, supporting British families.

“She talked about fairness to the British people. I was going to tell her that caring for British families is our own little way to show that we are contributing, and that we have earned our rights to stay in this country, a place we’re currently calling home.”

Kolade describes care work as the “most honourable work anybody can do”, a conviction shaped by his father’s death from diabetes when he was about 20. His father had concealed the severity of his illness, instructing the family not to tell Kolade until he had finished his university exams. But he died just a day before his final exam.

“Losing my dad at that age … created a vacuum, a space in my life to care for people,” he said. “When I started caring in the UK, I see everybody I care for from the lens I would see my dad. And this is what I would have said to Shabana Mahmood: I would give my best to that person as if I had a second chance to look after my dad.”

Kolade rejected the suggestion migrant care workers were simply waiting to secure permanent residency before abandoning the sector. Many were investing in qualifications to build long-term careers in British social care, he said.

“On the day that Shabana cancelled the meeting, one of us put on the group that he had just finished his NVQ 4 and passed with distinction. We were all very happy,” he said.

“People are developing themselves within the industry so they can take up more senior roles. So the fear around: ‘Oh, they’re just going to leave the sector’ – that’s not what we are saying.”

But he warned the proposals could push experienced workers to countries offering greater security. “I have a few years to my ILR [indefinite leave to remain], and so if they say: ‘Oh, you have to stay 15 years,’ I have to evaluate the other options I have. Today, Ireland, Canada and Australia are asking for people with my skill.

“So you would have trained people and then you would lose them to these countries.”

Kolade moved to Britain in 2022 with his wife, who is also a care worker, and two children. One of his children recently asked him: “If you don’t win, are we going to go back to Nigeria?”

“I couldn’t explain what was going to happen to us,” Kolade said. “This is our home right now. This is what we know at the moment. Our kids know this place already.”

Despite the cancelled meeting, Kolade remains committed to Unison’s campaign for a five-year route to settlement, sector-wide visas allowing care workers to change employers without risking their immigration status, and fair pay.

“Confidence is never down,” he said. “We are going hard. We are not stopping until we have everything we have on our list.”

Christina Applegate’s multiple sclerosis misdiagnosis is not an isolated event. I should know

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 14:00:44 GMT

Shakira Hussein’s concerns about her bipolar diagnosis were dismissed as common among ‘women like you’. Then she was found to have MS

In the five years since her diagnosis with multiple sclerosis, the Emmy award-winning actor Christina Applegate has become a prominent spokesperson for people living with the neurological disease. Both her memoir, published earlier this year, and the MS-themed podcast MeSsy that she co-hosts with fellow actor Jamie Lynn Sigler have significantly raised public awareness about multiple sclerosis and the broader topic of living with disability.

So Applegate’s recent revelation that her neurologist now believes that she does not have the disease after all came as a shock to me and to many other people living with multiple sclerosis. We understand why Applegate says that she does not regard her health update as good news. The undiagnosis is not a cure – she is just as sick as she ever was, but “back to square one” when it comes to explanations. Medical experts interviewed about Applegate’s case reassure us that most people being treated for multiple sclerosis can be confident in our diagnoses and advise those of us with concerns to consult our neurologists for reassessment.

But Applegate’s experience is not an isolated event. A 2024 systematic review found that about 15% of the MS cases it studied were misdiagnosed, with women twice as likely as men to be diagnosed as having the disease when they did not. And underdiagnosis is also commonplace, with many patients waiting months or years for their disease to be correctly identified and treated.

My own diagnosis with remitting-relapsing multiple sclerosis 20 years ago came after a long period of being misdiagnosised with bipolar disorder.

I had initially been referred to the psychiatrist who (mis)diagnosed me while I was recovering from trauma. The heart-stopping panic attacks gradually subsided thanks to cognitive behavioural therapy rather than the cocktail of antidepressants and antipsychotics that I had been prescribed for bipolar disorder, but my physical health continued to decline.

My psychiatrist’s response was to increase the dosage of my medication, dismissing any concerns that I expressed by telling me that “intelligent women like you” are often unwilling to accept that they have a psychiatric disorder. The words “intelligent women like you” came to sound like an insult as I heard them recited more and more often.

Eventually my health reached crisis point with a flare up that left me unable to stand without a walking stick for support; even then, the first neurologist I consulted dismissed my symptoms as psychiatric – “very common in women like you”.

It was the words “women like you” that motivated me to seek a second opinion.

By the time I saw the second neurologist and had an MRI scan, I had put my symptoms down to a madness caused by the political upheaval and bloodshed of the early 2000s. But when I tried to explain this to the neurologist, he paused for a long moment before saying, “The scan was abnormal”.

Of course, it is entirely possible (and not particularly unusual) to have both bipolar disorder and multiple sclerosis. My psychiatrist told me in our final phone call that “intelligent women like you” often seize upon the diagnosis of a physical disease to deny that they are also suffering from a psychiatric condition. But my health immediately improved once I was taken off the bipolar medication and began treatment for multiple sclerosis.

The years since the diagnosis have not been easy. As a disease of the brain and central nervous system, multiple sclerosis has an endless array of weapons at its disposal and the treatments have ranged from daily self-injections to monthly infusions to a demanding immune system reboot. But nothing that the disease has thrown at me has been as difficult as the fear and uncertainty of the gruelling pre-diagnosis period.

The boundary between the diagnosed and undiagnosed has become the border between worthy and unworthy, deserving and undeserving, entitlement to disability support payments and destitution. Applegate’s experience illustrates how uncertain and contested this boundary is. The legions of people like her who are sick but undiagnosed deserve better than to be stigmatised as grifters and malingerers. We should not be dismissed as time-wasters because the diagnostic process is complex and lengthy.

My symptoms ought to have been taken seriously regardless of whether their underlying cause was multiple sclerosis or bipolar disorder. And, once diagnosed, we should not have to fear that a doctor’s second thoughts will make us second-class patients.

The secret behind Lula’s win in Brazil may be an ‘army’ – of social media creators

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 13:37:39 GMT

There are many explanations for the incumbent president’s win over Flávio Bolsonaro, but analysts – and he – point to reinvention of his social media use

Four days before his stunning electoral comeback, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president, got his first smartphone.

Lula, who turned 81 last Tuesday, had long said he wanted to avoid an endless stream of calls during his rare moments off, and he began his presidential campaign by sticking to an old habit: using aides’ phones – only when necessary.

Then he suffered an unexpected first-round defeat to the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who had neither his father Jair Bolsonaro’s charisma nor much of a record as a two–decade legislator – and Lula realised he had lost both in the ballot box and in the digital arena.

The veteran leftist, who contested his first election more than 40 years ago, overhauled his digital strategy, began recording selfie-style videos – and went on to beat Bolsonaro by more than 4.4m votes.

There are many explanations for how he managed to boost turnout and win over other candidates’ voters. Some analysts point to an organic student mobilisation that held mass protests across Brazil, others to a package of government benefits Lula approved at the last minute in a transparent attempt to use government spending to curry favour with the electorate.

But many analysts, and the president himself, point to the incumbent’s reinvention of his social media use as a key reason for his victory.

Interestingly, neither Lula’s campaign created nor ran what was ultimately the driving force behind the shift: a WhatsApp group called “Lula’s Army”.

In the days leading up to the vote, its nearly 11 million followers – up from just 60,000 after the first round – received daily “missions” to try to win over voters and make pro-Lula content perform well on social media.

Leading the “army” was the man Lula praised in his victory speech as “our general”, whose role was “raising the morale of our troops every day”: 42-year-old congressman André Janones.

“I have no doubt that Lula’s army determined the outcome of the election,” Janones said, saying that he is not modest “because modesty sometimes comes very close to hypocrisy. I know how much bigger I came out of this election.”

In his view, the contest had three main fronts. The first was candidate versus candidate, “and on that Lula was winning by a mile because he had much more experience”. The second was mobilisation on the streets, “and we were bringing many more people out to the protests”.

But the third: “You don’t have to be very clever to realise that we were losing on social media.”

Although Lula had more followers, Bolsonaro’s content generated up to five times more engagement.

The incumbent’s campaign also complained to the electoral court of alleged interference by Meta in the senator’s favour, including a 24-hour period in which Lula was unable to boost ads on Instagram, which the company later acknowledged but blamed on a technical error.

Janones said he realised the solution was to boost organic engagement among Lula’s voters.

One of his most successful strategies came a week before the election, when “soldiers” were told to post a photo making an “L” sign for Lula with their thumb and index finger while wearing the yellow Brazil football shirt, a national symbol that had been appropriated by Bolsonaro supporters over the past decade.

Domestic worker Sidneia dos Santos Araujo, 63, took part “because the shirt of Lula supporters is the Brazilian one. Bolsonaro supporters should be wearing the United States shirt,” she said this week, citing the Bolsonaro clan’s “subservience” to US president Donald Trump and noting how the senator fled to Miami.

A day after Lula’s victory, Araujo created a template on Google Drive that allowed followers of the “army” to create their own “certificate”, which would declare that during their “military service” they “maintained excellent performance and exemplary conduct … and are therefore deserving of this distinction as a ‘soldier’”. The certificates, which went viral, came complete with copies of the signatures of “marshal” Lula and “commander” Janones.

Janones said that, above all, he wanted to create a “sense of community: the feeling that we are not alone”.

According to Raquel Recuero, a researcher at the Federal University of Pelotas, this was one of the channel’s biggest achievements: it gave voters “a sense of purpose and the chance to channel their energy into doing something to help Lula”.

Other young, digitally native politicians have also been credited with reshaping Lula’s social media strategy, including 21-year-old Ana Elisa Santos, known as Ana Elisa, who became the youngest congresswoman elected from Minas Gerais in this election.

The night after Lula’s first-round defeat, Elisa recorded a hugely popular video saying the left needed to be more “humble” and to “learn” how to use social media because “there is no longer any separation between social media and the streets … The grassroots are also on Instagram and TikTok.”

She was called to a meeting with Lula and is said to have persuaded the president to record the selfie-style videos he had previously refused to make.

Meanwhile, Janones urged each WhatsApp group member to bring in one more person. One day, while recording a video alongside the president, the congressman said that if they reached 5 million followers, Lula would buy a mobile phone and join the “army” himself.

“People think we only say that for the cameras, but it’s real: Lula really didn’t have a mobile phone,” said Janones.

The group hit its target, and when an allied politician gave the president a phone as a gift, Lula finally joined it. “I’m not going to say he’s an expert now, but he’s there, following it, and has been sending some content,” said Janones.

Recuero believes it will be difficult to keep “Lula’s army” engaged now because there is a “social cost” to being so digitally committed – Janones himself suffered a cardiac arrhythmia after the first presidential debate and had to spend 24 hours in hospital. It was the only day the group went silent.

But Janones believes there is a path forward for the group, perhaps not engaged 24/7 as it had been, but focused on special moments, such as trying to secure passage of legislation important to Lula.

“We can’t leave the campaign trail any more,” he said, noting that despite Lula’s election, Bolsonaro’s party secured an unprecedented number of seats in congress. The “army”, he said, is what will “guarantee Lula’s ability to govern”.

Starmer says UK must get closer to Europe as US relationship changes

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 13:32:25 GMT

Shift in dealings with Washington not likely to reset once Trump leaves Oval Office, former PM says

The UK and other European nations must draw closer together as the US becomes a less-reliable partner, Keir Starmer has said in his first significant political intervention since leaving No 10.

The former prime minister warned European leaders of the threat posed by Russia, among others, and said the shift in relations with Washington during Donald Trump’s presidency was not likely to reset once he leaves the Oval Office. He accused them of being caught out by these new realities twice already.

“A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,” Starmer told an audience at the British Irish Chamber of Commerce on Friday. “Europe has twice been caught asleep, failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events.

“First, when Russia’s attack on Ukraine exposed longstanding European weaknesses on defence and security, and second, when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up.”

Starmer had called for closer European ties before stepping down as prime minister in July. Three months earlier, amid Trump’s war with Iran and his threats to withdraw from Nato, Starmer said Europe represented a “partnership for a dangerous world we must navigate together”.

He said those ties should go further than just defence, adding that Brexit had done “deep damage” to the UK economy, and that he wanted to be “more ambitious”, including pursuing “closer economic cooperation [and] closer security cooperation”.

Starmer spoke after spending time in Dublin meeting senior business leaders and politicians, including the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, with whom he established the annual UK-Ireland summit.

“I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before.

“That doesn’t mean the US relationship is no longer important. On the contrary, the military, security and intelligence alliance is far too strong for that. But it does mean enabling Europe to take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security.”

His comments reflect a growing consensus on the left of UK politics that closer ties with Europe are essential to ensure economic and military security. Soon after taking office as Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham said that he intended to be “bolder” about closer ties with the EU.

Next month, Burnham will attend a crucial EU-UK summit where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus.

Burnham has also said he wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election. At a meeting of European defence ministers in Paris this week, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said that they were “united and unwavering” in support for Ukraine in the face of Russian hostility.

Starmer said: “We need to build up pan-European cooperation and coordination on defence and security – a common security framework as much as a common market. The EU is changing to respond to that, but it cannot be the EU alone when Europe’s periphery is core to its defence.

“Britain must be central to that project. We are one of two nuclear powers. We are a leading Nato member. We have a viable next-generation fighter jet programme. And we are pledged to work alongside European allies to guarantee security in Ukraine.

“Ireland and the UK stand side by side in the coalition of the willing and with Ukraine, working together to guarantee and shape the security of our continent. I hope and believe that Britain’s relationship with its friends and allies can and should be strengthened by this urgent and common security project.”

UK police should not have let US force take over airbase trial, MoD documents show

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 13:30:43 GMT

According to documents obtained by the Guardian, officials accused Cambridgeshire force of breaching US-UK deal by handing over case of woman strangled by US pilot

Ministry of Defence officials have privately accused a UK police force of wrongly handing over the investigation of an American fighter pilot who strangled a British woman to the US military, according to documents obtained by the Guardian.

Cambridgeshire police allowed the US military police to quickly take control of the investigation into Capt Jacob Wulfson after he had been accused of sexually assaulting Sarah Steele in his Cambridge flat.

The decision meant Wulfson was not tried in an English criminal court. Instead he was prosecuted in a military tribunal on a US airbase in neighbouring Suffolk.

Ministry of Defence officials said the Cambridgeshire force should “absolutely” not have let the US military police take over the investigation in a clear breach of a long-established agreement with the US.

The disclosure of the case by the Guardian in June provoked immediate criticism from Downing Street, which said it was “deeply distressing” and “very concerning” that the UK authorities were not involved in prosecuting Wulfson.

The government to set up a high-level inquiry to examine how and why police forces have been transferring investigations into serious crimes to the US military police.

The Ministry of Defence, which is responsible for handling the military relationship with the US, is one of the key departments taking part in the inquiry.

A batch of documents, disclosed via the Freedom of Information Act, revealed the private views of MoD officials about the Steele case, which centres on an obscure agreement signed by the US and the UK decades ago.

Under the terms of the agreement, police in the UK have the primary right to investigate alleged crimes by Americans stationed in the country.

The MoD officials made it clear the agreement was “pretty unambiguous” and only permitted the US military to acquire jurisdiction over investigations in a “narrow set of circumstances”. These circumstances are: if the offences were committed while the Americans were on duty, or if they were committed against another member of their armed forces or property.

In a memo written on 8 July, MoD officials based in Washington wrote: “The Steele case does not, on the surface, appear to meet the bar for a visiting force to be awarded jurisdiction.” In the agreement, the US military is formally known as a visiting force.

Four days earlier, the MoD officials had referred to the Steele case in an email to colleagues, saying: “The decision-making on this specific case seemed at odds with what is very clear” in the agreement.

Another MoD official agreed that “as best as we understand the facts, this should absolutely have been for the UK courts”.

An unidentified Greater Manchester police officer wrote in an email to MoD officials on 6 July that Cambridgeshire police had “wrongly, in my view” handed over the Wulfson investigation to the US military.

Cambridgeshire police said they were conducting a review of the case with what they called “the assistance of material provided” by US Air Force lawyers. The force said it “remained engaged with the victim”.

“We are working with government, wider policing and criminal justice partners to ensure greater clarity of jurisdictional decision making,” they added.

The US military aims to prosecute as many of its personnel as possible within the boundaries of its agreement with the UK.

The Americans often ask police in the UK if they can take over the prosecution of their military personnel – requests the police agree to, even when they have primary responsibility for investigating them.

A series of cases uncovered this year by the Guardian have highlighted concerns that British victims are required to give evidence in US courts martial, an unfamiliar legal system that often does not afford the same protections as that of a court in the UK.

Wulfson was off-duty when he assaulted Steele in his Cambridge flat in December 2023 after the pair talked on the Tinder dating app.

Steele testified at Wulfson’s court martial, which was held on his airbase at Lakenheath, Suffolk in April, that her experience was “degrading and distressing”.

The verdict and sentence were decided by an all-male jury of Wulfson’s fellow air force officers. All the lawyers were American. Steele was subjected to invasive and aggressive questioning by Wulfson’s lawyer.

Wulfson was convicted of strangling an intimate partner but acquitted of sexual assault. He was dismissed from the US Air Force and confined to a military jail on Lakenheath for six months.

The cross-government inquiry, which includes officials from the Home Office, Ministry of Justice and Foreign Office, is looking at how US military personnel are not being brought to justice in British courts.

The inquiry, which also involves police chiefs, is scrutinising a series of cases uncovered by the Guardian this year.

In each case, police handed over the investigations to US military police even though the American perpetrators were off-duty and the British victims had no connection to the armed forces.

They were tried in US courts martial on American bases. Tyrion Davis allegedly raped two women in Suffolk. He was convicted of one charge of sexual assault, but cleared of 10 further counts of sexual assault and abusive sexual contact.

Hannes Marschalek allegedly exposed himself to a 16-year-old girl and four young women in Littleport, Cambridgeshire. He negotiated a plea bargain at a court martial and admitted a charge of indecent conduct. He won an appeal in a US military court that quashed his conviction on technical grounds. This ruling is now being challenged.

The US has more than 12,000 US military personnel in the UK, stationed in at least 15 bases and facilities. The two biggest bases are at Lakenheath and Mildenhall, in Suffolk. Significant numbers of American military personnel live in East Anglia.

‘We freed Patrick Stewart!’ Star Trek’s Marina Sirtis on breaking in her beloved but very serious co-star

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 13:00:45 GMT

She was scared of him but soon loosened the Shakespearean up – then watched him give Star Trek depth, even insisting scenes be rewritten for her. Captain Picard’s right-hand woman salutes her fabulous friend

I’d been warned about Patrick by friends who’d worked with him at the Royal Shakespeare Company. They said: “Marina, you can’t be you around Patrick Stewart. He’s all about the work. He takes it very seriously and he won’t abide you mucking about and trying to make people corpse.”

We had been cast together on Star Trek: The Next Generation and, because of what I’d heard, I was a bit scared, a bit intimidated. And let’s be honest – Patrick was very serious about the work. But there was a concerted effort by the rest of us to beat it out of him. We were from a younger generation and we wanted to shake up this Englishman who was so typical of his generation – stiff upper lip and a Yorkshireman to boot. You know, the kind of person who was not exactly renowned for showing their emotions. Early on Patrick told us all that we weren’t there to have fun, and you should have seen the looks he got. I’m a cockney: I’ve got a Spurs tattoo and we all looked at him in the same way I look at an Arsenal fan. But we did loosen him up. And – he’s said this himself – I think we actually freed him. We gave him a freedom that he said he’d never really felt before.

Of course it went both ways. We learned so much from him, how could you not? We learned from his professionalism and his absolutely insane talent. He brought gravitas to the role. Star Trek was a bit of a punchline before Patrick came along – it’s not any more. Patrick gave it depth – here was this consummate Shakespearean actor playing the captain of a starship. It just shifted everything.

He had reservations about taking the role, and his friends – who loved him and were looking out for him – told him not to do it. They thought it would be the end of his career, whereas it was probably the best decision in showbusiness at that time. He handled fame with grace. He didn’t flaunt it. Never got too big for his boots. Early on, a review in a paper described him as an “unknown Shakespearean actor” and we blew it up and stuck it on his trailer door. Someone less self-deprecating might not have liked that but he left it up there for years. He knew it was all good fun.

Before meeting Patrick I was just a jobbing actor who did a bit of telly. I’d grown up dirt poor and had a difficult childhood, so we came from very similar backgrounds. I kept my cockney accent because I wanted people to know where I came from. Patrick was the same – not through his voice, but through his demeanour and actions. He was down to earth, a regular bloke. The fact that he supported Huddersfield Town shows you who he is – he didn’t go for Leeds or one of the glamour clubs.

We’d both experienced childhood trauma and came out with our stories after we had finished working together. We never sat down and went into it all. But when people have gone through something like that, there’s something in their demeanour, something that you can see in them, that you feel in them.

A month before Covid hit, my husband died. I was on my own in my house in Los Angeles for a year with just my dogs for company. Patrick was one of the very few people who invited me over for lunch, socially distanced in his garden. It had occurred to him that I was grieving and on my own – and he did something about that. It’s a mark of who he is.

He was always on my side. In one of the Star Trek movies we did there was a scene written for Picard and Data, where Picard tells the story of how his family were burned in a fire. Patrick went to the writers and producers and asked if they could rewrite the scene to have me be in it instead of Brent Spiner. He said that Brent’s character Data was an android, and that he really needed to look into my eyes in order to reach the emotions he needed. So our relationship on screen was a two-way street, which sounds ridiculous saying that out loud! I don’t know how I’ve got the cheek to say that when I’m talking about Patrick Stewart! But we did help each other.

It’s also because of Patrick that I am now in the annals of my football team. When Tottenham played Huddersfield in 2018, we both did interviews about the game and it was officially named in the match day programme as the Star Trek derby. That’s now a part of Tottenham history and, as anyone who knows me will tell you, that means more to me than winning an acting award!

It was the absolute privilege of my life and my career to work with him. We were very, very close and stayed in touch right to the end, even though it became difficult to speak to him on the phone because of his health. He went quickly in the end and it makes me very sad that I didn’t get a chance to say goodbye. To say: “Thank you Patrick. Thanks for everything, mate.”
