‘Dark green dust’: the best (and worst) supermarket green teabags, tested and rated

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 13:00:43 GMT

Green tea can be a mixed bag – we sipped our way through the supermarket shelves to find the ones worth boiling the kettle for

The best (and worst) supermarket teabags

My mother-in-law has a mug that reads: “By replacing your morning coffee with green tea, you can lose up to 87% of what little joy you still have left in your life.” Some people will never like green tea, while others will probably have tried only poor-quality, over-brewed bags filled with the dust and fannings left over from the production of whole leaf tea. Only one of today’s teas contains whole leaves, and the difference is hugely noticeable, though that’s not to say the more economical bags are undrinkable. Some are single-origin or organic, and are certainly satisfactory, so long as you brew them properly.

Due to the large surface area of these tiny broken leaves, you need to be careful not to over-brew them. To stand the best chance of making a half-decent cup, use water at 80C – you can achieve that temperature by quarter-filling a cup with cold water, topping it up with just-boiled water and leaving it to brew for about 90 seconds. You’ll end up with a much sweeter cup, with nuanced kelp, edamame and toasted-straw flavours (all of which are, admittedly, acquired tastes).

★★★★☆

Small, individually wrapped bags of green fannings and brown stems with a classic umami, earthy aroma. Chamomile-yellow in colour with a distinct, savoury scent alongside a sweet, brothy tone. Quite astringent, so I’d recommend a shorter brew time. Bags free from plastic.

★★★☆☆

Dark green dust fannings and brown stems with a seaweedy aroma, from a single estate (Korakundah in the Nilgiri mountains, southern India). A clear, buttercup-yellow brew that holds a bright and complex flavour with a sweet start, an astringent finish and a full mouthfeel. Organic and Fairtrade.

★★★★☆

A small, individually wrapped bag of organic dark green fannings and brown stems made from a blend of sencha, Vietnamese and Indian green teas, plus 2% South Korean matcha. A sweet, oceanic aroma, a golden-yellow colour and a honeyed, floral and grassy flavour with hints of citrus. Bright and sharp, with a mild astringency.

★★★★☆

The only whole tea leaf in the test comes in a plant starch pyramid teabag full of large, broken dark green leaves with a kelpy scent. A light and clear green-lemon colour and complex, brothy, seaweed aroma. Bright and crisp with an earthy-umami depth, bright, fruity quality and mild astringency. One star Great Taste award in 2025, industrially compostable bags, and this week’s best splurge.

★★★☆☆

Dark green fannings with brown flecks produce a chamomile-yellow cup with clarity, toasted straw aroma, vegetal notes and a strong, astringent finish. Good tannic structure, too. Rainforest Alliance-certified, and plant-based, compostable bags.

Hear me out: maybe Norway should give Melania Trump the Nobel peace prize

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 12:00:44 GMT

The first lady has been praised for ‘singlehandedly’ brokering a ceasefire in a Ukrainian city – though she might have had some help

Haters be damned: Donald Trump just keeps on winning. He won the inaugural Fifa peace prize last year and was presented with the completely real, totally not made-up “Man of the Century” award at a recent rally. The president has also spent the greater part of a decade claiming he was once crowned Michigan’s Man of the Year: a fantastic achievement considering there is no such award and Trump has never lived in Michigan.

But despite his many trophies, there is one honour that has proved elusive: the Nobel peace prize. Trump holds a bit of a grudge about that, recently terming Norway a “shithouse country” for passing him over for the award. In response, the country’s tourism board highlighted some of its nicest public lavatories with the tagline: “Norway makes shit houses great again!”

Speaking in my capacity as Philadelphia’s Woman of the Millennium, I’ve got a modest proposal for the people of Norway. The toilet gag was excellent, but if they want to do some top-tier trolling then I think next year’s Nobel peace prize needs to go to Melania Trump.

Some people would be thrilled for their spouse to be in the spotlight, but I’m not sure that’s the case with Donald. Indeed, the president has said: “You can only have … one star in a family; it doesn’t work with two.” If Melania got Trump’s coveted Nobel peace prize, it could spark a war in the White House.

But look, I’m not just suggesting the Norwegians honour Melania because it would raise Donald’s blood pressure. No, it seems Melania has become quite the diplomat. Last week, the White House announced that the first lady had “successfully secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, localized to the city of Oleshky”.

How on earth did she manage that? Apparently, Melania initiated discussions with Russia and Ukraine and “aligned the parties on the agreement’s objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary”.

Whatever all that means, it seems to have worked: the ceasefire went into effect on Tuesday in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city, which has been enduring a worsening humanitarian crisis. On Friday, hundreds of people were evacuated from the frontline town and emergency supplies were brought in for people who needed to stay.

Melania has been widely praised for brokering this ceasefire. Melania’s adviser has claimed she “singlehandedly” secured it, adding that no other first lady has ever achieved what Melania just pulled off, and she is “completely revamping the role of first lady … [and] saving lives.”

Perhaps. But if there is one thing that the Trumps are good at it, it is taking credit for other people’s work. So is the first lady really the great peacemaker that she’s making herself out to be?

To be fair, Melania has done some good work vis-à-vis Ukraine and certainly seems to be better at peacemaking than Jared Kushner is, who has made huge sums of money while operating as one of Trump’s top diplomatic envoys to the Middle East. Last year, for example, Melania wrote a letter to Vladimir Putin pleading for Ukrainian children seized by Russia to be returned to their families. Since then, her office has said she’s facilitated numerous rounds of family reunification.

However, despite the claim that Melania “singlehandedly” secured this ceasefire, it would appear she had a little help. Pope Leo XIV also personally appealed to Putin about the situation in Oleshky in early October. It’s unclear whether he had more or less sway than the first lady had, but the pope is certainly being rather more modest about his involvement.

So what’s next for Melania after her success in Oleshky? In an interview with Newsmax, her adviser Marc Beckman said Melania might help pave the way to “durable, everlasting peace” in Ukraine and Russia as a whole.

“She’s against war, she thinks it’s senseless … she wants to see peace all over the world,” Beckman added.

Does she indeed? In that case she might want to have a word with the president, who started a very bloody war against Iran and who is currently trying to use US taxpayer money to send 2,000lb bombs to Israel, a country accused of genocide.

Forget the Nobel peace prize. If Melania can do something about her husband, I’m crowning her Michigan’s Woman of the Year.

Last November, the FDA announced that menopausal hormone therapy medications would no longer require a scary “black-box” label on them, which is the highest safety-related warning a medication can have. This reassured a lot of women about the treatment and caused a surge in demand. Supply didn’t keep up, and there’s been a shortage of estrogen patches in the US all year because of an uptick in demand. Now Reuters reports that the shortage has spread beyond estrogen patches “with some injectable and vaginal estrogen products also in short supply”.

‘The sexy stuff has got to be coming to an end, right?’: Rivals star Aidan Turner on beards, ballroom dancing and putting Poldark to bed

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 12:00:43 GMT

His dashing lead role in Jilly Cooper’s bonkbuster didn’t hurt the actor’s pin-up status, but now, he protests, he’s 43 – and a dad

Aidan Turner has a tactical beard. For the last two decades or so, the actor has found himself in roles that have made him a smouldering pin-up. Audiences really love to look at him. You can buy mugs that say, “Today I don’t feel like doing anything … except Aidan Turner.” There are entire Reddit forums dedicated to sharing photographs of him looking hot. He knows this about himself, just like he knows that people want to ask him about it. “I do get asked these questions,” he says, a little wearily. “I do get the, you know, word ‘smoulder’ or ‘sexy’, and all that kind of shit.” So right now, he has a full beard, in the hope that he will not be accused of, for example, smouldering. “I thought it wouldn’t happen so much with the beard,” he sighs. “I thought I could get away with it. I was going for ‘dad’.”

The job of actors is to sell a story as well as they possibly can, and over the years plenty of the stories that Turner has sold have involved romance and sex. He appeared in Les Liaisons Dangereuses at the National Theatre in London this summer, and even the New Yorker noted how much he smoulders. In some ways, Turner is one of those male performers who is, well, a little bit objectified. The fact that he is a good actor, and also known for being sexy, places him in a peculiar bind. If he doesn’t gamely play along, if he points out that he’s getting a bit tired of it actually, then he risks being seen as a killjoy. Sure, there are worse burdens to bear, but at times the star of Poldark and Rivals finds himself in a curious position.

Turner is 43 now. (He is literally a dad – he and his wife, the American actor Caitlin FitzGerald, have got a small son.) His early roles showed off his ability to handsomely, pensively brood. He was a vampire in the sci-fi series Being Human, and played Dante Gabriel Rossetti in Desperate Romantics, writing moody poetry in soft light. Then, in 2015, he starred in the BBC’s hugely popular adaptation of Poldark, which turned him into a household name. As Ross Poldark, an 18th-century soldier, he loved, fought and, very famously, swung a scythe. The attention that came with it made his career, but it also put him off sexy roles for a while. Then a few years later, Rivals came along.

Rivals is outrageously fun and smutty. It adapts Jilly Cooper’s Rutshire Chronicles novels, the kind of books that would once have been known as bonkbusters, into big, brash television. In her fictionalised version of the Cotswolds in the 1980s, Cooper brought together aristocrats, MPs and cut‑throat television executives. Everyone is having sex with everyone; everyone is ready to stab their neighbour in their back, and probably have sex with them at the same time. Everyone, that is, except Turner’s character, Declan O’Hara, a serious‑minded broadcast journalist who is unusually faithful to his wife, Maud – and also dashingly handsome. So here Turner is again, fielding questions about intimacy coordinators, sex scenes and his very full moustache.

The moustache was his idea. “I say it was my idea,” he begins, then corrects himself. “It fucking was my idea.” Turner swears like it is going out of fashion. He has just finished today’s photoshoot, so we have gone to find a quiet spot to chat, and have ended up in a basement, surrounded by bikes and cleaning products and tools. He is out of the fancy clothes and back in his east London dad uniform of white T-shirt, navy chore jacket and jeans. He explains that he had turned up for the Rivals job with a full beard, and if they were going to shave it off, he told them, he had no intention of using a stick-on prosthetic. “You end up eating hairs all day and if you smile it falls off,” he says. “I think everyone on set has now learned the lesson of no stickies.” So they shaved him down to a moustache first, and decided they liked it, and that’s what stuck. It also gave Declan a bit more gravitas. “I don’t want to make this about getting into character or anything. All that stuff gives me the creeps, actors talking about that,” he says, squirming. “But [the moustache] is really helpful, because Declan feels older to me. Like, he’s a bit more of a grownup than I am.” Turner grew up in Dublin and has the accent to prove it, but Declan has a Westmeath accent, a bit deeper than his own, which he borrowed from his father, Pearse. “So with that, and the geography teacher outfits, everything feels more mature.”

Rivals has been a juggernaut for all involved. The TV series is nostalgic and knowing, horny and hilarious, but the new episodes find the show in a more gloomy mood. It opens with a funeral – don’t panic; I counted, and it only takes 15 minutes to get to a sex scene – and trouble is brewing for Declan and Maud’s marriage. “It’s a big one,” Turner nods, though spoiler etiquette dictates he cannot say too much.

The fact that Rivals can swing so comfortably between profound grief, camp backstabbing and joyful infidelity gives it a very particular tone. Why does Turner think that audiences have lapped it up? “I mean, I was born in ’83, and there is this yearning for that nostalgia, I suppose. And Jilly Cooper has a certain tone. She was looked over for many years. It was seen as this low-rent, smutty kind of literature, and I don’t know if a lot of people gave it a chance. That doesn’t seem to be the case any more.” He has noticed that it appeals to lots of age groups, and for the first time in a while people in their 20s are coming up to him in the street. “Rivals is funny, and it knows exactly what it is,” he offers. “It’s unapologetic. It’s on the front foot and it’s out there, going, this is what we’re doing, this is who we are.”

Cooper was heavily involved in the first season, and they were in the middle of shooting the second when the author died suddenly, at the age of 88. Turner has fond memories of her. “She was famous for throwing these parties at her house in the Cotswolds that were just exactly what you would imagine,” Turner says. “They were so much fun. The champagne never stopped flowing, and her dogs were everywhere. She was so spirited.” He was filming the immediate aftermath of those funeral scenes when he sensed that something was going on. “It was eerie already, and I mentioned to Victoria [Smurfit, who plays Maud] that this feels weird. It feels very dark, and, like, not Rivals. And then we took a break, and I knew something was up.” The line producer broke the news to the cast that Cooper had died.

Five weeks earlier, Turner says, he had been at one of those famous parties. “And she was making speeches and drinking champagne and introducing me to people. She was her brilliant, funny, filthy self.” Cooper would often swing by the set. “I’m just glad that she got a chance to see the show, to see where it was going and how it was looking, and she was really proud of it.”

Given the amount of sex involved in Rivals, it is no surprise that they use intimacy coordinators to assist with the choreography. Turner remembers the time before intimacy coordinators were commonplace, and he finds it much better, and much easier, now that they are readily available on sets. In the past, he remembers working with directors who were hands-off or awkward when it came to sex scenes. “They just kind of leave it to you. And I don’t know whether that’s a really good thing, you know, because it’s, like, what the fuck do we do? And is this OK? And does this work?” Having a professional who is there to figure that out is really useful. “I think it’s important, especially in a show like this, to sell the scene and to do what we’re doing, because there are so many different types of sex in this show. It helps us a lot.”

Turner was in his early 30s when he got the lead in Poldark, the BBC’s second adaptation of the Winston Graham novels, about a soldier returning home from the American revolutionary war. It turned you into a pin-up, I suggest. He takes a breath so deep that it could fill a Cornish tin mine. “I suppose they were positioning Ross to be that,” he concedes, carefully. “There was a sex in Ross, wasn’t there, I suppose,” he says, with a chuckle, “that previously wasn’t there.” He mentions the photograph of him taken behind the scenes, in a field, topless, with a scythe. For the last 10 years, it has appeared again and again, which, he says, is “all quite embarrassing. It kind of went everywhere.” In it, Turner is being touched up by the show’s makeup artist Jacqui Fowler, who is often airbrushed out of the shot, much to his disdain. “She’s there with the makeup brush, brilliant Jacqui, and I don’t know what she’s doing … ”

Was she painting his muscles? (I meant enhancing them, rather than adding them.) “No! That was something I fucking worked hard for,” he laughs. “I was 12 years younger. It was probably a lot easier to get in shape. But I was, like, no, this guy is a farmer. He’s on the horse all the time. We never really see him eating. When he is, it’s fucking gruel. He’s probably quite lean.” So Turner decided that he needed to get in shape, too. As with the Rivals moustache, it was his idea to go topless in the scything scene, and he had no idea that it would still be talked about a decade later. “I made some friends on the show that I’m still friends with now, and I’m proud of it. It had a really strong audience, and we tried to do something different with it, and I think we did. But all of that stuff was embarrassing, because it just kind of follows you around a little bit. But it might not have been successful if we didn’t have any of that at all.”

For a few years afterwards – until Rivals, in fact – Turner resisted taking roles that he knew would require him to be sexy. Did Poldark put him off? “It did, yeah,” he says. In photoshoots now, for example, he might politely decline to pose in a way that seems suggestive. “It just feels different, at 43, and being a dad,” he shrugs. Then again, he admits, he is here to talk about Rivals. Also, he has just finished Les Liaisons Dangereuses, that famously sex-focused play, in which his character Valmont manipulates women into bed, for sport and for the sheer sociopathic thrill of it. “And you’re, like, well, I mean, you’re asking for it, dude!” he laughs. He is nothing if not self-aware. “But then, I feel like this sexy stuff has got to be coming to an end. Right? Tell me it’s done.” I think that’s up to him. “For sure, and it is. But the roles are getting more interesting, and less about … that.”

Turner has never done social media and says he has never felt any pressure to sign up to it. “No. You would definitely get more free shit if you had a few million followers on Instagram. I do meet people and I’m, like, where did you get that? And they’re, like, oh, it got sent to me.” But he knows it’s not worth it. “I don’t need those trainers. Most people I know are on it, but I don’t really want to share those things. And I don’t think I’d be very good at doing it. I would probably get it wrong. I’d probably either overshare, or not do it enough.”

Turner does not strike me as an oversharer. He mentions early mornings taking his son to school after a late night at the theatre, or trips with him to the West End to see The Lion King and Paddington, but otherwise he is tight-lipped on life outside work. “I draw the line at the personal stuff. And plus, I’ve always just felt, like, who wants to hear from me? I always felt that, in the early days of Twitter or X or whatever. It takes so much confidence, doesn’t it, to go, ‘People want to hear exactly what I have to say in this sentence.’ Wow. The balls on that. Jesus. I’d love some of that courage.”

When not being forced to examine the embarrassment of being objectified as a man in your 40s by horrible, intrusive journalists, Turner is great company. He is funny; he is as charming, as you might expect; and he is more than happy to discuss big, state‑of-the-world stuff. Take this morning. He was listening to a podcast about Meta’s new AI assistant, he says. “They will do shit for you. They’ll order food and deliver it to a friend of yours, and they’ll make sure that if you want to get paid, you’ll get paid, and they’ll make sure your mortgage gets done every month, and they’ll do everything. But you’ve just got to give them all of you.” He realised, for the first time, that he was scared of what might happen next. “There could be a moment where it’s, like, no, sorry, Aidan, there is no money for you. We need that money for a datacentre.” The podcast talked about how helpful AI could be, as well as how destructive. “But this has already been downloaded by millions of people, and I’m, like, we’re walking straight into this fire, aren’t we? This might be coming for us faster than I thought.”

Does he worry about AI coming for his job? The late Gene Wilder’s voice has been reactivated for a Netflix reality show; Tilly Norwood, the world’s first AI actor, has been unleashed on Hollywood, to middling results. “It will get better and better, and it’s about how comfortable we are when it does get amazing and we can’t tell the difference,” he says. “I don’t know whether I want to read a novel from an AI author. I want the human. I want the connection.” Maybe he is showing his age, he says, “but I don’t want to write us off yet. I don’t want a painting that’s been generated by AI. I want to see oil and canvas and acrylic. Call me old school, but I want the humans to win that battle.”

Turner lives in London now, with FitzGerald and their son. He moved to the city in his 20s, after a few years of doing theatre in Dublin. “My first TV job brought me over, and I never really went back,” he says. “I love London. For me, it’s still one of the most exciting cities in the world.” The couple have lived in the US for short periods of time, too, though neither was keen on settling there. For political reasons? “I’m not going to lie. Guns scare me, and we have a young child, and I don’t want to worry about that every day. I know we have our own problems in this country, but the guns thing scares me. I think the healthcare system is completely fucked [in America]. God forbid you’re not very wealthy, because if you get sick and you don’t have much money, or even if you’re doing all right, it will take everything. That just seems crazy to me.”

Turner grew up in Clondalkin, in the west of County Dublin, with his brother and his parents. “We were a working-class family. My dad retired a few years ago, but he was an electrician, and my mum is an accountant.” He had a grandmother who did amateur dramatics, but otherwise there was no history of performing in the family. When Turner realised he wanted to go to drama school, at 18, “there was a certain mould being broken, there”. But, he says, he did have some experience of being on stage. “It would be remiss of me not to say that there was an unusual part of my childhood where I danced,” he begins.

He was not just a casual dancer. He danced ballroom and Latin American from the age of six to 17, and at one point he came third in the All-Ireland dance championships. “That’s weird as fuck,” he laughs. “I mean, not odd, but just not the norm for a kid from west Dublin, which is quite poor. My mum and dad spent a lot of money to fund that.” He describes the world of competitive dancing in vivid detail. “There were trophies everywhere, and we went to a competition and it was tails and suits and numbers on the back, and fake tan and Elnett hairspray and pushy mums.

“I went to schools that were quite rough, and I danced right up until I was 17,” he continues. “And I told everyone!” Was he given a hard time for it? “I don’t think they believed me, that’s my theory.” He has seen old friends who have since read about his dancing years, and they told him that they didn’t think he was being serious. “These are working-class boys, who are 14, 15, and we’re all drinking cider on a Friday night and smoking cigarettes and doing whatever else. And you tell them that you’re away to Blackpool this weekend, that you dance, and they might believe you. But they don’t want to take part in this conversation. They move away. They still want to be your mate, but they don’t have the faculties to deal with this conversation.” He gave up dancing when his dance partner got injured, and while on a break, he applied on a whim for drama school. “I was actually quite a shy kid, and there’s still a lot of that in there,” he says. Acting made him less self-conscious, and he knew straight away that it was the life for him.

Turner has roles coming up that take him beyond the heart-throb. He is waiting for work to start on Grendel, the live-action adaptation of the 1971 novel, which tells the story of Beowulf from the monster’s perspective. Is he playing a monster? “No, no, he’s a warrior. He’s a shit warrior,” he jokes. “I don’t even know how much I can talk about that. I hope it’s still happening.” He also plays the Apostle Andrew in Terrence Malick’s forthcoming biblical epic, about the life of Jesus Christ, currently known as The Way of the Wind, though Malick is, famously, not a fast worker, and it was filmed in 2019. “Surely it’s coming out soon? I don’t know,” he says.

But he has also, briefly, returned to The Diplomat, Netflix’s popular political thriller, reprising his role as the British spy Callum Ellis. And there is no denying it: Callum is a sexy guy. “Oh, come off it. I am not sexy in The Diplomat,” he says, firmly. “That is all you.” He really does think, or hope, that this era is almost behind him. “It must be coming to an end,” he says. But what if he’s got another 20 years of it left? “Oh no,” he says, laughing. Then groans, as if he cannot think of anything worse.

Rivals season two returns to Disney on 11 November.

Is AI your new wingman? How chatbots are transforming dating

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 12:00:42 GMT

Almost 40% of British singles have used AI for romantic advice, from writing messages to assessing potential partners

After Sam’s ex joked that her sister found him ugly, he turned to AI. Google Gemini had a look at the photo and politely disagreed. AI has been his wingman ever since, aiding his dating life by giving pep talks and vetting his messages.

The 27-year-old from Stoke-on-Trent is not the only AI-assisted romantic – a survey of 3,000 British singles published this month by Match Group, the owner of the Tinder and Hinge platforms, found 39% had used AI in their dating lives.

Relying on AI is bad, Sam tells the Guardian, adding he would rather begin dating in person, but there is a “paradigm shift in dating that’s occurring, which is really odd, where everything is expected to start online”.

The proportion of AI use in dating is even higher for younger generations, rising to 66% for members of gen Z (people born in the mid 1990s to early 2010s), and 53% of millennials (those born in the early 1980s to mid-90s).

Sam says pressure to make a good impression on dating apps means a misunderstood message could risk him losing out on dates. “Online dating … as a guy it’s a bit of a ghost town,” he says. “Rather than saying: ‘Hey, how’s your weekend going?’ it’s thinking about what I can pick up that might get a response.”

The most common use of AI across all cohorts, according to Match, is to get advice about someone they are talking to, plan date ideas, practise conversations, write a dating profile or messages, and vet whether profiles or photos are genuine. Using AI to alter a photo is a no-no for the majority of singles, the survey says.

A single mother from New Zealand, who asked to remain anonymous, says she has used AI as a dating mentor. “I did not really date before I met my ex-husband … with ChatGPT I set it up to coach me to become more secure – to not panic about any delay in messaging, to not rush into anything,” she says.

One man from Melbourne, Australia, who began dating after his 20-year marriage ended, says AI made finding his current partner faster by assessing people he “matched” with and testing his responses. “It was getting [to be] quite a lot of work, like all the chats and the profiles. So I thought: ‘How can I use AI just to sort of speed it up a little bit?’” he says.

The 51-year-old adds that the chatbot he was using helped him think twice about profiles he’d overlooked. “[With] my current partner, it was really aggressive with me saying that: ‘Nah, she’s your vibe, she just takes shit photos.’ And then I meet her at a cafe and she’s absolutely drop-dead gorgeous,” he says.

When he told his partner he had used AI in their exchanges, she also admitted to using Anthropic’s Claude chatbot to analyse his responses. He says she joked that the “two Claudes were probably just chatting away behind the scenes”. It is a risky admission, though – about a third of UK singles said they would end a date if they found out AI had been used to write a potential paramour’s messages.

But, while a few singles like to discuss how their date went with a chatbot (7%), far more prefer a group chat (29%) or their parents (20%), according to the Match survey. “Maybe our friends are becoming more distant because of technology, a little more hands off, compared to the generation before us [who] would get together in their flat or the pub and just absolutely dish the dirt,” says Dec, 31, from London, who uses ChatGPT as a “sounding board” when chatting with single men.

Dec says he uploaded his dating conversations to ChatGPT and gave it prompts such as: “Tell me what you think the red flags there are”, and: “What does this connection look like?”

Although deploying the chatbot charmer led to a number of dates, Dec worries that his “brain feels like it’s rotting because everything’s just offloaded to AI now”. He adds: “We all know it’s going to be a bit of a yes man sometimes.”

The Match survey also hinted at a robotic romantic future where autonomous AIs do people’s dating work for them. More than a quarter of respondents liked the idea of two people’s assistants talking to each other and reporting back before the people speak – even if a majority think the idea is “unacceptable”. Match’s head of trust and safety, Yoel Roth, says the company is taking a “hard stance” against bot-to-bot dating.

“In a world where people say that they’re more alienated than ever, are hungrier for connection than ever, we don’t get closer to that goal of human connection by having robots talk to each other,” he says.

Sam agrees that AI can only enhance his prospects by so much: “If I replace my humour with AI I think I’ve died as a person.”

Days away from a national verdict on Trump 2.0, we check in with nine voters across the political spectrum

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 11:00:44 GMT

Millions will vote to decide which party controls Congress – which will have a huge impact on Trump’s final years in office

US voters will soon deliver a national verdict on the second presidency of Donald Trump. On 3 November, millions of Americans will vote in midterm elections to decide control of the House of Representatives and Senate, as well as the governorships in 36 states and state legislatures across the country. The results could have a huge impact on Trump’s final two years in office.

Our reporters have interviewed nine voters across the country and the political spectrum about extremism in US politics, their confidence in the US voting system, what they hope Congress will tackle first and their views of the president’s secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth.

The answers – highlights of which are published below – offer insight into the national mood days before voters head to the polls. The Guardian will return to its voter panel after final votes are cast.

Sally Rasmussen 62; Medford, Wisconsin; independent/progressive

double quotation markThe times that we’re living through has created a certain extremism. My bias is that I see the extremism on the right. I see the extremism of Trump’s influence on the candidates, on the electorate and the people that I live with every day here in Taylor county. I’ve not been a fan of Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor in Wisconsin. He showed his extremism from the very start, seeking to undermine the 2020 election, voting for war, supporting tariffs, never swerving from the lockstep Maga extremist playbook, essentially.

double quotation markIt depends on what you mean by extreme. While this shift is seen as electorally threatening to some, most of these candidates who are typically the ones labeled as “extreme” have policy prescriptions that are very close to the average American’s views, especially when it comes to topics like healthcare reform or participation in forever wars. Looking at the other side of the aisle, I do think there has been an emergence of candidates who display an “extreme” level of corruption and bigotry typically only seen coming from the White House these days. Mike Rogers [Republican Senate candidate for Michigan] comes to mind, with his main campaign strategy seemingly being a desperate bid to tie El-Sayed to anything radical or Islamist, and so does Vivek Ramaswamy’s notable doubling-down on a campaign ad implying his gubernatorial opponent [in Ohio] lied about her childhood sexual abuse.

double quotation markMost of the Democratic candidates are extreme. This political cycle has produced more extreme candidates than ever before. I’m 70 years old and I’ve never been involved in active politics. I’ve always voted since I was 18 and I’ve always voted conservative Republican but I’ve never seen anything that’s so extreme. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan is one that stands out and some have already been elected like the mayor of New York [Zohran Mamdani]. I never thought I would see someone that far left voted in.

Sally Rasmussen 62; Medford, Wisconsin; independent/progressive

double quotation markI believe that at the most local level, it will overwhelmingly be free and fair. And by that I mean that I have a great deal of faith in the town clerks and the county clerks, the people who, at the ground level, oversee elections and whose livelihoods, whose reputations are on the line. On the national level, I have every expectation that the extremists that are currently in power will do whatever they can to, well, to cheat, to break the law, to violate constitutional rights of the people, and to try to deny election results, as happened after the 2020 election.

From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 11:00:40 GMT

A mile beneath the Black Hills, scientists are building giant detectors to analyse neutrino particles – and possibly find the answer to existence

For more than a century, the mining town of Lead, in the Black Hills of South Dakota, attracted workers with a taste for gold. Now, a flagship experiment being built in the old mine is drawing scientists in search of more intriguing riches: answers to the deepest mysteries of the universe.

Construction of the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (Dune) in the former Homestake mine is due to start on Monday. Engineers will begin assembling four giant detectors inside caverns blasted from rock a mile underground.

Once switched on, the detectors will quietly spark and flicker as ghostly particles called neutrinos hurtle through them. Some will arrive from the sun and distant supernovae, others in an intense beam sent through 800 miles (1,300km) of rock from a government laboratory near Chicago, Illinois.

Observing the neutrinos could uncover entirely new science and shed light on cosmic spectacles, such as the death of stars and the birth of black holes. Scientists are particularly hopeful of solving one of the most enduring puzzles in nature: why everything around us is made from matter and not its “evil twin”, antimatter. In other words, why we, and why anything, is here at all.

“It’s a super exciting time to be working on this,” said Dr Kate Shaw, an experimental particle physicist on Dune from the University of Sussex. “Neutrinos do not make sense yet and they could open a door to new physics.”

Neutrinos are the most abundant matter particles in the universe, outnumbered only by photons, the massless particles of light that illuminate the universe. They are produced in natural nuclear reactions, such as those that power the sun, in radioactive decay and in particle accelerators.

Even by physicists’ standards, neutrinos are oddballs. The chargeless particles barely interact with other matter: about a trillion pass unnoticed through your body each second. Neutrinos come in three varieties, all with minuscule but different masses. Weirdly, they change from one variety to another, a process called oscillation, as they travel. “It’s a very strange behaviour,” said Shaw. “It’s like me throwing you an apple and it turns into a banana.”

Lead has a history with these peculiar particles. In the 1960s, the physicist Ray Davis followed miners down the shaft and built a detector from a 100,000-gallon tank filled with dry-cleaning fluid. Shielded so deep beneath the ground, the detector became the first to record neutrinos from the sun as they struck chlorine atoms in the fluid and turned them into argon.

The mine closed in 2001 and transitioned, thanks to visionary forethought, into a dedicated subterranean laboratory, the Sanford Underground Research Facility (Surf). It is already home to the Lux-Zeplin (LZ) experiment which last month reported the first potential detection of dark matter.

“We’ve gone from mining the Earth to helping scientists explore the universe,” said Robin Lucero, Lead’s city administrator, whose family has lived locally for generations. “We’re incredibly proud and lucky that Dune is happening here, and Surf, which has other experiments like LZ. Having world-class science brings new opportunities, new people and new possibilities for our local businesses and especially our young people.”

Unlike Davis’s apparatus, the Dune experiment is enormous. Made from more than 4,000 tonnes of steel, the detectors will stand up to five-storeys high and hold a combined 70,000 tonnes of liquid argon that must be chilled to -200C. Assembling the detectors should take nearly three years. Filling them with liquid argon, another year.

“This is a heavy duty engineering operation,” and a partnership with the skilled local workforce, said Prof David Newbold, of the UK’s Science and Technology Facilities Council and a Dune spokesperson. “It’s like building a ship underground.” The UK is the largest international partner in the US-led experiment and is making core detector components, critical computing to reconstruct events in the detectors, and the graphite target needed to generate neutrinos at Femilab, a particle physics facility in Illinois.

Once operational, Dune will study an intense beam of neutrinos sent from Fermilab through 800 miles of the Earth’s crust and mantle. Most neutrinos will shoot straight through, but every so often one will strike an argon atom, creating a flicker of light and a pulse of electric charge. Analysing these will reveal intimate details about the mysterious particles.

One big question surrounds the masses of different neutrinos. Which is lightest and which heaviest? The answer could reveal fundamental new forces of nature. And in an attempt to answer the matter v antimatter question, Dune will look for subtle differences between neutrinos and their antimatter twins, antineutrinos.

Beyond the beams of particles sent from Fermilab, Dune will also study neutrinos arriving from space, carrying with them fresh information on stellar explosions and the formation of black holes.

Earlier this month, the Nobel prize for physics honoured the Belgian researcher Francis Halzen, who used a cubic kilometre of Antarctica to detect high-energy neutrinos from deep space. But detection is far from the end of the story. “This really is going to be a golden era,” Newbold said. “There’s a lot more of that to come.”

Streeting says he began stockpiling food weeks ago amid rising threat to UK

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 10:57:36 GMT

Defence secretary says value for money and modernisation key for spending to ‘fight the wars ahead’

The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, says he started stockpiling food and water weeks ago in case of a national emergency, as he talked up the threats to the UK and said his department had already begun ramping up its spending in response.

Streeting spoke after the chancellor, John Healey, said he wanted defence spending to reach 3% of GDP by 2030 and 3.5% by 2035; having already asked Whitehall departments to find 1% cuts in their budgets for long-term investment to fund defence spending.

“I’m glad the message is getting through because my mum got in touch and said ‘payday is coming up, how much do you think I need to buy because I’m just budgeting to the end of the month?’ I’m glad that people are beginning to think about their own household resilience, making sure we’ve got sufficient supplies of bottled water, canned goods, battery-powered torches. These are all just commonsense things for the everyday challenges,” Streeting told the Times.

The defence secretary says he has bottled water, a first aid kit and a battery-powered torch on standby. He added that he was stockpiling baked beans, sweetcorn, red kidney beans, tuna, protein bars and nuts. Streeting, who recently urged all Britons to follow suit, said he had started setting aside the supplies because he wanted to “lead by example”.

He told the Times he was determined the UK should be able to deter its adversaries and “should deterrence fail, to be ready to defeat them”. Streeting said: “That is the core job. We should never lose sight of that,” adding that any additional spending must be done carefully. “Spending more money badly is not virtuous,” he said. He also told the newspaper that value for money and modernisation needed to be balanced in order to ready the UK to “fight the wars ahead”.

In June, Healey’s resignation as defence secretary was one of the final nails in the coffin of Keir Starmer’s premiership. The man who now serves as chancellor in Andy Burnham’s government accused Burnham’s predecessor, as well as the former chancellor Rachel Reeves, of putting the country’s security at risk with inadequate funding for the defence investment plan (Dip).

“You have been unable and the Treasury has been unwilling to commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country at this time of rising threats. I would not be able to accept a Dip settlement that does not give our forces the resources they need. I am now left with no other option than to submit my resignation as your defence secretary,” he wrote.

Announcing his first budget on Wednesday, Healey said he was now fully funding the defence investment plan. He reiterated the target of defence spending reaching 3% of GDP; prompting the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, to say the UK was on “a credible path towards meeting the commitment made by all Nato allies in The Hague”. But Healey was criticised for leaving details of his plan to reach that target until next year’s spending review.

Besides spending, Streeting also discussed oversight of service personnel, telling the Times the courts were in the middle of an “active campaign” to “smear the reputation and integrity of our special forces”. He also left the door open to scrutiny of special forces and the UK’s nuclear weapons by MPs and peers on the intelligence and security committee, saying they could be trusted.

The real problem with Britain’s Political Traitors show is that no one is very faithful to anything for long

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 10:00:40 GMT

For Westminster’s special budget edition of the series, politicians have played to their strengths. Bombast, duplicity, distrust: it’s all second nature

You join us on a steam train in Scotland as we head to the next episode of the BBC’s hit show Political Traitors. It’s like the celebrity edition, except that everyone is less comely – politics being the practice of show business for ugly people. For this week’s task, the players have to construct a “budget” of tiny crowd-pleasing measures, carefully balanced by invisible tax rises.

What makes the show so compelling is that the players don’t know the whole story. Only those of us on the outside can see what’s really going on. While John and Andy run around shouting about how they have faithfully met their “fiscal rules” in the third year of the forecasts, on our sofas at home we know that this incantation is entirely meaningless.

But people who’ve been on the show say that when you’re in the midst of it, it feels completely real. So much so that there are ongoing questions for the producers about safeguarding. Liz, who was a sensation of chaotic energy when she briefly appeared in 2022, is the most obvious example of someone who shouldn’t have been allowed to take part. She was last heard explaining her plan to colonise Mars.

If the series has any value beyond entertainment, it’s for the insights it offers into human psychology, especially the way people convince themselves of narratives that are objectively nonsense. Take Kemi, from the current run. After the banishment of Keir earlier this year, she could be heard explaining to anyone who would listen that this was the result of her brilliant inquisitions at the roundtable.

We could all see that the other players, after debating why on earth Keir hadn’t already been stabbed in the back, had concluded that although he was 100% faithful, he was also 1000% loser.

Nevertheless, there’s something rather charming about Kemi’s total conviction that she’s a masterly player on course for triumph. It’s easy for us to laugh, but you have to remember that she doesn’t have access to the information we do, such as opinion polls and byelection results.

That information gap is the joy of the show. Several times Nigel has seemingly revealed himself to be a traitor, and his close ally Nathan was actually unmasked as one, but still no one seems able to put two and two together.

Some players adopt a strategy of trying to fly below the radar to avoid being noticed. One current player, Ed D, has been so successful that many viewers have forgotten he exists and refuse to believe he is part of the game at all, even after his triumph in the water slide task.

Each morning, the players meet over breakfast TV for a heated discussion in which they all insist that whatever has just happened proves their theory is right. Then there’s the dramatic moment of discovering who has been banished, or simply walked off the set. In one compelling episode in 2022, almost all the players quit in the hope of forcing Boris to admit he’d been lying. Even then, to viewers’ delight, he still had the support of the loyal Nadine.

In last month’s “conference” task, the players were handed the severed head of a deceased teammate and had to mimic their distinctive cry. Kemi, predictably, chose Maggie, although her impersonation looked more like pastiche. Andy, on the other hand, reckons he can do a mean Harold. He’s rejected any suggestion that he should try copying Tony, one of the game’s most successful players, but he’s failed to brush aside the lingering suspicion that he’s simply doing an impression of Keir.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The format has been sold around the world, with changes for local markets. The French edition involves a runoff vote. The Israeli version is so complicated that no one understands anything about it except that somehow Bibi keeps winning. And the American one is louder, brasher and far more expensive. It also seems to be played entirely by idiots who have failed, despite an impossible number of very clear clues, to identify their obvious traitor.

Although the players change at an alarming rate, the one constant in the British show is the host, Lindsay. With his ridiculous outfits and his catchphrases – “Order! ORDER!” and “Mr Holden, I think you need to leave” – he is fast becoming a national treasure. And now, as he says at the end of every roundtable, the time for talk is over.

I’m joking, of course. In this version of the show, the time for talk never ends.

Robert Hutton is a journalist and author

The staggering $446m Elon Musk has spent on the US midterms – visualized

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 10:00:40 GMT

In May 2025, Elon Musk said he would do “a lot less” political spending in the future.

The tech mogul’s midterm donations backing Republicans have made him the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history

Elon Musk has poured so much money into US politics this midterms election cycle that his donations could fund half a dozen SpaceX rocket launches or buy thousands of Tesla Cybertrucks. At the Tesla Diner in Los Angeles, Musk could order more than 31.9m cheeseburgers with the money he has spent on the midterms.

Musk, the world’s richest person, has funnelled at least $445.77m into Republican-aligned political action committees (Pacs) and groups since last year, according to US Federal Election Commission data as of 29 October. The contributions have made him the Republicans’ most prominent financial backer and the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history.

Musk’s spending is a staggering example of the SpaceX and Tesla CEO’s political influence, as he seeks to help Donald Trump’s administration retain control of Congress in the upcoming midterm elections, though current polls predict Democrats achieving a majority. The contributions are at a scale that is difficult to fathom and dwarf efforts from big name megadonors like George Soros or Michael Bloomberg, setting a new precedent for how the rich and powerful attempt to shape politics.

Only last year, Musk claimed he would step away from making large scale political donations after putting nearly $300m towards Trump’s 2024 presidential election campaign. FEC data since then shows he has not only leaned back into financing campaigns, but that his spending has dramatically ramped up as election day approaches, increasing by about $200m in the final two months of campaigning.

Musk’s money has primarily flowed into several Republican-aligned Super Pacs, with his largest contribution of $216m going into his own America Pac. The Pac has targeted 43 House and Senate races across the US, blanketting voters with television commercials, digital ads, text messages and mailers.

America Pac made 839 independent expenditures in House races and 623 in Senate races in 17 states across the country. The spending varies greatly depending on the state, however, with campaigns in battlegrounds such as Michigan and Arizona receiving more of the Pac’s support.

Musk’s Pac has spent the most in his home state of Texas, where a closely fought Senate contest between Democratic candidate James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton has turned into the most expensive race of the midterms. America Pac has overall poured more than $33m into efforts to elect Paxton, while Musk also made a $168m contribution to the Senate Leadership Fund which supports the Paxton campaign.

A large portion of America Pac’s output focuses on attack ads against Democratic candidates such as Talarico, often accusing them of being radical socialists or targeting them over supporting transgender rights. The Pac has spent $28m on anti-Talarico content, including between $300,000 and 350,000 in October on a single Google ad targeting the Texas Senate candidate.

“James Talarico supports parents being charged with child abuse if they do not support transitioning their children,” stated the ad, which was shown more than 10m times over an eight day period.

Musk has also reposted America Pac’s content to his more than 200m followers on X, the social media platform he owns. One of Musk’s posts in October amplified an America Pac attack ad and claimed: “Talarico wants to trans your kids and destroy the border.”

The nearly $446m that Musk has donated this election cycle far exceeds his contributions in the 2024 presidential race, when the tech mogul also held rallies and appeared on stage next to Trump during the campaign. While Musk has been a less visible presence in the midterms, potentially reflecting the US public’s dislike of him, behind the scenes he has greatly upped his financial support for Republicans.

Musk’s spending far outpaces all other donors in the elections, including fellow tech and finance moguls like Marc Andreessen, who also started his own Super Pac. Musk has put more money into this election cycle than what every top Silicon Valley donor, including himself, spent on the 2024 presidential election combined.

The stakes of the midterm elections are potentially high for Musk, who has closely aligned himself with the Trump administration and benefited from its lax policies toward regulating tech and artificial intelligence. SpaceX has also intertwined itself into the government more extensively, landing lucrative contracts this year for Trump’s missile defense program and the use of Musk’s Grok AI chatbot in the Pentagon.

Despite the immense and unprecedented scale of Musk’s political spending, his contributions this election are still only a tiny fraction of the centibillionaire’s overall assets.

How ‘sin bin’ for red light jumpers saves cyclists from being saddled with a fine

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 10:00:39 GMT

Police scheme in City of London offers errant cyclists a choice – watch a roadside safety video or pay a £50 penalty

When Aman cycled through a red light in the City of London this week, he was surprised when the police pulled him over. He was positively shocked when, instead of giving him a fine, officers took him into a gazebo to watch a bike safety film.

Aman was one of 30 cyclists caught in the first 20 minutes that morning, as part of a new scheme by City of London police to dissuade cyclists from running red lights.

Many concerned pedestrians have celebrated the time-out zone and, perhaps more surprisingly, cyclists have too.

The new pop-up scheme, called “stop, look, listen, change”, gives offending riders the chance to view an educational film about the dangers of red light jumping. Those caught by police who do not want to pay a £50 fine are taken to a “sin bin” by the roadside, where they watch testimonies from visually impaired road users.

“It is about taking that time away,” said Rob McTaggart, media and engagement manager at City of London police. “Time they didn’t stay waiting for the light is now the time they’re having to spend watching the video. It’s a bit of instant justice in that regard.”

As cyclists continued to be corralled into the time-out zone, McTaggart said the police team had noticed no difference between the numbers of red light runners on hired e-bikes versus those on regular bicycles.

When the sin bin was first launched two weeks ago, roughly 70 people were brought in within 90 minutes, McTaggart said. None of the halted riders opted to take the fine.

Watching the safety film, McTaggart said, was useful for spreading road education.

“Right now you can jump on a bike without any training whatsoever,” he said. “It’s about that understanding that just because you can go, it doesn’t mean you should go. We’re not going to enforce our way out of it.”

Sgt Stuart Ford, who helped create the scheme, said it was inspired by the Exchanging Places initiative, where cyclists are brought into large goods vehicles to understand risks like blind spots and difficulties in manoeuvring.

Ford said he was sympathetic to cyclists – “You can quote me: I like bikes” – but added that police “get more complaints than anything else in the city around cyclists jumping lights and their behaviour”. He added: “I’m afraid to say it but a lot of the time, the cyclist is the protagonist here.”

Ford collaborated with the National Federation of the Blind UK (NFBUK) to understand how vulnerable road users are affected by riders skipping lights or riding on the pavement.

Hyacinth Malcolm, who is fully blind, said: “I’m just lost for words as to why they [cyclists] are behaving the way they’re behaving.”

Malcolm said she had to rethink before going out for a daily coffee because of the risk of cyclists colliding with her.

Sarah Leadbetter, a disability activist with visual impairments, also said the footways were not safe for disabled people and that things were getting worse.

She said she relied on a cane, her guide dog and the rotating cone at pedestrian crossings – a small, unassuming plastic or metal cone which is attached to the underside of the push-button unit.

But, she said, she could not be certain of her safety because cyclists “suddenly come through the red light and go straight into you”.

McTaggart said the scheme had sparked discussions across the country and that there was a “huge appetite for what we’re doing here”. In the last week, pedestrians have complained of cyclists riding through the recently pedestrianised Oxford Street.

Sarah Gayton, street access campaign coordinator from NFBUK, commended the new education scheme, but hoped to see the fine increased to £300 and further action taken by the government. “Something has got to give,” she said. “We need designs that work for everybody.”

While some have pitted cyclists and pedestrians against each other, Tom Fyans, CEO of the charity London Cycling Campaign, said he also wanted to see more changes in London’s road designs to better suit all road users.

Standing at the busy junction of Old Street roundabout in the east of the capital, he said: “London isn’t designed for cycling, it’s getting better, but it’s designed for cars. What we need to see is far more cycle-friendly, pedestrian-friendly designs where the car is less important. Then you’ll see a much safer environment for everybody.”

On the new scheme, Fyans said his charity supported the measures over what he believed to be ineffective monetary penalties. He said: “Punishing cyclists with fines and criminal prosecutions, it doesn’t really work. But getting them to think about their impact on other road users – hearts and minds – is much better.”

Fyans said most cyclists do follow the Highway Code, but that a focus on bicycle users was “disproportionate” and a result of the rising number of bike users on London’s roads.

“I think there’s double standards quite often,” he said. “We’re not the biggest danger. It’s cars and speeding and drivers not paying attention that kill people on our roads. That’s the biggest challenge that needs addressing.”

Fyans, who works with Wheels for Wellbeing – a cycling disability group – said he understood the dangers for visually impaired pedestrians and wheelchair users.

But can relations between cyclists and pedestrians be improved? “Let’s address it, but let’s be proportionate about what the real problem is,” he said. “Cyclists are not really the main problem on the road when it comes to danger.”

‘Never big enough’: inside the booming penis enlargement industry

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 09:00:38 GMT

In a revealing documentary, a looksmaxxing-influenced world where ‘your social capital is tied to your appearance’ has led to more men wanting more

Man’s obsession with his member is a tale as old as time, writ large in sky-scraping edifices, in allusions that flatter (big dick energy) or offend (prick), in the countless artifacts across the ages that venerate male potency – a porn star’s description of Donald Trump’s “toadstool” penis. But it’s the booming intimate wellness industry – AKA the rash (ahem) of fillers, therapies and cosmetic procedures that have come into vogue since the little blue pill rocked the market – that most intrigued Daniel Lombroso, the esteemed documentarian who made his name at the Atlantic and the New Yorker dissecting male fragility.

“A lot of the stories I worked on at those places were kind of fringy subculture and oftentimes adjacent to white nationalism,” says Lombroso, who became aware of the rising demand for penile enhancement procedures while reporting on plastic surgery trends at the New Yorker. “I started calling all these practitioners. But to make an embedded film the way I do, you need someone who’s very open.”

A 2024 study of US Google searches noted an increase in interest in penile-enhancement injections from 2013 through 2022. Lombroso’s 90-minute film, Manhood, puts male self-esteem issues at the heart of the trend on a cold, chafing examination table. Our guide throughout is Bill Moore, a capitalist in scrubs who gives fresh meaning to the phrase bedside manner. We meet him at home, tongue-kissing a pet lap dog while snuggled up under the covers with his male partner. We behold the full splendor of his naked body, nipped and tucked in retreat from the ravages of time and his own unforgiving eye. “Nobody would suspect I’ve ever had anything done!” he says with bracing cluelessness.

We see Moore hawk outpatient penile enhancement procedures from his Dallas strip mall office for $15,000 and $20,000 a pop and tout the lowly glow-ups as career-changing, sex-life turbocharging, depression-curing – whatever patients need to hear to fork over the dough, really. “Everybody wants a boat that’s one foot longer,” one guy says as Moore sticks a long numbing needle into his nether regions. “The boat is never big enough.”

We see many of these patients (though customers is the better word, since, again, Moore is not a doctor), their faces more obscured than their ink-marked private parts. The inclination toward anonymity owes as much to the physical embarrassment Moore’s clientele bring into the room as to the irony of receiving this kind of care from an out-and-proud gay man – the megachurch pastor, the border patrol agent. It’s wild to see Moore act as a machismo whisperer to men who might perceive him as less than masculine, especially as he reflects on the guilt and fear of rejection he experienced before coming out to conservative Christian family members in the deep south (not that his mother having dementia doesn’t help).

Throughout the film, Lombroso manages to point out these and other paradoxes without casting judgment. “I’m not deep in the looksmaxxing world, but part of what Clavicular and those guys understand is that your social capital is tied to your appearance,” Lombroso says. “Does your penis size matter? Probably not. But there are all these stats about the huge percentage of American men who obsess over it, which was foreign to me. And it connects all these other things we talk about – like how many older American men don’t know how to make a best friend.”

None of Moore’s customers embodies male loneliness quite like Ruben, a father of five who is so desperate to enlarge his penis that he moves his family in with an ex to raise money for an enhancement procedure. “I have to sell my house this weekend, and I’m going to Bill after.” Lombroso recalls Ruben telling him in a phone call. “I was like, ‘OK, I’ll be there tomorrow.’ The only way to make a film like this, because I’m in New York and this was in Texas, was to fly out on a whim every time and just capture things as they happened.”

Ruben fills his days listening to Joe Rogan prattle on about the marginalization of manly men and spends nights performing at comedy open mics in bars to crickets – and zero friends in the crowd. His jokes about child abuse are as wince-inducing as the circular logic of upgrading his manhood. He believes it will help protect and provide for his family, even as it fundamentally destabilizes them. “He’s actually a very loving father,” Lombroso says. “A good guy. But he escapes into these worlds like many of us do, and I think eventually it caught up to him.”

Meanwhile, Lana, Ruben’s poor wife, overwhelmed by the succession of shocks his big dick sidequest has imposed on their lives, is pushed ever closer to divorce. “With very few exceptions, almost none of the partners in the movie wanted them to do this,” Lombroso says. “You see Lana kind of against it, but not taking too strong of a stance.”

But the film takes its strangest turn with David, a handsome young man who seeks out Moore’s help repairing the damage from an enhancement procedure botched by another dubious quasi-physician – Victor Loria, a gruff George Costanza-type who brags about growing up in a “connected” family (“We lived the Goodfellas life,” he says, wondering “when are we going to jail, basically”) and keeps a large malpractice insurance disclaimer nailed to his front office wall like Martin Luther’s 95 Theses. Loria is the film’s villain, in case that wasn’t clear.

David seems plucked from a casting call for the reality TV series Botched, a naive keen to hit control-Z after going under the knife too young and, perhaps, steer others away from rushing down that same path. But as his arc unfolds and his OnlyFans porn-acting past is revealed, it turns out he and Moore have more in common than just deeply religious parents who viewed homosexuality as an abomination. They share a bed, too – with Moore’s partner and the dog. That David risks permanent damage from this corrective procedure only heightens the stakes around the throuple bombshell.

Lombroso calls the effort to compel David’s participation in the film “one of the hardest acts of persuasion I’ve ever done. It took the entire film to convince him. We were going to use AI face replacement. But right around the rough-cut stage, when we realized he was the heartbeat of the story, we flew him into New York and showed him – and he loved it. Told his family everything. Now he’s touring with the film. It’s the best.”

Weaving between David’s feelgood story, Loria’s villainy and Ruben’s allegory is Moore – the honest broker who still lulls customers into thinking he’s a doctor, who travels to conferences to show actual doctors how to get in on the male-enhancement gold rush, and who sells his wares as an antidote to all the cosmetic procedures women can get to feel better about themselves. His massive house and impressive car collection speak more plainly to his motives in this space than his riffs to customers about self-esteem or the blarney about posting their post-op results on his company website.

Moore’s company PhalloFill, which specializes in “girth enhancement”, has expanded to 32 locations across the country. He hopes to make the procedure as common as Botox. “Bill tried to get me to have my penis enlarged,” says Lombroso. The thought never occurred. “I said my mom would never forgive me.”

But the great shame in Manhood isn’t that Moore and other practitioners in this charcoal gray area of medicine lavish their customers with patience and empathy. It’s that few see the tender treatment for what it is: gender-affirming care. “That’s why this movie has a very light touch,” Lombroso says. “So many of these things are funny and self-evident, especially to smart viewers. It’s fun to have these tough conversations and not tell people exactly how to feel in every moment.”

Manhood is now playing in select US cinemas with UK and Australia dates to be announced

Relying on AI is rotting your brain. But here’s what you can do about it

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 08:00:37 GMT

Each new tech product is designed to make our lives easier and keep us mindlessly entertained. Switch off: embrace discomfort – and boredom

Ever longed for your own personal assistant? In the ever quickening tech race, Meta has recently launched Muse, a new AI personal agent. Unlike traditional chatbots, this little AI tool will be able to fill out forms for you, organise calendars, pay bills and make reservations. Meta describes Muse as a personal agent “built for everyone”. The launch comes at a time when AI agents have been making headlines for hacking into government websites, public agencies and businesses. However, my immediate concern is a little closer to home.

I work as a psychologist, and I’m often talking to clients about lifestyle habits that lead to short-term gain but incur long-term pain. Our brains have a beautiful way of preferring the path of least resistance, of doing what is easiest to preserve our resources. And with the demands of modern life feeling so overwhelming for so many people, the urge to scroll after a long week or defer to a chatbot because you are exhausted is incredibly seducing.

Tech bros pushing their products on to us is nothing new (we all remember the metaverse, right?), but the message is now seemingly at fever pitch for mass AI adoption and how integral it is for human development. It is helpful to remind ourselves what we are being asked to give up, to whom and why, and to consider the potential risks before we hand over our precious data.

Some technology, such as large language models (LLMs) and social media that has an infinite scroll algorithm, seem to have a dose effect: too much reliance on this technology can lead to particular cognitive biases being activated, brain chemistry being depleted, moods and mental health being affected, and even neurological skills being atrophied, to name but a few of the documented risks.

Overusing artificial intelligence affects the brain and learning by bypassing the mental effort required to build deep neural connections, a process known as cognitive offloading. Frequent AI use fosters a passive acceptance of information, reducing the internal friction and inquiry that drive genuine curiosity and problem-solving. The brain depends on mental struggle and overcoming failure to rewire and strengthen our neural pathways. Bypassing that friction reduces our overall cognitive reserve over time.

Our tendency to favour or give greater credence to information supplied by technology (such as ChatGPT or Claude), and to ignore a manual source of information that provides contradictory information (a textbook, for example) even if it is correct, illustrates the phenomenon of automation bias. Automation complacency is closely linked – an overlapping concept that refers to the monitoring of technology with less frequency or vigilance because of a lower suspicion of error and a stronger belief in its accuracy, even when we know that LLMs often generate inaccurate answers.

Social media is designed to be so addictive because its business model relies on maximising user attention, while people give up their privacy because the immediate psychological rewards outweigh the abstract risk of data exposure. Most people say they value their privacy, but their behaviour says otherwise. This contradiction is known in behavioural economics as the privacy paradox.

Digital tools make life incredibly convenient – you can order a car with the touch of a button, a hot meal can be delivered to your door, and you can order and return outfits without ever exchanging a word with another person. People gladly trade their location data, contacts and browsing history in exchange for free maps, personalised shopping recommendations and seamless communication. Many individuals falsely believe that because they aren’t committing crimes, their data isn’t valuable. They don’t realise that aggregate data is used to manipulate purchasing habits, influence political votes and predict private life events.

Privacy policies are also intentionally long and confusing, and written in dense legal language that is inaccessible to the vast majority of users. Users face “consent fatigue” and simply click “Accept all” whenever the pesky window pops up while they are browsing because they feel they have no real choice.

There is a way out of the muck, though. Become more discerning about what information you share online; consider turning your location off unless you’re using navigation apps; reject cookies tracking you; hell, even start to poison your data if you really want to engage in some online anarchy. Does the online store you bought a T-shirt from once really need to know your full legal name and date of birth?

To avoid AI overreliance, you need to start introducing “friction” into your days – deliberate obstacles that break the automatic loop of seeking instant gratification. From a psychological perspective, AI is highly addictive because it eliminates this friction, offering immediate rewards with zero cognitive effort – and our brains need cognitive effort to remain sharp. Every time you try to work out a problem or read a book instead of the comments section, that is your brain doing a push-up.

If you’re struggling to rein in your social media or AI usage, a good way to start is by logging out of online sessions. Forcing yourself to manually type your credentials every time creates a massive psychological barrier. Also, try restricting your AI usage strictly to a desktop or laptop computer: removing ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini from your phone eliminates the urge to use it while walking, lying in bed or waiting in line. Scrolling on our phones or talking to a chatbot impedes much of the necessary mind-wandering time that our brains need to function at their best.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

When you feel the urge to ask an AI a question or have it write something for you, force yourself to wait about 30 minutes. Use this time to brainstorm, look at a book or simply sit with the problem. Often the urge passes or you solve the problem yourself. Commit to writing the first draft of any email, letter or presentation entirely by yourself. Embrace the discomfort of maybe getting things wrong. Instead of asking an AI for a recommendation or an explanation, ask a friend or colleague, or check a reputable website. The delay in waiting for a human response builds patience, and we need to practise this skill in order to retain it.

Dedicate specific hours of your day to completely screen-free activities. Read books, write with pen and paper or go for a walk without your phone and see how differently things feel for you after six weeks of consistent effort. Intentionally building friction into the frictionless online experience is hard – but I promise that your brain will thank you for it.

Carly Dober is a psychologist living and working in Melbourne
