Nigel’s ‘chiselled cheekbones’ make the news – Reform’s the Reformer, digested by John Crace

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 07:00:37 GMT

Editor, agony uncle, crossword compiler – he even interviews himself. Our sketchwriter finds there’s no end to Farage’s talents

Welcome to your new super, soaraway Reformer. The paper that aims to take you back to the 1950s with all the stories that the mainstream media don’t want you to read. Free to all patriots. And those who happen to have found a copy on the floor of the bus.

We are living in dangerous times. The chances of finding an immigrant ahead of you in the supermarket checkout queue have never been higher. Now more than ever you need a newspaper you can trust. One that isn’t afraid to tell you the truth about Broken Britain, and where you can find a grievance on every page. So let me introduce you to the Reformer team. There’s me, Nigel. I’m the editor-in-chief. And then there are seven or eight other nobodies whose names escape me. Here is my promise to you. If you are not fully satisfied with the Reformer in the first 100 days then I will sack all the people I have already forgotten.

by Nigel Farage, agriculture editor

A sensational report that has been hushed up by establishment figures linked to the European Union reveals that migrants are responsible for the failure of this summer’s harvest. The report, which has been leaked to the Reformer by a source who wishes to go by the name of Nigel, reveals that officials have tried to blame the crop failure on climate change. “It’s a total scandal,” said Nigel. “What’s been going on is that immigrants have been bringing their hot weather over to the UK with them in small boats. Global warming is a hoax perpetuated by leftwing politicians who want to encourage unlimited illegal immigration. But there’s no denying the facts. Back in the days when you seldom saw a black or brown face, British summers were much cooler. It’s time for everyone to start telling the truth.”

by Nigel Farage, home affairs editor

In one of the country’s biggest surveys of two families, the Reformer can exclusively report that white people much prefer to live next to white people. The families in question say their lives are being made a misery by having a man called Zia Yusuf as their next door neighbour. “It’s got nothing to do with Zia being a brown Muslim,” said Trevor Bloke. “I don’t care what colour or religion he is. What’s intolerable is that he is a deeply unpleasant person who goes out of his way to be rude to everyone. He thinks he owns the whole street. We all just wish he would leave. It’s doing my head in. I’m now on maximum Pip payments for my anxiety and I can no longer work.”

by Nigel Farage, consumer affairs editor

We’ve all had it. An email from someone who is clearly black. A telephone call from someone who is also clearly black. You know they are black because deep down, every black person wants to try to scam your bank account. Not a nice feeling when you’ve just been transferred £5m as a gift from a Thai-based billionaire. It’s the new something-for-nothing society. Say what you like about Oswald Mosley, but he would never have tolerated such behaviour. Now we just accept that immigrants are trying to take over our country. What is the easiest way to spot a Nigerian scammer? Just go to the House of Commons. There you will find the criminal mastermind. A woman called Kemi. She claims to be the leader of the opposition, but all she really wants are your credit card details.

Our features editor, Nigel Farage, interviews Nigel Farage. With additional reporting by Nigel Farage

It’s late afternoon in autumn. The sun streams through the window, its rays dancing off Nigel’s chiselled cheekbones. Nigel is at his most relaxed, mainly because he has just sent his valet, Richard Tice, to the off-licence for a third bottle of champagne. He smiles kindly at me. Reform are well ahead in the polls in third place and he is busy putting the finishing touches to his first speech as prime minister. “Tell me, Nigel,” I say. “Why is it that God has sent you down into the world to save Great Britain from all the illegal immigrants? Please can you also talk me through your magnificent byelection victory against a comedian with a bin on his head?”

Continues for another 1,500 words …

by Nigel Farage, football editor

In a stunning triumph for Brexit Britain, England’s Harry Kane has seen off countless other black and foreign footballers to be crowned the world’s best footballer in a glittering Ballon d’Or ceremony in London. Speaking exclusively to Reform, Kane’s best friend, Nigel Farage, said: “It’s about time a white Englishman won this. Harry would never have been able to do this if we hadn’t left the European Union. Just think what might have happened if footballers had freedom of movement. Harry might have ended up playing for some deadbeat team like Bayern Munich. Then he would have remained an unknown. So, really, Harry owes it all to me.”

by Nigel Farage, agony uncle

Dear Nigel, I recently got married and it should have been the happiest day of my life. Instead it became the worst. First, discovered that the man who had promised me he was rich enough to be worth divorcing my first husband for had only bought premium economy seats for our honeymoon in the US. Then I discovered that British Airways – a disgrace of a national carrier – had deliberately delayed the departure of our plane to maximise our inconvenience and then lost an item of luggage. My husband, Thicky Dicky, as I affectionately call him, yelled: “Don’t you know who I am?” and the person on the desk said: “We know exactly who you are.” Please help us seek redress. Dear Isabel, I am sorry to hear your distressing story. Please send me £80 and I will do a Cameo video calling for every foreign-looking baggage handler at Heathrow to be sacked. PS: BA is now owned by a private Spanish company.

by Nigel Farage, competitions’ editor

Call 0800 001 for Tommy Robinson who has recently been found guilty of harassing journalists in a massive miscarriage of justice.

Call 0800 002 for cheeky chappy Raheem Kassam, who asked the Guardian to correct a sketch that said he had deleted a racist tweet.

Calls will cost £5 plus normal charges. Winners will receive something worthless in bitcoin.

by Nigel Farage, literary editor

My Struggle, by Nigel Farage.

In which the Reform leader hilariously recounts the ways he made antisemitic remarks in front of Jewish boys at school on his way to becoming the most consequential politician of the last 200 years.

‘Almost as good as Liz Truss’s Bank Job’ – the Guardian

by Nigel Farage, transport editor

In the first of an ongoing series, Nigel Farage, discusses his favourite pothole and how he got it filled. “There was this fantastic pothole near my house in Kent,” he said. “We filled it up with loads of dead immigrants and the rubber of small boats the navy had sunk in the Channel.” Doing good with a smile on your face. by Nigel Farage, the Reformer’s eye-in-the-sky

Avoid travelling on the M6 north of Birmingham. Traffic is at a standstill due to too many foreigners driving on English roads. It’s a nightmare. And I can promise you that I will stop all immigrants driving when I become prime minister.

When you’re traduced, abused and gaslighted – believe me, Black History Month matters

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 06:00:38 GMT

There is always debate about the concept’s necessity and efficacy. But with nativists in their pomp, it’s good to focus on who we are and why

What forces shaped four generations of Black Britons? | The panel

Pity Black History Month UK, assailed on all sides. Those on the right seek to end the celebration on the basis that it amounts to special treatment for a group that doesn’t deserve it. History should be colour-blind: society should not differentiate, they say. We are not racist, we just want fairness. But often, they are – and they really don’t.

On the other side of the argument are the progressives, notably minority progressives, who say the idea of a month to consider Black history is demeaning because it should already have a year-round place in our teaching and consciousness. There is a further view that any beneficial effect the month once had has been diluted by unimaginative repetition and commercially motivated virtue signalling. Players taking the knee in the Premier League? Been there, done that: yawn!

I have long taken the glass-half-full approach. The ideal would be for Black history to be incorporated into the social and educational culture – and perhaps one day it will be. But in the meantime, I’ll take a mandated, month-long focus on the Black contribution to the way our society has evolved. And it seems very necessary this year, when the very notion of belonging in Britain and other major western countries has been so under attack.

A year in which we have clearly seen that a political party, with pretensions to lead the country, attracts activists with ugly racist and nativist views – at national and local level – with the same efficiency that magnets attract iron filings. Our expectations are different now. When transcripts of the things Reform folk say in private reach the public domain, the old-fashioned Tory dog-whistle seems comparatively quaint.

This is a year in which we have again seen the confidence and daring of those who cuddle close to pseudo-scientific theories asserting white superiority and black inferiority. The racial eugenicists are back from the fringes, championed down their venal path by Donald Trump, whose leadership of the free world gladhands nativists, targets Black officials and routinely belittles Black enemies as “low IQ”.

It’s been a year in which toxic politics and the mainstreaming of intolerance – against minorities of many categories – has led to racist unpleasantness on our streets and in the workplace. There is a snapshot from the Royal College of Nursing: racist abuse of NHS nurses – including use of the N-word – up 86% in the recent past. All part of what one NHS official called “a rising tide of racism”.

Another snapshot of the increasingly hostile environment is from parliament. What happened, via social media, when Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy posted a video in support of Black History Month? Vile abuse, of course: “Some of a kind that I had not necessarily seen in that volume before. I had people calling me the N-word, people telling me to eff-off and go back to where I came from, and people sending monkey photographs.”

Another snapshot from Chichester, Sussex, where a diverse group of actors recently went to perform A Midsummer Night’s Dream and were shamefully menaced. “I don’t know if I have witnessed and/or experienced as much racism, xenophobia and homophobia as I saw in those six weeks,” said the actor and comedian Munya Chawawa. Britain is a good place. The vast majority of our fellow citizens are decent and kind. But it’s now easy, far too easy, to unwittingly enter hostile territory.

So in years like this, when there are obvious, concerted, targeted, and well-funded attempts to undermine Black people and the Black experience – not least the targeting of books by Black authors by “anti woke” crusaders – it becomes more difficult to be sanguine about concepts such as Black History Month. It then becomes a good thing, perhaps an essential one, to remember and to highlight – if only over a calendar month – who we are, who has shaped us and how we have indisputably helped to shape Britain as a vibrant, diverse, first world power.

Today, at the end of this Black History Month, Guardian Opinion has asked Black Britons representing four generations to tell us how their own Black British identities have evolved, for we have been here long enough now to compare notes on the different stages of our lives on this island. A twentysomething sees the joy and pain of being here very differently to their elderly siblings, to their parents, to their grandparents.

after newsletter promotion

Call it reflection with a purpose. In a time like this, it seems more vital than ever to know who we were, who we are – and the foundations on which we all stand.

Hugh Muir is executive editor, Opinion

Winston Taylor Photo Portrait prize National Portrait Gallery, London, 5 November to 17 January The biggest photographic portraiture prize in the country has rebranded – you might know it better as the Taylor Wessing – but is otherwise unchanged: expect the finest photography by established pros and amateurs alike, featuring work from James Clifford Kent’s long-term project Yuma, including his portrait of aspiring pentathlete Neisser Yoel Gálvez Tabares.

Mad Bloomsbury Charleston Firle, Lewes, 4 November to 11 April Coinciding with the centenary of Virginia Woolf’s essay On Being Ill, this show looks at how the Bloomsbury Group – the likes of Roger Fry, Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant – dealt with ideas of madness, disability and neurodiversity.

Steve McQueen: Resistance Leeds Art Gallery, 6 November to 25 April Deeply moving documentation of how acts of resistance and rebellion have transformed the UK, all conceived by the brilliant Turner prize-winning artist and Oscar-winning director Steve McQueen.

The Nue Black Aesthetic Design Museum, London, 6 November to 8 August This display of more than 100 objects celebrates the black creatives who are shaping the future of design in Britain, including Taiba Akhuetie, Ini Archibong and Tejumola Adenuga. Eddy Frankel

Jordan Brookes Touring to 27 November; starts Bristol In 2019, the Surrey-raised standup expressed his long-held ambition to become “the existential Michael McIntyre”. In his excellent new show, The Part of You That’s Always Screaming, Brookes reaches those heights, with an unlikely combination of laugh-out-loud observational comedy and genuinely terrifying evocations of the abyss. Rachel Aroesti

Peanut Butter and Blueberries Leeds Playhouse, to 7 November After opening to strong reviews at Kiln theatre, Suhaiymah Manzoor-Khan’s thoughtful romcom transfers to Leeds. It’s about two university students and practising Muslims who move to London from the north, fall in love – but come up against harsh realities and rumbling racism. Miriam Gillinson

Hamlet Hail to the Thief Barbican theatre, London, to 23 January Steven Hoggett and Christine Jones’s music- and movement-infused Hamlet lands in London. The backbone of the show is Radiohead’s 2003 album Hail to the Thief, which frontman Thom Yorke has stripped back, rewired and threaded through the show with electrifying intent. MG

Luail: Nōs The Mac, Belfast, to 7 November Only formed two years ago, Luail is Ireland’s all-island national dance company, spanning Northern Ireland and the Republic. Their triple bill includes works by Belfast’s own Oona Doherty, Liz Roche and a classic from Akram Khan. Lyndsey Winship

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

Yaga Sky Atlantic, 31 October, 9pm Hudson Williams swaps romance for folklore fantasy as he follows his star-making turn in Heated Rivalry by playing two characters – the missing scion of a wealthy family and his odd housemate – in Kat Sandler’s adaptation of her own play. Could a witchy professor be the key to it all?

The Rise of the Rockstar Chef BBC Two/iPlayer, 5 November, 9pm The collective yearning for 2000s monoculture continues to be stoked with this documentary series about three of the decade’s rule-breaking, gamechanging chefs: Marco Pierre White, Heston Blumenthal and Gordon Ramsay (whose own production company is behind the show). Catnip for 00s nostalgists.

The Greatest Prime Video, 4 November Boxing dramas are a Hollywood mainstay, but this year the genre is migrating to the small screen with the likes of Fightland, A Thousand Blows and this new Muhammad Ali biopic, whose first season chronicles the vertiginous early 1960s rise of the then Cassius Clay (Jaalen Best).

Allies in Exile BBC Four/iPlayer, 3 November, 10pm BBC Four’s Storyville strand has long brought the world’s best feature-length documentaries to television. Now briefer films will be showcased too, starting with this one following the arduous journey of two Syrian film-makers through the UK’s asylum system. An Unknown Substance, about the poisoning of a Russian politician, airs afterwards. RA

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Switch 2; out 5 November The only major game challenging GTA 6 this month is this lively, stylish remake of Nintendo’s 1998 adventure classic, in which series hero Link becomes a time traveller to save the land of Hyrule from evil warlock Ganondorf. A nostalgic treat for the ages.

Where the Seeds Fall PS5, Switch 2, PC; out 5 November An intriguing action adventure which follows the human inhabitants of a vast tree as they set out to descend its branches and rediscover the land they were once forced to flee. Part mystical role-playing game, part climbing challenge. Keith Stuart

Ex:Re – Save As Out now With her band Daughter currently between albums, Elena Tonra returns to her Ex:Re solo moniker via this second album of textural alt-rock. Songs such as Sleep creep along with a hint of menace, while opener Radio Station spins off into a trippy road trip anthem.

DIIV – Zirp! Out now American alt-rock curios DIIV return with this AG Cook-produced fifth album. While steeped in their typically opaque, shoegazey textures, songs such as the pop-adjacent Kid and chunky lead single The Fountain dial up the melodies and frontman Zachary Cole Smith’s hushed vocals.

Chloe Qisha – Fantasize Out now After quitting a psychology degree for pop stardom, Malaysia-born, UK-based singer-songwriter Qisha found instant success with 2024’s sultry I Lied, I’m Sorry. She increases the sex chat on this debut album, specifically on gloriously overblown banger YDH, AKA young, dumb and horny.

The Big Moon – Forever Out now London quartet the Big Moon return with a sunnier take on their brand of indie rock. Created as an imaginary utopia after a period of upheaval in frontwoman Juliette Jackson’s life, songs such as the buoyant Three Things and Fun offer sweet solace. MC

Provocations Podcast For the numerically challenged, this new series hosted by Nihal Arthanayake is essential listening. Experts break down the big stories in finance, such as changes in lending policies and how technology can affect banking.

Interior Motives YouTube On the surface this video series looks like a flippant guessing game pairing pictures of domestic interiors with their owners, but it in fact uncovers fascinating truths about the ways our homes reveal our hidden selves.

Concorde: The Untold Story PBS America, 2 November, 8.40pm Encompassing everything from engineering breakthroughs to espionage and political hand-wringing, this film on the race to build the first supersonic airliner between Europe, the Soviet Union and the US makes for surprisingly engaging viewing. Ammar Kalia

The cursed cruise: how the dream of never-ending luxury at sea became a nightmare

The Guardian Sat, 31 Oct 2026 03:00:31 GMT

The MV Odyssey was billed as the ultimate escape from Donald Trump. Instead, the oil shock caused by his war has left passengers unceremoniously dumped in Cambodia

The idea was a never-ending retirement at sea, a continuous voyage around the globe. The promise to the passengers of the MV Odyssey cruise ship – many approaching the autumn of their lives – was that on the open seas they could cut loose from the troubles of the world. But the world had other ideas.

The end came in an announcement as stark as it was brief: they had seven hours to get off. They were going no further than Cambodia.

The Odyssey, owned by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, which had first set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024, made an explicit offer: Donald Trump had been re-elected to the White House, and this was a way for those ill-disposed to the president to enjoy a four-year “skip forward”.

For $319,998, a couple seeking such an escape could head off to the high seas for the length of a presidential term and come back from their journey to nowhere when the danger had passed – or not. For those who had simply had enough, there was a permanent residency option for a few hundred thousand more. Depending on the package, there were also monthly fees on top, which covered food, drinks, wifi, wellness programmes and room cleaning. They would have access to a pool, a pickleball court, a theatre, several bars and a gym. Exotic port destinations would be visited along the way.

It was by no means cheap – but the Odyssey was quite accurately billed as the “affordable” option for those interested in such a cocoon. The pioneer in the world of “residential ships”, a vessel called MS The World, offered apartments that typically ranged from $2m to $15m, with the pampered passengers getting to choose where it would go. For that experience, there was a waiting list.

The Odyssey was not in that league. Rather than built as a residential ship, it had previously been a traditional cruise liner named MS Braemar. Under that name, it had been turned away from several ports in the Caribbean during the pandemic when its passengers became ill. Cuba finally allowed it to dock, but the vessel never went into service as MS Braemar again. It was sold off by Fred Olsen cruises and adapted by its new owners. Villa Vie described the three-decade-old restructured vessel as “an intimate residential cruise ship offering a new way to live”.

At 642ft (196 metres) long, it was a relatively small ship, but at such prices, and with the world being held firmly at bay, what could go wrong? Neither the more than 200 passengers on the Odyssey nor its cruise operator foresaw the consequences of Trump’s war in Iran. The reality was, there was no escaping the US president.

On Tuesday, Villa Vie Residences issued a statement. It had run out of money owing to the soaring price of oil. Monthly fuel costs per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, placing it “under unsustainable financial pressure”, it announced.

“Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company said, explaining the slow death of its business model. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses.”

The Odyssey’s passengers were told to pack up their belongings before being transported on buses into the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand. “We are working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and temporary living arrangements, and are supporting residents, crew, and employees as we evaluate restructuring and recapitalisation alternatives over the next 60 days,” the company said.

“People were shell-shocked, numb, crying,” said one passenger, Kit Cassingham from the US, who spent two years on the ship with her husband, Randy. They had made their cabin into a home, putting down their own rugs and pictures on the wall. “People were angry. They were hysterical. They were sad … Disbelief,” she added. “I mean, that whole gamut of, what is it, the five stages of grief.”

Most of the passengers on the Odyssey were Americans, travelling with an international group of 156 crew members, including a ship’s doctor and two nurses. Many of the passengers were retired or digital nomads. One woman, Holly Hennessy, had been living happily with her cat, Captain, since the ship set sail two years ago.

One couple, Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin, who said they had bought a cabin with a 15-year guarantee, had been documenting their life at sea on YouTube, including the lead-up to the fateful announcement. The signs of financial distress had been apparent for weeks, they said.

“I’m Mr Super Positive, and I’ve felt really drained the last two months,” Bodin recounted in a video.

Footage from inside the ship’s lounge on the final night showed residents drinking, as rumours spread that their voyage might be over. Cruise ship staff had requested each passenger contribute $1,800 to ensure the ship had funds to travel to Bangkok.

The next day, the couple posted an update showing the inside of their cabin as a voice on the loudspeaker said the ship’s operator had “unfortunately” been “unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations”. An email was sent requesting that everyone disembark by 2pm.

“We knew the worst-case scenarios, but we didn’t think it would come to reality, which it did,” said Rina Cavazza, a pilates instructor from Brisbane, Australia.

Another passenger, Sherrie Cornett, wrote on Facebook that they were “dropped unceremoniously in the middle of town, left to our own devices”.

The company has not provided financial aid, passengers said, or even supplied a list of hotels in Cambodia. It later offered tickets for a charter flight to the US, although many passengers had already left. The company has been contacted for comment.

Kit and Randy Cassingham, now in a hotel in Cambodia, reflected on how life changed on the ship once the Iran war began, with ominous signs that the company was running out of money. The food quality began to deteriorate, and there was less of it; there were fewer excursions on shore, they said.

“I realised as soon as the strait of Hormuz incident came along, the energy of the ship changed,” Kit said. “I think it was because the ship management realised how much more this was going to cost. And then they were starting to do cutbacks that we weren’t aware of yet.”

Far from being a haven, the ship became a microcosm for the global economic turmoil. “I watched the world, and I don’t even pay attention to the news, but I’ve watched it just kind of crumble and shatter,” said Kit. “And I’m thinking, ‘it’s going to be difficult no matter what’.”

Randy said the writing had long been on the wall. They were, after all, on a ship that “drinks petrol by the metric tonne”. “You know, literally they’re buying 150 metric tonnes of fuel at a time,” he said. “We’re talking about $800,000 if we tried to get a full tank.”

While docked in Singapore in August, passengers had already been told the company did not have enough money to continue cruising, and several of the residents had contributed their own funds to get it moving again.

“Very few expect to get any money back because we know that they [the company] have been in terrible money problems from the beginning,” said Randy. Passengers had also passed a jar around for money for the crew, who are also stuck in Cambodia, he said.

Will the story of the Odyssey put people off cruises? It is unlikely, said Prof Andrew Coggins, an industry analyst, who pointed to an unprecedented boom since the end of the Covid pandemic, with global passengers reaching a historical high of 37.2 million in 2025.

Those numbers were in part because of “pent up demand” from those who had been unable to enjoy a cruise during the pandemic years, he said. But it was also the case, he said, that a cruise could offer good value for money. “You get to be pampered, you pack and unpack once, but you see different places, you eat better food than you would get at home, and then you have the romance of going to sea,” he said.

Residential ships such as the Odyssey were, though, in a very small category of their own, Coggins added. “The World is the only other one I know about and I think there are a couple that are trying to start up,” he said. But the finances are notoriously difficult. In 2023, a three-year cruise offered by Miray Cruises, with fares starting at $30,000 per person per year, including accommodation, food, drinks, laundry and even health care, was cancelled weeks before its due departure date owing to an inability to make the sums add up.

To survive choppy world markets, charges to the passengers have to be high, necessitating a concomitant level of luxury. “The World was actually built as a residential ship,” Coggins said. “The cabins or the state rooms are much bigger.”

Speaking earlier in the week, Mikael Petterson, who launched Villa Vie Residences in 2023, accepted that he was the “villain in the story” but said he was doing everything he could to help the stranded passengers. “Nobody that’s tried residential cruising has succeeded and we have gone further than anyone else,” he said. “But I think we would have been absolutely fine and we would have seen this through, if there was no Iran war.”

Back in Cambodia, Randy has been blogging to keep people updated while they work out what to do next. But he isn’t bitter. For all the promises, he said, all good things must come to an end. “Our message is that we’re not saying ‘poor me’. We know that people are having trouble, that they’re trying to put fuel in their cars, food in their mouths. And we’re very lucky. We’re not crying in our soup. So we are completely aware that we’re very lucky and that we’re going to land on our feet and be OK.”

Kit, a transformation coach, agreed. “This isn’t a pity party for us,” she said. “We actually want to say to people: ‘Live your dreams. Go for the gusto. Live life while you can because you don’t know how the adventure will turn out’.”

Five Great Reads: Elections, eugenics and high school reunions

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 21:21:44 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden and Miles Herbert

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend. It’s been a big week around the world, with results of three major elections taking many people by surprise. And away from the news cycle, our journalists have been asking some big questions – about birth, death, cocaine and why on earth anyone wants to go to a high school reunion.

At a time when populist leaders and the far right appear to be on the rise, Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s extraordinary victory on Sunday offered more than a glimmer of hope. As Jonathan Watts writes: it “should provide much needed inspiration and, more practically, a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections”.

So what do we do? Many analysts have put Lula’s win down to galvanising the streets and social media, and that campaign group – in particular the WhatsApp group ‘“Lula’s Army” – gathered up about 8% of the electorate by voting day. But that’s far from the only mechanism – political messaging, challenging tech giants, standing up for the environment and sheer determination are among some of the big takeaways here.

Notable quote: “Brazil has given the world a remarkable example of hope through action.”

How long will it take to read: Just under three minutes.

Further reading: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback; In Serbia, a new type of democracy is taking hold, and Europe is watching closely.

You may have noticed it – at the pub, with friends at dinner, or maybe even brazenly, out in the open – people shamelessly snorting cocaine. Journalist Robyn Vinter had been observing the uptick in drug use for some time and wanted to know “how did cocaine conquer Britain?” Here, she lays out some sobering findings.

From the middle class to the far right: “It is just staggering the amount and the accessibility of it,” a West Ham pub owner says. Wastewater analysis suggests people in England consumed 123,000kg of cocaine in 2024-25, a rise of 26% since 2021. And the class A drug, once firmly associated with middle classes, has moved around the demographics, including now appearing to be a drug of choice for the far right.

Fuelling crime: The Guardian’s investigation found a 10% rise in recorded crimes where the drug was mentioned since 2019, and Home Office figures sent to the Guardian show nearly six in 10 police drug tests carried out on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine between July 2025 and June this year.

How long will it take to read: Three and a quarter minutes.

Further reading: ‘I thought the baby would change him’: the women whose pregnancies are blighted by domestic abuse.

Most people do their best to avoid talking about death. But as of now, science has yet to find a cure for the affliction that comes for us all. So why the social taboo? In the final instalment of the Guardian’s series about death – Memento mori – Meaghan O’Connell documents the journey her mother took after deciding she wanted to donate her body to science. O’Connell wasn’t prepared for what came next but says, “In some ways, it was absolutely perfect”.

Why would you donate your body to science? Demand for medical cadavers far outstrips supply. More than 25,000 Americans donate their bodies for research purposes after their death but, according to Tamara Ostervoss, director of Oregon Health & Science University’s (OHSU) body donation program, “it remains an unpopular choice”. For medical students, the ability to practise procedures on the real thing versus a human model is like “the difference between a flight simulator and piloting an airplane”.

The emotional cost: Not knowing exactly what happened to her mother’s body weighed on O’Connell’s mind. But she says going down the donation route also offered an element of simplicity. No being upsold by funeral directors, no grief-stricken decisions about embalming, or what goes on the gravestone. Just a quick phone call and a short physical assessment, then “voilà, off my mom went to fulfil her destiny”, O’Connell says.

Notable quote: “Was it odd to feel jubilant on the same day I watched my mother take her final breath”? – O’Connell, after learning her mother’s body was accepted as a medical cadaver.

A memorial of sorts: After fulfilling her mother’s posthumous wishes, O’Connell was invited to a “body ceremony”, a 25-year tradition where students from OHSU memorialise body donors and their families. Two students offered their thanks through an aerial yoga routine; others sang Taylor Swift. O’Connell was looking for closure but all this offered was amusement.

How long will it take to read: Just under six minutes.

Further reading: More from the Guardian’s Memento mori series.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

It may be Greek for “good birth” but the term eugenics has, for the past century at least, been seen as a racist and repulsive movement. But whether you like it or not, eugenics is back in a new guise, this time by companies offering prospective parents the problematic promise of delivering the “best baby”. Jan Grue, who has a form of spinal muscular atrophy, considers the ethical implications.

What is ‘the best’? Adverts on the New York City subway offer embryo scans for every genetic disorder under the sun, eye and hair colour, and for traits ranging from strength and longevity to insomnia and male pattern baldness. Whether the promises are credible is one thing but a more important one might be: what is “valuable and worthless in a human life?”

Notable quote: “I think it is crucial to acknowledge disability as part of human variation. In treating ever more traits and qualities as things to be measured, ranked and diagnosed, we are doing the opposite – turning variation itself into something like disability.”

How long will it take to read: Eight minutes.

Further reading: The girl with a will to live: the love, hope and pain of raising Elsie – my one in 163 million daughter.

High school reunions are notoriously awkward; just ask Romy and Michele. While some look forward to reconnecting with friends, others see reliving the past as “a potential hellscape”. But can you go in prepared? The Guardian asked a mix of experts and reunion-goers for their advice on tackling one of life’s most fraught social situations.

Should you even go? Psychologist and author Amberley Meredith says it is normal to ruminate over reunions, and you should expect to not be the only one with existential questions about your place in life. If you are on the fence, experts say avoid making a pros and cons list – instead, just focus on the potential positives.

The dos and don’ts: Still feeling nervous before the big day? Etiquette expert Jodie Bache-Mclean says you can come prepared with a few conversation starters and a bit of background on your past classmates, but while “a little homework is helpful; a full social media investigation is not”. What about alcohol? Should you drink to calm your nerves? “A glass of wine may help, four may not!” Bache-Mclean says.

How long will it take to read: Just under four minutes.

Further reading: Why are class reunions so terrifying? And are they even good for us?

The Guardian view on Labour’s fiscal devolution: the future of Burnhamism will play out in municipal England

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 17:56:11 GMT

Replacing government grants with revenue streams from taxation will not in itself reduce regional inequalities. But the political implications are radical

Following Wednesday’s budget, the Treasury minister, Torsten Bell, was challenged by the BBC’s Evan Davis on whether its modest series of “breathing space” measures could truly be said to have ended “40 years of neoliberalism”. This line of questioning is becoming a familiar one. Andy Burnham’s ringing declaration of long-term intent is now being regularly deployed by commentators to suggest an emerging gulf between rhetoric and action.

Mr Bell’s response was a good one. Recalling how “Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s hugely hollowed out local government [and] tried to emasculate our big cities”, he called the fiscal devolution roadmap unveiled in the budget a step change and a really big deal. From 2028, mayoral strategic authorities will for the first time receive a share of income tax receipts, and from next year they will be allocated 20% of business rates revenue. That figure will potentially rise to 100% by the end of the decade, while a new overnight visitors levy will add another local income stream.

These are structural changes that will transform the relationship between local government and a notoriously overly centralised state. They have so far failed to generate anything like the coverage that accompanied the Conservatives’ levelling-up programme, which degenerated into a tawdry pork barrel exercise for “red wall” Tory MPs. But it is on this municipal terrain that Mr Burnham’s aspiration to rebalance the country, reduce regional inequality and “roll back” the 80s will be played out.

Replacing government grants with guaranteed income streams will give strategic authorities more certainty over future revenue – against which they will be able to borrow – and the ability to plan flexibly according to locally set priorities. The devil will be in details to be announced in next year’s spending review, in particular regarding mechanisms to ensure poorer areas with a smaller tax base do not lose out. But the roadmap is a first move towards restoring proper agency to local authorities struggling to cope with the disastrous twin legacy of deindustrialisation and austerity.

Further steps will need to be taken if, as the prime minister intends, local government is to drive “good growth” that improves general living standards and prospects throughout communities. As the Local Government Association pointed out, cash-strapped councils on the frontline face a £7bn funding gap by 2028-29, and are in a perennial struggle merely to meet their statutory obligations on social care. Strategic authorities need to be given the capacity to gradually reassume control of priorities in sectors such as care, housing and the utilities. That will take time and investment at scale in forms of community provision that can offer an alternative to a model in which services have been outsourced and profits offshored.

Devolution will not of itself reduce inequalities or restore a degraded public realm. But this week’s budget measures began the necessary process of rewiring British politics. Mr Burnham’s core conviction is that radical devolution can redistribute power to those who know their own community best, and allow councils to rebalance the relationship between the public and the private sector. After decades in which the latter has profited hugely from calling nearly all the shots, that is very much the right direction of travel. The starting gun has been fired in a process that can lead to a genuine renaissance of municipal England.

The Guardian view on 50 years of The Selfish Gene: flawed, outdated, yet still a model of truly popular science writing

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 17:56:07 GMT

Richard Dawkins’ first work has thrilled fans and frustrated critics for five decades. The science has moved on, but any writer looking to supplant its place must learn its lessons

Richard Dawkins’ The Selfish Gene was not predicted to be a success. Its initial print run, published this week in 1976, was just 5,000. It went on to sell millions, and is perhaps the most influential work of pop-science ever. For 50 years, it has been the go-to resource for the layperson seeking to understand evolution.

What accounts for its enduring power? Prof Dawkins’ central claim, that “we are survival machines – robot vehicles blindly programmed to preserve the selfish molecules known as genes” was provocative, stripping the messy stuff of human and other life down to a simple law. And yet the book is primarily concerned with proving that complex, selfless behaviour such as altruism in animals can emerge from these basic “selfish” drives, satisfyingly resolving an apparent paradox. Prof Dawkins – a zoologist by training – also succeeded in conjuring entertaining, vividly drawn vignettes of the lives of animals, from lions and ants to hawks and honeybees, to make his points.

Nevertheless, 50th anniversary celebrations have been somewhat muted. In an essay in the journal Nature, the historian of science Nathaniel Comfort suggests there is something almost malign about The Selfish Gene’s commitment to a simple kind of determinism.

There is certainly that and more to take issue with. Prof Dawkins fought publicly with eminent biologists such as Stephen Jay Gould about whether genes were the primary target of natural selection, rather than the individual organism or group – a legitimate clash between differing theories that was mirrored in the scientific literature. More quietly and damningly, many biologists bemoan the way the book seems to assume every trait is some kind of adaptation – hardly the textbook view, which has long recognised the role of randomness and chance in evolution. It also focuses almost exclusively on animals. And it is hard to read Prof Dawkins fresh, without the knowledge that the later books are repetitive and that his comments outside his field – including on feminism, disability and describing Islam as “the greatest force for evil in the world today” in 2013 – don’t suggest a great or sensitive thinker.

Perhaps the best way to read The Selfish Gene is alongside its critics. Prof Dawkins’ Oxford tutor Arthur Cain called it a young man’s book, pointedly suggesting that the author would come to regret or recant his most bombastic claims. Prof Dawkins never really did, but his intransigence brought out the best in his critics, from Prof Gould to Richard Lewontin or Hilary and Steven Rose. Read all together, it makes for a full and rollicking picture of modern evolutionary debate

It also remains a model of style. The philosopher John Dupré, no fan of Prof Dawkins’ scientific thought, nonetheless calls it a paradigmatic example of successful popular science writing. The book works on this level because it takes a point of view in a live scientific debate, and argues its side with engaging dash and zeal. Prof Dawkins is often too polemical, but most science writing tends to be heavily didactic, with little argument or rhetorical flourish. And it is possible to both inform and persuade: Sean Carroll’s Endless Forms Most Beautiful and Nick Lane’s The Vital Question take a similarly clear, provocative line.

The science has moved on, and The Selfish Gene has flaws. But any writer looking to supplant its place in the public imagination with a more capacious vision of evolution must reckon with the reasons for its long-running success. For all its problems, it remains a model of its genre.

This budget fails to live up to Andy Burnham’s grand rhetoric

The Guardian Fri, 30 Oct 2026 17:11:06 GMT

Caitlin Boswell of Tax Justice UK and others on what Aditya Chakrabortty described as a ‘Martin Lewis budget’

Aditya Chakrabortty was spot-on in his analysis of John Healey’s budget (Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budget, 28 October). It was a drop in the ocean of what is needed to bring about the scale of change this country needs and, importantly, was promised by Andy Burnham.

As the affordability crisis rages on, people may feel some relief at the small cost of living measures announced for households and businesses. But when we’ve been told we’ll get a wholesale reset and an end to neoliberalism, 4p off the price of gherkins and a temporary tiny bank tax isn’t going to cut it.

So, what’s the solution? The government must fairly tax the vast fortunes of the richest people and corporations, left mostly untouched. Recouping the massive wealth and profits siphoned off to shady tax havens each year, equalising how the tax system treats income from wealth and work, and building HMRC’s capacity to properly measure and collect tax from the very richest would raise tens of billions to help pay for targeted, meaningful cost of living support and Burnham’s ambitious plans to fix the housing crisis, fund social care and devolve power and wealth to every region.

Reforming capital gains tax – a proposal supported by members of his own party – would make things fairer and raise around £19.7bn a year, enough to build 90,000 new council homes (the number needed each year to end the housing crisis) and train 128,000 new NHS nurses.

This government cannot survive much longer on vibes alone, and Labour is already on its last chance. Burnham must use his 10-year plan and spending review to lay out a proper roadmap to genuinely improve lives and transform the country, otherwise he risks being remembered for gherkins, which isn’t much better than Liz Truss’s lettuce. Caitlin Boswell Deputy director, external affairs, Tax Justice UK

Aditya Chakrabortty is right to say that Andy Burnham’s grand rhetoric and romantic notions need to be translated into a bold programme of change. Unless this government tackles income and wealth inequality seriously, people’s anger will unceremoniously sweep it from office at the next election. Hugh Firth Newcastle upon Tyne

Living in a rented band B property, my “breathing space” was short-lived on budget day. The £100 energy payment announced by the chancellor will be entirely swallowed up by Northern Energy’s own announcement via email at 5pm the same day: “a temporary fuel surcharge of £17 per delivery will be applied to LPG deliveries as from your next delivery”.

Although this is “temporary”, customers are warned that the need to cover the elevated fuel costs is likely to remain for the foreseeable future. I had six deliveries of LPG last year – do the maths. Juliet Lunn Cockermouth, Cumbria

Once again, tax thresholds are frozen. What a missed opportunity. It would have been so easy to raise the threshold in line with the state pension, and keep them aligned. This simple mechanism would ensure that those with no other income pay no tax, and keep a little more money in the pockets of working people and others on very low incomes. Maybe next year? Jack Kenward South Molton, North Devon

Although abolishing the standing charge is something I agree with, presumably one of the groups that will benefit are second (and third) home owners. This includes approximately 177 MPs, Airbnb properties and holiday lets. John Victor Davies Hastings, East Sussex

I know that things are tight, but could the government not have funded a red box with “CR III” painted on it rather than the “ER II” sported by Mr Healey? Robert Bowden Bristol

‘We Are Coming From Hell’: A Ukrainian City’s Evacuees Tell Survival Stories

The New York Times October 31, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Safely out of Oleshky after enduring years in the combat zone and a harrowing 24-hour journey, weary civilians reunited with family and friends.

Safely out of Oleshky after enduring years in the combat zone and a harrowing 24-hour journey, weary civilians reunited with family and friends.

Ukrainians evacuated from the frontline town of Oleshky, Ukraine, on Saturday. Credit...

Supported by

By Carlotta Gall and Oleksandr Chubko

Photographs by David Guttenfelder

Reporting from northern Ukraine, near the border with Belarus

A rasping scream rang out as a teenager recognized her father. He was one of the hundreds of people who had escaped: years of Russian occupation, months of hunger under a deadly drone war, and then a truce backed by a first lady and the pope and an odyssey back to their loved ones.

A fleet of buses brought the evacuees from the embattled Ukrainian city of Oleshky out of the war zone on Saturday, the passengers waving and wiping tears as they swung into the parking lot and ended their journey back.

Draped in Ukrainian flags, the evacuees stepped down gingerly from the buses, weary after a 24-hour journey, which took them from the front line and through Russia and Belarus before returning to Ukraine. Many were gaunt from living months with little food, dark rings round their eyes from lack of sleep.

“We are coming from hell,” said Oleksandr Styopin, 75, lighting a cigarette. “It’s a kill zone there.”

Trapped close to the front line, with Russian soldiers living among them, the residents of Oleshky have been living under occupation for more than four years since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

Their predicament worsened this year, when Ukraine drastically increased its drone attacks on Russian forces in the area, said Mr. Styopin, a retired electrical engineer.

The roads came under fire and supplies dried up as fewer and fewer drivers dared to risk the trip. Some residents tried to drive to the nearby town of Radensk to buy provisions, but many were killed on the road when drones struck their vehicles, he said.

Bodies of Russian soldiers were left lying in the road, he said, since no one would risk collecting them.

Mr. Styopin would push his bike to a local store once in a while and stock up on as much food as he could carry. Once he passed the burned body of a girl beside her own bicycle, he said. “That was from a mine, I think,” he said.

Some drones hovered close as if to look at him, and then let him be, he said.

But they hunted down the Russian soldiers relentlessly, he said.

“They pinned them down so hard, they could not step out of the building,” he said of the Russian soldiers. A group of soldiers had moved into an apartment in his building, he said.

Some of the evacuees described the hardships they endured with a lightness that verged on humor as they recalled destruction and loss.

“There was no electricity and no water. Then the house got bombed. Then the food ran out,” said Halyna Lohvynovska, 65.

“We got used to everything,” her husband, Ivan Lohvynosky, said with a smile. Their house was hit several times, he said. “When something fell on your head, you moved to another room. When the house was destroyed more, you moved house.”

There were some young families and even young children among those evacuated.

Vladyslav, 24, came out with his sister and mother. Thin and watchful, he declined to give his surname for security, he said.

The family had stayed in Oleshky because they had been scared that the Russian authorities would prevent him from leaving; he was of the age to be drafted into the military in Ukraine.

They survived by growing vegetables in their garden and raising a few animals, he said.

To some of their fellow evacuees, that was good fortune.

“The past two years were terrible. We had nothing to eat,” said Anatolii Honcharov, 53. His 61-year-old brother, Valerii, had not heard from him for three years because communications were so bad. Only families who lived close to the river could pick up a Ukrainian cellphone signal.

Things became so dangerous in recent months, Mr. Styopin said, that he did not dare leave his apartment. He sat listening to the radio, a cigarette permanently clamped between his teeth, he said.

His wife, who left at the onset of the full-scale invasion in 2022, joining their son in Queens, New York, called him many times urging him to leave.

“If I try to leave, I will step on a mine,” he told her.

“For the last two months I was living with a drone above my head,” he added. “It’s more than fear,” he said, “it’s an internal dread that’s always present inside you.”

But the plight of Oleshky drew international attention, helping to push for a rare localized truce in a war where each side has pressed for every advantage. Pope Leo XIV, just three days after surgery for lung cancer, spoke with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and called for a cease-fire to evacuate the city, and then the American first lady, Melania Trump, announced a local truce last Friday.

When the cease-fire began on Tuesday, Russian soldiers appeared to demine the roads and clear the streets of the dead.

“The Russians cleared up everything,” Mr. Styopin said. “There was a destroyed armored personnel carrier with bodies inside,” he added. “There was a body in pieces, half here and half there. The Russian took them all away.”

Many residents did not trust the news of a humanitarian convoy. Several said they had tried to leave in convoys early in the war only to retreat after the vehicles came under fire.

But Mr. Styopin packed his things. Then, on Friday morning as he was leaving his home, a blast knocked him back. During the Russians’ demining an explosion went off, and shrapnel ripped into his suitcase, he said.

He went back to find another case and then rushed through heavy rain for more than a mile to the bus.

“My heart was burning,” he said. “I thought I would crawl there in order to leave.”

Vladyslav said he and his family feared to trust that they would truly escape.

“These last four days, we didn’t believe we would make it out,” he said. “We thought it was just another provocation — they would declare a cease-fire and then blow us up along the way,” he explained. “We were terrified, but we went anyway, because there might not be another chance.”

Many of the evacuees and their families said they were surprised at the scale of the seriousness of the operation to get them to safety, and said it raised hopes for an end to the war.

Standing in the parking lot looking around, Vladyslav still looked uncertain.

“I can’t quite make sense of my mood yet,” he said. “Happiness. Being back under my own flag, hearing my own language.”

Carlotta Gall is a senior correspondent, covering the war in Ukraine.

David Guttenfelder is a Times visual journalist based in Minneapolis.

Susan Collins Is Always Keeping Score

The New York Times October 31, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

House

Governor

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

The long-serving senator has delivered millions of dollars to every corner of her state. But in Maine, people say, it’s best to avoid getting on her bad side.

By Michael Kruse and Lisa Lerer

Jordan Wood, a Democrat from Lewiston, Maine, was the first person to announce a 2026 campaign challenge to Senator Susan Collins, and he made a priority of winning the endorsement of the mayor of his hometown. He met with Mayor Carl Sheline, a fellow Democrat, in his office and over drinks at a local Italian restaurant. They had a series of phone calls. But ultimately Mr. Sheline declined to back him.

Ms. Collins, the longtime Republican incumbent, was not in the room, at the bar, or on the line.

But she had made her presence known.

Mr. Sheline had various reasons for withholding his support, he said in an interview. Among them, he acknowledged, were a housing project, a food distribution center, and a mill museum in Lewiston. Ms. Collins had helped with the finances for all of them.

“It’s just an environment of possible retribution,” Mr. Wood said. “It is that fear she instills.”

Over nearly 30 years, Ms. Collins, a self-styled moderate in a familiar Maine mold, has cultivated a public persona as a workhorse and a fastidious maestro of constituent services and pork-barrel disbursements, using her Washington know-how to get her constituents what they need.

But for just as long, her detractors say, she has managed to mostly mask another reality. “The gentlewoman from Maine,” as her colleagues say on the Senate floor, is a formidable power broker who can play a fierce brand of politics with a how-dare-you air. According to more than 40 interviews with Republicans and Democrats in Maine politics, former staff, colleagues and longtime observers, Ms. Collins has wielded power not so much as a Yankee Republican but as a shrewd machine politician.

“It’s almost like Tammany Hall,” said Amy Fried, a retired political scientist from the University of Maine. “You’re going to get this benefit here if you vote for me.”

Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist and former aide to Ms. Collins, did not disagree.

“That’s exactly what it is,” he said. “She’s openly discussing the fact that Maine is going to be set back if she’s not in that position,” he added. “It puts people in the position of very clearly understanding that voting against her is a vote against their own well-being.”

Ms. Collins’s staff stresses that she has worked to bring money back to all communities in Maine — regardless of whether they support her.

Annie Clark, a longtime aide to Ms. Collins, provided The New York Times an exhaustive list of projects, from Orono and Ogunquit to Belfast and Blue Hill, for which the senator had secured funding since 2021. The senator got $234 million for 96 projects in Cumberland and Knox counties — the only two counties she lost in 2020. In Portland, where she received just 21 percent of the vote: $51.2 million for 28 projects.

“Senator Collins has been extraordinarily effective,” said Blake Kernen, a spokeswoman for Ms. Collins. “She works tirelessly to deliver results for the state, meets with thousands of Mainers every year, and she secures billions of dollars for communities in all of Maine’s 16 counties whether they vote for her or not.”

Ms. Collins, 73, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, is running for re-election this fall the way she always has — no clickbait TikTok posts or big, rah-rah rallies, but a relentless focus on stops in small towns where she has brought home federal dollars for boat landings, emergency operations centers and wastewater treatment facilities.

At her campaign events, supporters hold signs that underscore the point she is trying to make: “Thank You, Susan.”

In debates this month with her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, a former logger and Maine Senate president, Ms. Collins was unsubtle about the crux of the deal.

“In the past five years I’ve secured $1.5 billion for properties all over the state,” she said.

She was even more blunt in a radio interview this week, citing 672 projects that she had secured across the state, including 45 new fire stations.

“All that goes away,” she said, “if Troy were to be elected.”

Her whole life has been a lesson in the accrual and use of power.

Ms. Collins was born and raised in Caribou in Aroostook County, the state’s most northern terrain. The Collinses didn’t just own and run the local lumber company and hardware store. They were politicos too.

“My parents,” Ms. Collins told The New York Times this past summer, “both served as mayor of Caribou. My father was in the State Senate, my grandfather, great-grandfather served in the state legislature.”

Her parents were supporters of William S. Cohen when he ran for Congress in 1972 and beyond, and Ms. Collins was a driver and an intern for Mr. Cohen when she was in college at St. Lawrence University in Canton, N. Y. After she graduated, she was hired as an aide and was on his staff for a dozen years, known by her colleagues and peers as a meticulous note-taker and over-preparer.

She ran for governor in 1994 when she was 41 and lost. She ran for Senate in 1996 and won. She said she would serve no more than two terms but then ran for re-election in 2002, 2008, 2014 and 2020.

Over the course of her three decades in the Senate, drafting off the renown of her cordial, consensus-building Maine forebears like Mr. Cohen and Senator George Mitchell, Ms. Collins has emphasized her image as the last of a vanishing breed. She has bucked her party, and in particular President Trump, more than enough to frustrate many Republicans — albeit not nearly enough to satisfy most Democrats.

“I’m consistently sought out by both sides for cosponsorship of bills,” she told The Times in her first year in the Senate. “I have a lot of power — I like that.”

Behind closed doors, though, she long has had a reputation as a lone wolf.

Her relationship with Olympia Snowe, the Republican who was elected to the Senate from Maine two years before Ms. Collins and served three terms, was marked by rivalries and perceived slights, according to former aides to Maine lawmakers on Capitol Hill. Publicly, they issued joint statements and often voted together. Privately, the relationship was far more fraught, as is sometimes the case when a state is represented by two senators of the same party.

“She was just hypersensitive to Olympia getting more credit than she was,” said Kurt Bardella, a former press secretary for Ms. Snowe.

“It was very machine-politicky: ‘I am owed a certain level of stature and respect,’” Mr. Bardella recalled.

Ms. Collins has a bristly relationship with Angus King, the independent junior senator from Maine, who defeated her in the governor’s race in 1994 and succeeded Ms. Snowe in 2013. While they exchange occasional text messages, the two haven’t spoken in months, according to people familiar with their communications who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private matters. They last texted Oct. 12, according to Ms. Clark. Aides in Mr. King’s office often are instructed to let Ms. Collins get the lion’s share of the credit, they said, if that’s what it takes to get a policy initiative accomplished.

When Mr. Wood announced his candidacy for Senate, he thought he knew what he needed to know about Ms. Collins. His campaign quickly became a window into what he did not know.

Elected Democrats and political donors, Mr. Wood said, told him Ms. Collins reviewed the lists of who gives more than $1,000 to whom — and kept score.

“People told me they could not give me money because they knew she would look at the report,” he said. “Democrats.”

Ms. Clark, the spokeswoman for Ms. Collins, said the senator does not review such lists.

Ultimately, Mr. Wood’s fledgling campaign was overwhelmed by the unexpected rise of Graham Platner, whose subsequent fall precipitated Mr. Jackson’s selection as the Democratic nominee. Still, he got an eye-opening tutorial in the sway of his state’s senior senator.

Last November, when he ended his Senate campaign and switched to run instead for the Maine’s Second Congressional District, Mr. Wood couldn’t help but notice the difference.

This time, Mr. Sheline, the Lewiston mayor, endorsed him right away.

This month, politicking her way through the annual fall fair in Fryeburg, Maine, Ms. Collins walked from a cattle auction to a livestock barn, putting up with out-of-town press asking her questions about the president while trying to steer clear of manure.

“I know you don’t like me,” she told one reporter, “but don’t make me walk through shit.”

She quickly changed the subject — to $38 million in federal aid for heating oil.

“I was delighted,” she said, “that I was successful in expediting the funding.”

That matters a lot, said Mr. Dutson, the senator’s former aide.

“Federal money is incredibly important up here,” he said. “The choice a lot of people are facing right now is: OK, well, I can listen to the noise out of Washington or what my party tells me to do — or I can support the lady who got me a new fire truck in my 500-person town.”

In the past few weeks in Maine, as Mr. Jackson has campaigned in front of large, loud crowds alongside progressive megastars such as Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, Ms. Collins has brandished a shovel at a groundbreaking at a boat landing in Orrington and attended a grand opening of a wastewater facility in Windham.

And in the stretch run of the race, people all over the state have received targeted text messages from her campaign.

“Susan Collins delivered $33 million for Knox County …”

“Susan Collins has delivered nearly $59 million for the City of Bangor …”

“Susan Collins is delivering real results across Kennebec County — 50 projects totaling more than $109.3 million …”

Her supporters say it’s why they trust her and one of the main reasons she should be re-elected.

“What she produces is real — it’s tactile,” said Chris Gardner, the executive director of the Eastport Port Authority, who has appeared in an ad for Ms. Collins. “We should be thankful.”

Kevin Raye, a former Maine Senate president and Ms. Snowe’s former longtime chief of staff, is an anti-Trump former Republican who is now an independent — “rooting,” he said, for Democrats to take control of Congress. “But I’m in the Collins camp,” Mr. Raye said, citing her record of bipartisanship. “The thought of replacing her with a reliable partisan vote, no matter the party,” he said, “is so the wrong direction for America.”

But the calculation, her critics counter, is more complicated. Her vote to advance Mr. Trump’s big domestic policy bill before she ultimately voted against it, her initial votes against setting congressional limits to military actions in Iran followed by eventual votes to do just that — all of it costs her constituents, they say, contributing to cuts to health care and higher prices for fuel, food and more. Many remain furious about her vote to put Brett Kavanaugh on the Supreme Court, a move that ultimately led to the end of Roe v. Wade.

“She’s very good at cutting ribbons,” Betsy Sweet, a Democrat who ran unsuccessfully for governor in 2018 and for Senate in 2020 against Ms. Collins. “She’s also really good at cutting your health care.”

Moreover, as she works to fend off her challenger in a tough year for Republicans, Ms. Collins’s sharp political style has been apparent not just to political insiders but to voters as well.

In a recent interview with Politico, Ms. Collins was startlingly cutting about her opponent.

“I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin,” she said. “I don’t know whether people know that or not.” They did now.

“This is a Susan people haven’t seen,” said Tony Payne, the executive director of the Republican Party of Maine in the 1970s who became an independent after the rise of Mr. Trump and a longtime critic of Ms. Collins. “This is the peeling off of the veneer.”

Last week, the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing the Republican Party’s candidates, aired a radio ad about Mr. Jackson with a crude jingle alluding to the relationship. After it had made the rounds, Ms. Collins told reporters she “had nothing to do with that ad,” saying it should be removed from the air.

This week, Ms. Collins’s campaign has been airing a TV ad that many in Maine considered elitist. “We’re not talking about a cord of wood here, we’re talking about the U. S. Senate, and Troy doesn’t have the tools he needs to be effective,” Bill Green, a well-known, retired local sportscaster, says in the ad.

“For more than 30 years, Susan Collins has carefully concealed her intrinsic arrogance,” Sam Patten wrote in a post on social media castigating the ad. (Mr. Patten, a former aide to Ms. Collins, pleaded guilty during the first Trump administration to failing to register as a foreign agent.)

“She’s very smart, and she works very hard,” Mr. Patten told The Times. “There’s an arrogance in everyone in Washington,” he added, “but she never showed it before. She’s always been careful not to.”

Ted O’Meara, a former aide to Ms. Snowe who also worked for Mr. Cohen alongside Ms. Collins and managed Eliot Cutler’s campaigns for governor in 2010 and 2014, described it as a sense of entitlement. “The sense that there’s nobody else that can do this job but me or do it as well as me,” he said.

He stopped himself.

“Is this on the record?” he asked.

It was.

“She’ll be pissed,” he said.

Kitty Bennett contributed research. Tim Balk contributed reporting from Fryeburg, Maine, and Esmé E. Deprez from Caribou and Casco, Maine.

Michael Kruse is a politics correspondent for The Times.

Lisa Lerer is a national political reporter for The Times, based in New York. She has covered American politics for nearly two decades.

Iran Braces for More War, No Matter the Outcome of the U. S. and Israeli Elections

The New York Times October 31, 2026

news analysis

With Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fighting to stay in power and President Trump facing a tough midterm, Iran’s leaders expect no major shift in policy.

By Yeganeh Torbati

Yeganeh Torbati is the Iran correspondent.

Little is clear about the power dynamics that will govern Israel and the United States in the coming months after pivotal elections in both countries. But Iran’s leaders are watching the contests closely, analysts said, and bracing for a renewed round of conflict whatever the outcome.

In Israel, this week’s national elections showed that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right alliance nor the main opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, the country’s former top military official, won enough votes to form a government. That has set the stage for weeks of uncertainty.

In the United States, Democrats appear to be in a strong position to at least take control of the House in the midterm elections next week. But the exact size of their win, and whether they secure a majority in the Senate, will determine if they can actually put a brake on President Trump’s policies, including the war with Iran.

Tehran expects more attacks whoever takes control in Israel or of Congress, and has shown little willingness to make concessions demanded by the Trump administration to seal a peace deal.

On Saturday, Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s supreme leader, said on social media that he had met with senior leaders of the armed forces and directed them to respond to any kind or level of threat with an immediate response in order to establish “maximum deterrence.” He also directed them to be prepared to target all types of U. S. and Israeli assets.

“They have been expecting a new round of war already for a few weeks, and they’ve been preparing accordingly,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, said of the Iranian government.

In Israel, Iran would welcome the removal of Mr. Netanyahu from power, said Mohammad Saleh Sedghian, director of the Arab Center for Iranian Studies in Tehran. The Israeli leader helped persuade Mr. Trump to attack Iran this year and sought to orchestrate new airstrikes on Iran ahead of the election. But Iranian leaders believe that changing prime ministers would probably have an impact only in the short term rather than leading to a fundamental shift in Israeli policy, Mr. Sedghian said.

“Iranian and Israeli policies toward each other have remained consistent regardless of which government has been in power in Israel since the 1980s,” he said. “Any changes would likely be temporary rather than strategic.”

Mr. Azizi said there were several scenarios for how the Israeli election results could unfold, but that “we should not expect a fundamental change in the hostility between Israel and Iran.”

Even if Mr. Eisenkot or another opposition leader takes power and shifts Israel back into deploying covert tactics against Iran rather than all-out war, Iran’s response could still be escalatory.

“The Islamic Republic’s strategic thinking has undergone a significant shift, involving, first and foremost, a greater willingness to take risks and a move away from its long-established policy of strategic patience,” Mr. Azizi said. “As a result, Iran could still respond to indirect Israeli operations through direct military action.”

When it comes to the United States, Iran’s leaders are keenly aware of how the costs of the war, including higher gasoline prices for Americans, have affected Mr. Trump’s popularity and the Republican Party’s prospects in the midterms. Their assessment appears to be that a deal with Iran would benefit Mr. Trump politically, giving Tehran leverage in any negotiations to end the war. Iran, on the other hand, has already borne enormous costs including spiraling inflation, without its leaders changing their stance.

Mostafa Najafi, an analyst who is said to be close to Mr. Rezaei, wrote on social media on Wednesday that the Trump administration was pursuing a deal with Iran in the days leading up to the midterms as Republicans face a difficult fight to retain control of Congress.

“They want to leverage the agreement for the elections and insist that nuclear concessions also be part of the pre-election deal, which Tehran does not accept,” Mr. Najafi wrote. “If no agreement is reached in the next two days, the atmosphere will likely shift toward confrontation in the first week after the elections.”

Last week, Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to a top Iranian official to propose a new round of comprehensive peace talks, a senior U. S. official and an Iranian official with knowledge of the communication have said. Mr. Vance bypassed Iran’s elected government and President Masoud Pezeshkian and instead addressed the letter to Mohsen Rezaei, the top national security adviser and the former longtime commander of the powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. The outreach to Mr. Rezaei reflected the Trump administration’s view that it needs to deal directly with an Iranian official with influence over hard-liners, who have opposed agreeing to a deal.

On Friday, a Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran for talks, Iran’s state news outlet reported. Qatar has been mediating discussions between Iran and the United States.

The burst of recent diplomacy comes at a significant moment. Mr. Trump has been weighing whether to renew attacks on Iran, potentially after the midterms, and the United States and Israel have drawn up specific plans for new strikes, U. S. officials and other people briefed on the deliberations have said. But there are major obstacles that would need to be overcome for the United States and Iran to reach a final agreement.

“The two sides remain far apart on several critical issues, including the Strait of Hormuz, sanctions relief, oversight by the International Atomic Energy Agency and the scope of Iran’s nuclear commitments,” said Mehrzad Boroujerdi, an Iran expert at Missouri University of Science and Technology. “My sense is that Tehran will pursue a dual-track strategy, engaging in intermittent diplomatic negotiations while simultaneously preparing, to the best of its ability, for a possible resumption of hostilities.”

Mr. Najafi, in his social media post on Wednesday, said that Iran “insists on the fulfillment of its seven conditions” before agreeing to any interim deal. Iranian officials have referred frequently to the conditions in the past month without fully explaining what they are, and framed them as a prerequisite for new talks or the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, the critical shipping waterway on Iran’s southern coast.

Mr. Najafi said in a voice message to The New York Times that the conditions included lifting the U. S. naval blockade on Iran and sanctions on Iran’s oil sales; ending the war on all fronts, including in Lebanon, where Israel has been fighting with Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed group; releasing frozen Iranian assets; and accepting Iran’s management of the Strait of Hormuz.

“Iran has put forth these to the American side as preconditions for the opening of the Strait of Hormuz,” Mr. Najafi said. “The American side must first fulfill these preconditions, and then the negotiations will enter the main phase.”

Mr. Najafi also expressed deep pessimism about the prospects of a lasting agreement between the two sides, saying that Iranian officials have no trust in American intentions or promises.

“Here, the messages exchanged with the United States are viewed with profound skepticism,” he said. “The issue of Iran-U. S. relations has become so complex that even if Iran were to agree to nuclear negotiations and make concessions, it is highly unlikely that this tangled web of conflict between the two nations will reach a meaningful resolution or result in a lasting agreement.”

Leily Nikounazar contributed reporting.

Yeganeh Torbati is the Iran correspondent for The Times.
