Doctors in Ukraine Try Treating Infections Like Biological Warfare Attacks

The New York Times October 31, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

As many as 40 percent of injured soldiers face severe infections that can lead to amputations and death. One initiative is trying to fix that.

By Gina Kolata and Marc Santora

Gina Kolata heard about a new effort to reduce infections in Ukraine while moderating a wartime medicine discussion. Marc Santora visited the site of the dress rehearsal in Poland and spent a day reporting from the disinfection unit in Dnipro, Ukraine.

The injuries to soldiers arriving at Ukrainian hospitals are horrific. Instead of bullet wounds, blast injuries from drones dominate the scene: Calf muscles are blown away, chunks of tissue are missing from thighs. Soil and debris thrown up from the blast are lodged deep in lacerations.

By the time they arrive at a hospital, which can take days, weeks or even months of travel under cover of darkness, 30 to 40 percent of soldiers are not just injured but have severe infections. And their infections often involve microbes that are untreatable — resistant to antibiotics. When the injured soldiers are admitted to civilian hospitals, they risk spreading the bacteria to other patients.

Now there is an effort to counter this scrouge.

It started with a realization by Hailie Uren, a clinical pharmacologist and disaster medicine specialist who works in Ukraine. The situation, she reasoned, resembled nothing so much as a biological warfare attack. “If we don’t have antibiotics to treat these patients,” she said, “how different is that from when a patient is exposed to anthrax?”

Hospitals already have plans in place to treat victims of biological warfare, she noted. All the hospitals had to do was carry out those same urgent protocols on the battlefield. Ms. Uren proposed the idea directly to Ukraine’s surgeon general, and received support from the defense and health ministries.

The effort began in September, in a large tent outside a hospital in central Ukraine.

The objective, which Ms. Uren had developed with colleagues, would be to disinfect injured soldiers before they entered a hospital; remove their dirty clothes and bandages, wash them with an antiseptic and give them a shower.

That alone would be a big change from the status quo, with soldiers going directly into the hospital, and possibly sitting in a crowded emergency room, or going straight into surgery, wearing soiled clothing and used dressings. Those items are often rife with potentially deadly microbes.

At that point, lifesaving treatments for these severe infections can be horrendous. “If a guy has infection in his leg and it is resistant to antibiotics, you sometimes have to cut the leg off,” said Dr. John Holcomb, a retired Army surgeon who served in Iraq and Afghanistan, and worked with Ms. Uren.

The infection problem is not just a challenge for Ukraine, Ms. Uren said. One hospital she worked in is about only 40 miles from Poland, where some injured soldiers are being treated. The spread of antibiotic-resistant microbes is “a huge biosecurity risk for the rest of Europe,” she said.

The U. S. Army colonel serving as the command surgeon for Special Operations Command Europe, overseeing the training, explained that these bacteria are a threat to everyone.

“If they enter the general hospital system, they endanger a 70-year-old with pneumonia, or a 25-year-old with appendicitis, if we cannot control their spread,” the colonel said. He spoke on the condition of anonymity in keeping with military protocol.

Infections have always been a problem in warfare, said Dr. Holcomb.

In war zones, Dr. Holcomb said, “infection control procedures are not always adhered to.” Basic handwashing, wearing gloves and wiping down beds between patients all can go out the door. So can standard practices around limiting the use of antibiotics.

“It’s not one thing. It’s all of them” he added. “They generate multidrug resistant organisms.”

But the scale of what is happening in Ukraine has no precedent, in large part because of how drones have transformed the battlefield.

The crisis begins at the point of injury. Blast munitions can tear away soft tissue, shatter bone and pack manure-rich soil deep into exposed cavities. The soil bacteria are “tough mothers” that can grow onto any surface they find, said Dr. Paul Pottinger, an infectious diseases specialist at the University of Washington who was not part of the Ukraine project.

“Any breach of human skin,” he said, “the germs like to crawl up.”

Washing the wound with water immediately, cutting off injured tissue and applying an antiseptic could stymie infections, but that seldom happens during prolonged combat.

The “golden hour” of modern military trauma care — evacuating a wounded soldier to a site that provides surgery within 60 minutes — has been dismantled by the saturation of drones. Wounded fighters often spend days or weeks sheltering in tree lines and trenches.

Every delay compounds the risk of infection, especially because patients — who have often lost blood and are frequently malnourished — have a weakened ability to fight off infections. And within eight hours, bacteria can form slimy biofilms across the wounds, shielding the microbes from antibiotics and from being flushed away with water.

Doctors along the evacuation route do their best to prevent infections, but their tools are limited and sometimes misused. They often do not have enough water to irrigate wounds, face shortages of antiseptics and lack diagnostic tools. They often provide the most powerful antibiotics out of desperation, encouraging the rise of microbes that resist the drugs.

By the time a casualty moves through the chain — often traversing up to eight separate handoffs and regional facilities — bacteria on the surface of a wound have time to migrate into bone and tissue and cause an infection. Rather than treating a clean trauma wound, surgeons at that point are confronted with patients with complex, extensively drug-resistant infections.

Many combatants have infections deep in their tissues, said Dr. Evhen Filonenko, who works at Pirogov Vinnytsia Regional Clinical Hospital. “These patients are very complicated,” he said. “You need to remove all infected tissue. We are doing huge surgeries.”

Some lose their legs or arms because amputation is the only way to control infections in their bones. Once a bone gets infected and bone cells die, there is virtually no way to even deliver an antibiotic; dead bone does not have a blood supply.

“I’ve never seen anything like this,” said Dr. P. J. Brennan, an infectious disease specialist at the University of Pennsylvania. Dr. Brennan is part of a group of specialists there that fields calls from Ukrainian doctors at 6 a. m. on Tuesdays.

“There are numerous instances in which we literally could find no drugs to treat the patient,” Dr. Brennan said.

Making matters worse, it can be hard to find out what these patients are infected with. “Not every hospital has a lab, so cultures get sent to other labs,” Dr. Brennan said. “It can take time before the results are sent back.”

“We might be looking at cultures obtained three weeks ago,” during which time different microbes may have colonized the wound, Dr. Brennan said.

The experiment to stop the spread of infections ran a four-day dress rehearsal in Poland in June, led by U. S., Polish and Belgian special operations forces.

Inside what observers nicknamed “the carwash,” Ukrainian doctors, nurses and medics practiced stripping blast victims of mud-caked uniforms, cutting away soiled dressings, throwing out pre-hospital IV lines and scrubbing exposed flesh and wounds, first with warm water and then with warm antiseptic solutions. Then they wheeled the injured soldiers into a separate, sterile area known as the clean zone.

Now, about a month after the official effort began, medical personnel in a decontamination tent in eastern Ukraine have treated about 150 injured soldiers, Ms. Uren said.

To see if the procedure is helping, the team swabs the soldiers when they arrive, and again on Days 2 and 5 when they are inside the hospital. The members also record heart rates and body temperatures before and after the soldiers are decontaminated. A high heart rate can indicate pain, and an inability to regulate body temperature can indicate infections. They also do blood tests every other day, looking for evidence of sepsis, the body’s life-threatening reaction to an infection.

It can take time to get the results from the swabs, Ms. Uren said, but what they have seen is encouraging.

One soldier, for example, came in with Acinetobacter baumannii in one of his wounds. That is a dreaded strain of bacteria that can be resistant to antibiotics. But the bacteria had not yet established an infection — they were still lurking on the wound’s surface. The disinfectant cleared them. On Days 2 and 5, the swabs showed no evidence of that microbe.

Ms. Uren said one surprise was the psychological effect of the decontamination on the soldiers. “The casualties consistently are telling us they feel like they are a human again,” she said. “It’s like we are washing off the war from them.”

Encouraged by their initial results, the investigators are now going to set up decontamination units outside two other hospitals. But they also have bigger plans.

They want to start controlling infections from the time a soldier is first injured, interrupting a chain of events that starts when a blast injury shoots debris and soil into a wound.

“I think it’s very smart,” said Dr. Pottinger, the infectious diseases researcher. “We will treat you right from the get-go as though you were contaminated. I admire them for doing it.”

He hopes the lessons from the experiment in Ukraine will be broadly applied.

“It seems to me,” he said, “that those in leadership positions at the Pentagon should pay very close attention to this threat — and to the countermeasures.”

Liubov Sholudko contributed reporting.

Gina Kolata reports on diseases and treatments, how treatments are discovered and tested, and how they affect people.

Marc Santora has been reporting from Ukraine since the beginning of the war with Russia. He was previously based in London as an international news editor focused on breaking news events and earlier the bureau chief for East and Central Europe, based in Warsaw. He has also reported extensively from Iraq and Africa.

Syria Weighs Joining Saudi Mutual Defense Pact as Yemen War Rages

The New York Times October 31, 2026

Houthi-Saudi War

Advertisement

Supported by

A move to join Saudi Arabia’s agreement with Turkey and Pakistan could entangle more countries in the kingdom’s escalating conflict between the Iran-backed Houthis.

By Euan Ward and Vivian Nereim

Euan Ward reported from Beirut, Lebanon, and Vivian Nereim from Manama, Bahrain.

Syria is considering joining a regional defense alliance with Saudi Arabia, its foreign minister said on Saturday, raising the prospect that Damascus could become involved in the kingdom’s widening conflict with the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen.

Asaad al-Shaibani, the Syrian foreign minister, told the Manama Dialogue security conference in Bahrain that “discussions are currently underway to evaluate Syria’s entry into the Mecca alliance,” referring to a mutual-defense pact signed in August by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan.

Under the terms of the pact, known as the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, an armed attack on any of its three members would be considered an attack on all, mirroring NATO’s collective-defense principle. The countries agreed this month to prepare for the rapid deployment of military forces to Saudi Arabia as the Houthis have intensified their attacks on the kingdom.

Mr. al-Shaibani said that Syria regarded the defense of Gulf Arab countries as essential to its own security. “Syria will stand beside all of the Gulf countries,” he said, adding that they faced challenges from “militias that cross borders.”

It was unclear, however, whether that potential support would extend to sending Syrian troops to Yemen.

Since sweeping to power almost two years ago, President Ahmed al-Sharaa of Syria has sought to stay out of regional conflicts, as his government has struggled to rebuild the country after nearly 14 years of civil war. The Syrian authorities denied reports this month that Saudi Arabia had requested that Syrian troops be deployed, saying Damascus was focused on reconstruction.

But Syria’s growing ties with Saudi Arabia could complicate that position, analysts say. Saudi Arabia has become a major diplomatic and economic supporter of Syria since the country’s longtime dictator, Bashar al-Assad, was overthrown by rebels led by Mr. al-Sharaa. The Assad family, which ruled Syria with an iron fist for more than five decades, had been closely allied with Iran, Saudi Arabia’s regional rival.

This month, Mr. al-Sharaa met with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader, in Riyadh, where they discussed investment and regional security, according to a statement from the Syrian president’s office.

Syria has raised the possibility of joining the defense pact as fighting in Yemen and attacks on Saudi Arabia have intensified after years of relative calm.

After the Houthis seized the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, in 2014, Saudi Arabia began a disastrous bombing campaign the following year in support of the country’s internationally recognized government. The fighting largely subsided after a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022, but it has escalated this year amid the broader U. S.-Israeli war with Iran.

The renewed fighting has killed at least 1,677 people and wounded more than 7,300 in Yemen since August, according to the World Health Organization. Nearly 300,000 Yemenis have been displaced, the United Nations has said, deepening a devastating humanitarian crisis in one of the world’s poorest countries.

In Saudi Arabia, Houthi missile and drone attacks on airports and vital infrastructure have killed at least 19 people and wounded hundreds more, according to the Saudi-led military coalition. The escalating attacks, which have severely disrupted air travel, have increasingly threatened the kingdom’s ambitions to become a global tourism and business hub.

As the attacks have intensified, Egypt — which is not part of the Mecca pact — this week authorized military aid to Saudi Arabia, another sign of the growing regional response to the conflict.

On Saturday, the Saudi-backed coalition said it intercepted three drones over the kingdom, including one near the capital, Riyadh. In Yemen, six people, including three children, were wounded in what the Houthi authorities said was a Saudi airstrike on a grocery store in Taiz Province.

Taiz, one of Yemen’s largest cities, has become a major battleground in recent weeks. The Houthis have cut road access to the strategically located city, leaving its residents with dwindling supplies of food, water and fuel.

Taiz is at a crossroads between Houthi-held territory in the north of the country and the government-controlled south and the Red Sea coast. Taking control would help the Houthis increase pressure on government forces and cement control of coastal areas on the Red Sea.

In another development, the Houthis have come under renewed scrutiny for arresting a number of U. N. personnel and aid workers two years ago. On Saturday, the United Nations said that Mohammad el Shami, a Yemeni employee of its human rights office who had been detained since June 2024, had died in custody.

Volker Türk, the U. N. human rights chief, called for an independent investigation into his death.

Euan Ward is a Times reporter covering Lebanon and Syria. He is based in Beirut.

Vivian Nereim is the lead reporter for The Times covering the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. She is based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

How Binance’s $6.3 Billion Hack Went Down

The New York Times October 31, 2026

Binance Hack

Advertisement

Supported by

A war room. A global conference call. A founder who live-posted about the largest crypto heist in history. Inside a frantic 24 hours at the world’s biggest crypto exchange.

By David Yaffe-Bellany

David Yaffe-Bellany reports on the cryptocurrency industry.

At about 4:20 p. m. on Thursday, a string of unusual transactions started to cause alarm at Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange.

Money was pouring out of the company’s accounts, a multibillion-dollar deluge of digital coins. It had all the hallmarks of a crypto heist — a high-speed bank robbery conducted over the internet.

As the news spread, Binance’s top executives put together an informal war room on Wea, the company’s internal messaging system, with about 100 participants, including specialized cryptocurrency tracers and security personnel.

They eventually transitioned to a mass conference call, with 100 boxes on the screen, where employees took turns muting and then unmuting, communicating in a mixture of English and Chinese. Among them was He Yi, Binance’s co-chief executive, who is seven months pregnant, and worked through the night from her base in Abu Dhabi, taking a call at 3 a. m. local time.

Ms. He and her colleagues were navigating one of the most damaging crises in Binance’s long and troubled history. A team of North Korean hackers had penetrated the exchange analysts said, and drained more than $6 billion in the largest crypto heist of all time. Binance was forced to halt deposits and withdrawals, and posted a series of frantic messages on X, promising that it would cover any losses.

It was a surreal situation made even more surreal by the actions of Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, who spent the evening narrating the events to his 12.9 million followers on X. He posted prayer hand emojis, publicly jousted with the site’s owner, Elon Musk, and insisted that “user funds are SAFU” — using a bit of crypto slang to reassure customers that hundreds of millions of dollars in deposits would not simply vanish into thin air.

“It hurts, but we will survive,” Mr. Zhao declared.

The impact of the Binance attack rippled across the crypto industry, from Abu Dhabi to New York, setting off a frantic effort to salvage some of the stolen funds and prompting law enforcement inquiries. This account of how the hack unfolded is based on interviews with four people with knowledge of the events, as well as analyses by crypto forensics firms and documents reviewed by The New York Times.

For years, Binance has been the most important and contentious company in the crypto world. After Mr. Zhao founded it in 2017, it quickly turned into a behemoth, the No. 1 destination for customers looking to convert traditional currencies into digital coins like Bitcoin and Ether.

It also became a haven for crime. In 2023, Binance pleaded guilty to anti-money-laundering violations that had allowed criminals to move money and paid $4.3 billion in penalties to U. S. regulators. Mr. Zhao was sentenced to four months in prison.

For all its troubles, however, Binance never lost popularity among the crypto faithful. It remains the world’s largest exchange by a distance, and Mr. Zhao, who lives in Abu Dhabi, is something of an industry folk hero. Binance’s main platform is banned in the United States. But last year, the company forged a business relationship with World Liberty Financial, the Trump family crypto start-up. President Trump granted a pardon to Mr. Zhao last October, paving the way for Binance to expand into the U. S. market.

But on the night of Oct. 29, the company had to deal with the aftermath of the $6 billion hack.

Such attacks have become commonplace in the crypto world. In February 2025, the North Koreans stole $1.5 billion from Bybit, a rival exchange. Bybit was breached after Ben Zhou, its chief executive, approved a seemingly routine transaction that granted the thieves access to the exchange’s internal system.

It’s not clear precisely how the North Koreans got around Binance’s defenses. An initial investigation pointed to a compromised laptop, Binance said Friday. But the company later said it had uncovered “additional points of breach.”

Much of the drama played out in public. Almost all crypto transactions are recorded on the blockchain, a ledger of money movements that anyone can look up. That meant crypto analysts could see funds leaving Binance in real time.

On Thursday afternoon, Jonathan Levin, the chief executive of the crypto analytics firm Chainalysis, was on a video call with a former senior U. S. official, discussing the need for the U. S. government to deploy cyber attacks against adversaries. Then Mr. Levin got the news about Binance.

“I looked at my phone and was like, ‘Oh, this doesn’t look good,’” he said in an interview.

A group of Chainalysis employees gathered in a conference room in New York named “Silk Road,” after another crypto platform that was famously hacked. They worked until the early hours of Friday morning, eating Malaysian food and analyzing transactions to get a clearer picture of what had happened.

Soon both Chainalysis and another analytics firm, TRM Labs, attributed the attack to an elite North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor. North Koreans have targeted crypto companies for years, using the proceeds of those thefts to fund its nuclear program, according to Western officials.

The hackers have developed increasingly complex strategies to steal crypto and launder the proceeds, a painstaking endeavor that can take months to complete. In a blog post on Friday, Chainalysis said the attackers had deployed “laundering patterns we have not seen before,” conducting thousands of transactions over a short period, probably with the help of automation.

At the same time, Binance’s colleagues in the industry mobilized to intercept some of the laundered crypto. Certain digital coin issuers can freeze funds, allowing them to halt a money-laundering operation in its tracks.

Soon after the hack, Tether and Circle, two major issuers, announced that they had frozen stashes of their own coins that the hackers had seized from Binance, a combined total of more than $2 billion in crypto. Binance is now working to gain access to those funds, the company said.

But $2.4 billion in crypto is already “beyond any issuer’s reach,” according to TRM. In a social media post on Friday, Binance said that it had set aside $6.34 billion to cover losses from the hack.

How much money Binance has in reserve is not publicly known. After midnight, Mr. Musk posted a grimacing emoji underneath an X post comparing Mr. Zhao to Sam Bankman-Fried, the disgraced crypto mogul whose FTX exchange collapsed in 2022.

“Bad time to troll,” Mr. Zhao responded. “Please stop.” He noted that Binance owns over $1 billion in shares in SpaceX, Mr. Musk’s rocket company.

Mr. Zhao’s comment got the attention of Ms. He, Binance’s co-chief executive and his longtime romantic partner. (Mr. Zhao is Binance’s majority shareholder but doesn’t have a formal role at the company.)

“Our company’s revenue for the year is sufficient to cover the losses, so we do not yet need to sell the SpaceX shares,” Ms. He wrote.

With the industry reeling, Ms. He and her co-chief executive, Richard Teng, told Binance employees to “stay disciplined,” according to a message reviewed by The Times.

"Do not speculate internally or externally,” the message said. “We know this is an intense moment, and we deeply appreciate everyone working overtime to make this right.”

They also tried to address the growing unease in the crypto world. Speaking in Mandarin in a video posted to X on Friday, Ms. He said that the rise of artificial intelligence had turned hacking into “a threat to the entire industry.”

“Of course, there are many things that we have done wrong,” she said. “We should have invested in security much earlier and more extensively, and established more rigorous standards.”

Word of Binance’s hack even reached Mr. Trump, who was asked about it by a reporter on Friday. “People never see the money anymore,” he said. “I’ve always felt it was a little bit dangerous. But they say they have it pretty much under control. We’ll see.”

Among the companies that rushed to Binance’s aid was the Trump family firm, World Liberty, the issuer of a coin known as USD1.

Zach Witkoff, the company’s chief executive and the son of one of Mr. Trump’s top advisers, announced on X that World Liberty had frozen $27 million in USD1 that was “associated with the Binance hack.”

“We stand by our industry partners,” he wrote.

“Thank you!” Mr. Zhao responded, followed by three prayer hand emojis.

Michael Forsythe and Dustin Volz contributed reporting.

David Yaffe-Bellany writes about the crypto industry for The Times from New York. He can be reached at davidyb@nytimes. com.

How Trump Is Dismantling America’s Scientific Research Machine

The New York Times October 31, 2026

Videos by Salwan Georges For The New York Times

The system that has driven life-altering discoveries and helped make the United States a superpower is now under intense strain.

Videos by Salwan Georges for The New York Times

Supported by

The system that has driven life-altering discoveries and helped make the United States a superpower is now under intense strain.

By Christopher FlavelleIrena HwangAdam SellaAlan BlinderSheryl Gay StolbergBenjamin Mueller and Michael C. Bender

This is the first in a series of articles examining how the Trump administration has upended the pursuit of science.

The warning, buried in an obscure government report this summer, was unflinching.

The Defense Department’s vaunted network of research laboratories — whose scientists helped develop satellite communication, radar technology, and even the computer mouse — was in trouble.

The labs lost a significant share of their staff last year, largely in response to the Trump administration’s efforts to thin the federal work force, the report found. Refilling critical positions was proving difficult due in part to President Trump’s demand that new hires be screened for their loyalty to his goals. The report, issued by the Pentagon, pointed to “potentially grave consequences for the future of national defense.”

The turmoil inside scientific research has extended beyond the Pentagon. The Energy Department, a key hub of nuclear and quantum research, has lost more than 1,000 scientists and technical staff. The National Science Foundation, for decades a primary backer of long-term, foundational research, has withheld more than $1 billion in funding. And at the National Institutes of Health, the biggest funder of medical research, officials delayed or canceled more than 2,000 grants to biomedical researchers focused on topics such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and other diseases.

Under Mr. Trump, the federal government is still spending roughly as much on research — about $200 billion this year — as the administrations that came before. Scientists across the country are still receiving grants; universities are still being funded. But beneath the surface, the system of federally funded science that helped make the United States a global superpower is under intense strain from Trump policies, jeopardizing the nation’s advantages in defense, medicine and technology, a New York Times examination has found.

The White House regularly proclaims that it is advancing American interests. Yet its actions are eroding the country’s scientific edge as global rivals challenge U. S. dominance in fields that will help define the 21st century, according to interviews with scientists, university leaders, government officials and analysts and a review of documents and budgets.

The damage is the byproduct of three pillars of Mr. Trump’s broader agenda.

One is the sweeping job cuts and grant cancellations engineered last year by the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, the Elon Musk-led effort that viewed much of federal spending as wasteful and whose effects are still reverberating across the bureaucracy.

A second is the administration’s continued pressure on research universities, in which the White House used funding cuts to push schools into adhering to its demands for ideologically driven policy shifts.

The third is a campaign by Mr. Trump’s budget director, Russell T. Vought, to impose more political control over how the government spends money appropriated by Congress, further infusing politics into decisions around scientific research.

If not for the courts curbing the administration’s campaign against universities and lawmakers in both parties rejecting cuts to research funding, the impact on science would have been far deeper. Still, the effects of the broader agenda have rippled through nearly every facet of the nation’s research machine.

Aspiring scientists have seen their career paths thwarted, with fewer available spots for Ph. D. students. The number of Ph. D. applications from foreign students, typically a significant share of U. S. science programs, shrank by 21 percent this year at leading universities, according to data gathered for the Association of American Universities. Total Ph. D. admissions at those schools have dropped as universities try to make do with less resources.

Even the agencies working on topics that Mr. Trump and his aides have called priorities — including national defense, artificial intelligence, quantum computing and nuclear energy — have been depleted.

Taken together, the changes underscore how Mr. Trump’s policies have disrupted scientific research beyond the areas the administration has targeted more directly, such as vaccines and climate science, endangering U. S. power and pre-eminence.

By many measures, China is closing the gap with the United States as the world’s research leader. Some organizations that rank global universities show China’s best schools increasingly displacing American universities at the top. And the impact of Chinese research papers, as measured by citations from other scientists, has caught up with the United States, according to Clarivate, a data and analytics company.

By the time the full consequences of the administration’s actions become apparent, experts warn, it could be too late to fix. That’s because basic research funded by federal grants often takes decades to mature into the technology, medical treatments and consumer products that change American life.

Federally funded work on atomic clocks starting in the late 1940s, for example, paved the way for GPS technology. In 1976, federally funded research yielded a major discovery about the origins of cancer-causing genes, which led to a Nobel Prize and, two decades later, lifesaving cancer drugs. Some of the early precursors to artificial intelligence date to U. S.-backed research in the 1980s, which used an algorithm to teach neural networks to learn from mistakes.

“Science is the long game,” said Marcia McNutt, who was president of the National Academy of Sciences, the country’s top scientific advisory body, until this summer. “By the time we no longer win any Nobel Prizes, we will have lost the capacity to ever recover.”

In response to The Times’ reporting, officials from the White House, Pentagon and other science agencies disputed that administration policies were hampering science. Rather, said White House spokeswoman Liz Huston, the administration is reinvigorating American science by transforming organizations in need of change.

“President Trump is ushering in a new golden age of American science by modernizing our research institutions, refocusing on ambitious national missions, and fully leveraging super intelligence for scientific discovery,” Ms. Huston said in a statement, using Mr. Trump’s preferred term for artificial intelligence. “Revitalizing our national scientific enterprise requires supporting the best American scientists and funding the best research based on merit.”

The White House said the administration has expanded a number of programs that support young researchers, and noted that the decision to reduce Ph. D. admissions this year was made by the universities themselves. The Association of American Universities said schools’ decisions to reduce admissions were largely the result of “federal research funding uncertainties.”

The White House also said that most of the scientists who have stopped working for the federal government since Mr. Trump came back to office were not fired, but instead left voluntarily. And it noted that the methodologies for ranking universities, such as comparisons between the United States and China, are limited.

The rest of the world now sees an opportunity.

Australia, for example, announced its “global talent attraction program,” calling it “an urgent and unparalleled opportunity to attract the smartest minds leaving the United States.” Canada dedicated more than $1 billion to bring in 1,000 international researchers, drawing American leaders in fields such as biochemistry and neuroscience.

Even China, a country not known for academic freedoms, has been luring researchers away. A winner of last year’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry left the University of California, Berkeley, to lead an institute in Beijing using artificial intelligence to accelerate the discovery of new materials — two fields the Trump administration has said it wants to dominate.

The roots of the United States’ science empire can be traced to a landmark 1945 report issued during the Truman administration, “Science: The Endless Frontier.” It described a vision, inspired in part by the Manhattan Project that led to the atomic bomb, for how science would power U. S. dominance in the world.

The federal government went on to establish a network of science agencies with distinct missions. The National Science Foundation supports theoretical or experimental work, which often lays the groundwork for future technologies years or even decades later. The Department of Energy was established to pursue advances related to power generation, as well as managing the nation’s nuclear arsenal. NASA, created in response to Soviet advances in space, put a man on the moon. The National Institutes of Health, which traces its roots to 1887, funds biomedical advances.

The federal government also provides tens of billions of dollars each year to the nation’s research universities while funding national labs, private industry and other institutions — a system built up over 80 years by presidents and lawmakers from both parties.

American universities spent $65 billion in federal money in 2024, accounting for more than half of their total research and development spending.

In less than two years, Mr. Trump has shaken that system to the core.

The upheaval began early in the administration.

DOGE engineered staff firings, and encouraged others to resign across the federal bureaucracy. Within a year, N. I. H. staffing had shrunk by one-fifth. The N. S. F.’s ranks were reduced by a third. Even NASA, which shrank less than other science agencies, lost 20 percent of its employees with Ph. D. s. Those who left included its chief scientist, a climate science expert whose job the administration eliminated.

NASA said it will keep recruiting staff as needed. In a statement, Nicky Fox, the associate administrator for NASA’s Science Mission Directorate, said the agency is working to get “more science into space for lower cost.”

DOGE and the White House directed agencies to search for terms in grant descriptions that might reveal science the administration viewed as liberal, including anything that appeared to promote diversity, equity and inclusion.

The cuts cascaded through the country.

Ann D. Cohen, a neuroscientist who co-directs an Alzheimer’s research center at the University of Pittsburgh, had been working on a five-year study looking at how people’s exposure to stress and health problems earlier in life can affect their odds of developing the disease.

The research was critical to developing better treatments and health interventions, Dr. Cohen said. “If the triggering event is poor cardiovascular health in midlife, we can actually deploy public health strategies to improve those things, and potentially have an effect on Alzheimer’s,” she said.

Recruiting people from different backgrounds was difficult, because people who volunteer for scientific studies tend to have higher than average incomes and education levels. So Dr. Cohen and her colleagues recruited from rural Western Pennsylvania, whose residents were more likely to be white and low-income, as well as from Black communities in Pittsburgh.

This past August, the N. I. H. terminated the grant, effective immediately, on the grounds that the project was focused on structural racism — an argument that fundamentally misunderstood the work, Dr. Cohen said.

Emily Hilliard, a spokeswoman for the U. S. Department of Health and Human Services, which includes the N. I. H., did not comment on specific grants. In a statement, she said N. I. H.’s commitment to Alzheimer’s research has not decreased.

“N. I. H. is focused on funding innovative projects led by a new generation of health researchers, and on allocating funds for research that will lead to better health for the American people,” Ms. Hilliard said.

Some researchers who lost funding acknowledged having framed their projects in the language of D. E. I. But, they argued, that was what the Biden administration had emphasized.

Jessica L. Rosenberg, director of education for the Quantum Science and Engineering Center at George Mason University, had received N. S. F. funding to research ways to encourage more American students to seek careers in quantum technology, an emerging field that has led to innovation by vastly expanding computing power.

The N. S. F. canceled the grant last year, about four months after the project started. Dr. Rosenberg said she suspects the grant was targeted because her application mentioned students from diverse backgrounds.

“That was what we were supposed to be doing at the time,” she said in an interview.

Trump administration officials argue that the push to incorporate D. E. I. degraded science, and that scientists who embraced the approach had themselves to blame for losing support.

“We cannot afford for America’s scientists to be in the business of scoring points for an ideological agenda,” Michael Kratsios, Mr. Trump’s science adviser, told a meeting of scientists last year.

Mr. Trump and his aides returned to the White House wanting to punish elite schools like Columbia and Harvard, ostensibly for transgressions like tolerating antisemitism.

But when cuts to research funding became the White House’s weapon of choice, professors and administrators had to decide whether to fight or acquiesce.

Harvard sued. Other schools negotiated. And even at universities that were not explicitly targeted, researchers made changes in hopes of keeping federal money that was foundational to their work — softening the language in their proposals, narrowing their projects and debating the line between fair-game government oversight and improper political interference.

The cuts fell across disciplines. Projects on epilepsy, Lou Gehrig’s disease, tuberculosis and even astronomy outreach and education sputtered. Work on cancer and heart rhythms was imperiled.

The administration ultimately restored billions of dollars in funding, either because of court orders or settlements with universities. But researchers said the interruptions and changing priorities delayed or derailed experiments.

“You can’t run a research operation when you have to constantly pivot,” said Dorota Grejner-Brzezinska, vice chancellor for research at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, which was swept up in the administration’s funding cuts and participated in more than a dozen legal challenges.

“The current state of affairs is that it’s really very hard to plan long term,” she added, “and research is a long-term kind of enterprise.”

May Mailman, a former White House aide who helped lead the pressure campaign against universities, said the administration wasn’t overly concerned about the effects on research. Funds taken away from one university could eventually make their way to other schools whose behavior and ideology the White House approved of, she said. In the meantime, Ms. Mailman said, the administration tried to minimize the disruption to fields of research it supported, including artificial intelligence and some types of energy.

But much of the work coming out of universities, she said, may not have merited the taxpayer money going into it.

“There’s a feeling that there is more spent on research than comes out of it — that the system is a little bit broken,” Ms. Mailman said.

The administration also sought deep funding cuts to federal science agencies. Last year, when Mr. Vought presented the administration’s annual budget request to Congress, he called for reducing research funds at the National Institutes of Health by 41 percent; cutting the National Science Foundation by 55 percent; and reducing NASA’s budget for science by almost half. No previous administration, from either party, had sought such deep cuts.

Congress rejected those cuts. But Mr. Vought began finding novel ways to slow grants and redirect funds.

One of the offices that Mr. Vought targeted in his budget request was the N. S. F.’s “woke social, behavioral, and economic sciences” — an apparent reference to an N. S. F. division that funded social science. Not long after, the division began reducing its grants.

An N. S. F. spokesman, Michael England, said in a statement that the agency’s funding decisions “reflect a strategic alignment of resources in a constrained fiscal environment.”

The loss of those funds affected researchers like Priti Shah, chair of the University of Michigan’s psychology department. Dr. Shah had applied for a grant to study how people evaluate and make decisions based on scientific information. In the summer of 2025, the N. S. F. told her that her application had been put on hold because of funding issues. It was later rejected entirely.

“It is so important to understand what people assume and what errors they make when they’re thinking about science,” Dr. Shah said. “People are very poor at reasoning about scientific evidence.”

The administration’s actions also hurt agencies central to its political agenda.

The Defense Department’s assessment of science and research capabilities published this summer said changes during the first year of the Trump administration had degraded the department’s highly regarded network of research laboratories, due largely to DOGE cuts and obstacles to hiring.

“Without a swift and sustained reversal of these policies,” the report warned, the Defense Department’s “innovation engine is at risk of stalling.”

The labs lost about 14 percent of their staff, the report found. Among those mentioned were the Naval Sea Systems Command, charged with developing ships and weapons; the Air Force Research Laboratory, which helped develop stealth aircraft and laser systems; and the Army’s Aviation & Missile Center.

External research laboratories, which are funded by the Pentagon but staffed by civilian researchers and develop technology for use by the military, were also suffering from the administration’s policies, the report said.

Much of the work at those labs, some of which are attached to major research universities, is classified, and the report did not disclose specific examples of research that has been affected. But it warned that staff departures inside the labs and among agency employees who coordinated with them “jeopardized the execution of critical defense research.” Without key points of contact between the agency and the labs, the report said, efforts that support “time-sensitive, real-world operations are in some cases at a standstill or delayed.”

Because the labs aren’t financially connected to defense contractors, they play an added important role helping the Pentagon objectively evaluate contractors’ claims about new technologies, said Heidi Shyu, who oversaw the Pentagon’s research operation as under secretary of defense for research and engineering in the Biden administration.

A Pentagon official acknowledged that, during the first year of the administration, there was a “retraction in the number of scientists and engineers across the research enterprise.” But, the official said, the agency has “hired to fulfill the mission and mitigate any impacts from the loss of personnel.”

Defense Department funding changes also affected university researchers.

Randall Engle, a psychologist at the Georgia Institute of Technology, was working on ways to help the Navy select air traffic controllers, pilots and other applicants for complex jobs.

The Navy needs to train roughly 1,000 new air traffic controllers each year, Dr. Engle said, at a cost of about $100,000 per trainee. But because the job requires intense focus in difficult conditions, nearly a quarter of trainees typically fail.

So he received funding to develop diagnostic tests to determine a person’s ability to maintain focus.

Dr. Engle tested his new approach at the Navy’s air base in Pensacola, Fla., and found that it did a better job identifying people likely to succeed as air traffic controllers. He was in the midst of refining those tests, when the Office of Naval Research told Georgia Tech that the grant was canceled.

Dr. Engle said he believes the grant was canceled simply because it was happening at a university.

“There was no wokeness,” Dr. Engle said of his project. “There was no diversity, inclusion.”

The uncertainty over the future of American science is reflected in the events that have unfolded at the Department of Energy.

The agency is a critical engine for research in the physical sciences, and it houses the Genesis Mission — a marquee Trump administration initiative that officials say will drive discoveries across a range of topics, from quantum computing and particle accelerators to microchips that can operate in outer space. In an executive order, Mr. Trump called it a “dedicated, coordinated national effort to unleash a new age of AI-accelerated innovation and discovery.”

But the Energy Department’s central role on a Trump-driven project came with a glaring contradiction: It was also hammered by DOGE.

The agency has lost about one-quarter of its staff since the start of the administration, according to a Times analysis of federal data. And the amount of grant money awarded by its two major science offices dropped by more than one-quarter during the administration’s first year, before Genesis began — a reduction of more than half a billion dollars.

Darío Gil, the agency’s top science official, rejected the idea that its science mission has suffered, noting that much of the department’s work is done by 17 national laboratories, where most staff are not federal employees and so not affected by DOGE’s staff-reduction programs. He said the agency is hiring.

“Staffing is always a challenge” Dr. Gil said. “We continue to recruit good people.”

He added that the goal of Genesis is to double the productivity of America’s science industry within a decade. The program has selected almost 300 projects to fund at universities, private companies, national labs and other research organizations.

“The outcome we seek,” Dr. Gil said, “is that this transformation impacts the entire American economy.”

In July, just a few weeks after the Pentagon published its warning about defense labs, Mr. Kratsios, the White House science adviser, issued a report of his own.

The document emphasized many of the administration’s goals: Increasing the role of private industry in federal research. Bypassing the traditional peer-review process for deciding who gets research grants, instead giving individual reviewers the chance “to make bold scientific bets” on researchers of their choosing. Redirecting more money toward younger researchers.

Mr. Kratsios barely mentioned a crucial part of the administration’s agenda: a proposed rule issued by the Trump administration this past May, which would require that Mr. Trump’s political appointees approve which researchers get funding — taking power away from nonpartisan science officials who have typically been the deciders.

Under the proposal, researchers seeking funds “should commit to complying with administration policies.” Officials would screen and reject applications for projects that “promote anti-American values.”

The day after Mr. Kratsios released his report, he appeared before the House science committee to discuss it. Some committee members seemed perplexed by his promise to usher in a scientific golden age, given the tumult over the previous year and a half.

“All I see is tarnish and deterioration,” said Representative Gabe Amo, Democrat of Rhode Island. “Do you commit to not leaving our scientific apparatus in shambles?”

“I don’t think, sir, I would be doing my job if I wanted to leave the scientific enterprise in shambles,” Mr. Kratsios responded. “So I will commit to not doing that.”

This spring, my colleagues and I set out to understand the lasting impact of the Trump administration on scientific research — from attacks on universities and DOGE to the fight against “woke” — and what it could mean for America’s decades-long scientific dominance.

Reporting was contributed by Mark Arsenault, William J. Broad, Kenneth Chang, Carolyn Y. Johnson, Sarah Kliff, Ryan Mac, Katrina Miller, Brad Plumer, Tony Romm and Theodore Schleifer. Research was contributed by Susan C. Beachy, Kitty Bennett, Alain Delaquérière, Georgia Gee, Sheelagh McNeill and Kirsten Noyes.

Christopher Flavelle is a Times reporter covering how President Trump is transforming the federal government.

Irena Hwang is a data reporter at The Times, using computational tools to uncover hidden stories and illuminate the news.

Adam Sella covers breaking news for The Times in Washington.

Alan Blinder is a national correspondent for The Times, covering education.

Sheryl Gay Stolberg is a correspondent based in Washington for The Times, covering Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and President Trump’s health agenda.

Benjamin Mueller reports on health and medicine. He was previously a U. K. correspondent in London and a police reporter in New York.

Michael C. Bender is a Times correspondent in Washington.

The Marathon Is as Popular as Ever. It Remains Inaccessible to Many.

The New York Times October 31, 2026

N. Y. C. Marathon

Advertisement

Supported by

Running has long been celebrated as a cheap and accessible sport. But the culture of racing, especially in New York, is often anything but.

By Santul Nerkar

When Michael Conway lines up for the New York City Marathon on Sunday, he will have spent thousands of dollars before even starting to run across the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge.

Mr. Conway, 30, is serious about his running. He owns five pairs of running sneakers, each of which cost at least $160 and serves a different training purpose. Edible liquid gels to sustain him set him back hundreds more each year.

Then there are the fees for New York’s many competitive races, which he needs to run to gain entry into the marathon. And if his friends and family want to see him cross the finish line in Central Park, they’ll have to pay $60 to watch from the metal bleachers.

“A lot of people talk about just wanting to finish,” said Mr. Conway, a creative strategist based in Brooklyn. “If I don’t have a sub-4 time, I’ll be pissed.”

He represents one of the millions of people who have taken up running seriously in recent years. But while the sport has long been celebrated as cheap and accessible, the culture of racing — especially in New York — is often anything but.

Amateur athletes now routinely shell out thousands of dollars each year on carbon-plated shoes, track club memberships and race fees, not to mention fuel pouches and flashy apparel.

It can be a pricey endeavor, but the challenges of marathoning are not purely financial. Plenty of runners reach the finish line each year without premium gear. The recent boom in the sport’s popularity has made Sunday’s race an experience that not many are able to access.

Nearly a quarter of a million people applied to run the New York City Marathon through the lottery this year. Those runners are effectively throwing their names in a large hat and hoping their entry gets pulled. Just 1 percent, or 2,400, gained access that way.

In some sense, the problem is one of supply and demand, as the city’s physical size isn’t getting any bigger. Yet some have argued that the organization behind the marathon, New York Road Runners, could do more to make racing more affordable and accessible for ordinary people.

Roughly 60,000 people are set to run this year’s race.

Thousands of bibs are reserved each year for those who gain entry through time qualification. About a quarter of the bibs are set aside for people who raise money for charity. This leaves relatively few ways for everyone else to squeeze into the marathon — that distinctly New York experience.

One option is to participate in Road Runners’ popular 9+1 program, which requires runners to complete nine races and one volunteer opportunity in order to qualify for the marathon.

However, that program was overhauled in June, drawing sharp criticism from some runners.

Starting in 2028, participation will be based on a drawing, and runners will have to pay $99 to join 9+1. They will then have to pay more to enter each of the required races.

Mr. Conway described the new policy as forcing runners to pay for “the privilege to buy the privilege to buy the privilege to get into the marathon.” He said he spent roughly $350 to participate in the nine runs for this year.

New York Road Runners argues that it has taken serious steps to ease various costs associated with the marathon. It points to the fact that it has not raised its $255 marathon entry fee for its members in a decade, and that Mayor Zohran Mamdani has provided 350 free tickets to spectators for the finish line.

“Our goal as a local nonprofit is to have a positive impact on the city, its residents and visitors,” Road Runners said in a statement. “Through our work, we center making running more accessible for all people — maintaining affordability for our community.”

New York is not alone in facing skyrocketing demand. In June, the London Marathon announced that it would be expanding the 2027 race to two days.

Sunday will be Matt Portillo’s sixth New York Marathon and seventh overall. Mr. Portillo, 38, has time-qualified for all but one race in his life, allowing him to save on hundreds of dollars in race fees each year.

In that way, he considers himself privileged, but he wants to see fewer people taking part in the New York Marathon who are “already good at running” or who have the financial resources to compete in race after race.

“I want to see opportunities for people where they don’t have to pay to play or perform to play,” Mr. Portillo said.

In Mr. Conway’s view, running in races requires a certain level of materialism. But, he added, you can always “opt out of the system,” lace up your sneakers and enjoy the crisp fall air as you run on your own.

“There’s nothing stopping me from going to Central Park tomorrow morning and running 26.2 miles,” Mr. Conway said. “That’s still a marathon.”

Santul Nerkar is a Times reporter covering federal courts in Brooklyn.

Republicans Tried to Turn the Cheesecake Factory Against Democrats. It Flopped.

The New York Times October 31, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Michelle Goldberg

By Michelle Goldberg

Opinion Columnist

In the waning days of the midterm election campaign, Republicans have finally stumbled on a closing message: defending the honor of the Cheesecake Factory.

Last week, Barack Obama made a viral crack about Donald Trump’s renovations: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” Conservatives feigned outrage on behalf of the humble American volk for whom the Cheesecake Factory is the height of sophistication. Fox Business interviewed the centimillionaire Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, after lunch at the restaurant; he sniffed, “I would tell the Martha’s Vineyard set to give it a try.” (His Massachusetts beach house, which he sold for a couple of million dollars in 2012, was in Provincetown.) The Wall Street Journal suggested that Democrats had shot themselves in the foot in their quest to win back “the working man in Middle America.” The White House posted a list of Trump’s “accomplishments” in the style of a Cheesecake Factory menu.

Republicans have been trying to brand Democrats as the party of out-of-touch elitists since at least the 1960s, but this time, it felt particularly forced and desperate. After all, it’s become screamingly obvious which party represents billionaires and unchecked plutocratic power.

On the stump this week, an increasingly disinhibited Trump scoffed at the idea of “suffering at the pump” while boasting that high oil prices have been a windfall for the energy industry. Elon Musk, the richest person on earth, is almost single-handedly funding the Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton’s campaign. Susan Collins ran a closing ad in which a retired broadcaster seemed to mock her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, for being a logger, saying, “We’re not talking about buying a cord of wood here; we’re sending someone to the U. S. Senate.”

Meanwhile, Democrats all over the country are running against the ultrarich. “The biggest divide in this country is not left versus right,” the Texas Senate candidate James Talarico says on the campaign trail. “It’s top versus bottom.” In the Michigan Senate race, Abdul El-Sayed is a political protégé of Bernie Sanders who accuses his opponent, Mike Rogers, of being bought by corporations. Former Senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio, defeated with the help of crypto dollars two years ago, may regain his seat thanks in part to widespread fury at data centers and the tech billionaires behind them.

If Democrats win big on Tuesday after running such populist campaigns, it will be more than a victory over Trump. It will be an opportunity for them to once again develop an image as the champion of working people against predatory elites. That, in turn, could realign American politics. But it will happen only if Democrats can resist the entreaties of the tech donors and lobbyists who, having realized that going all in on MAGA was a bad bet, will now spend big to rebuild bridges to the center left.

For decades now, American politics has been shaped by two very different conceptions of class. Liberals tend to view class as a primarily economic distinction: a millionaire car dealer in the Midwest has a class advantage over a Brooklyn adjunct professor on food stamps. Conservatives, by contrast, are more likely to understand class as a matter of taste, culture and education. They’ve long seen America as riven between what some called a “new class” of intellectuals, professionals and bureaucrats and an alliance of capitalists and traditionalist blue-collar workers. “The simple truth is that the professional classes of our modern bureaucratized societies are engaged in a class struggle with the business community for status and power,” wrote Irving Kristol, godfather of neoconservatism, in 1972. (He very much sided with the beleaguered businessmen.)

Neoconservatism fell out of fashion, but Kristol’s ideas about class didn’t. If anything, as the two parties sorted by education, they became a kind of cultural common sense. Obama, who was still paying off student debt in his 40s, was tagged as an elitist, while Trump, who loves to brag about his wealth, was not.

The 2024 election was a triumph for the right’s conception of class politics, with Trump making gains with low-income voters while Kamala Harris won those earning over $200,000 a year. In surveys and focus groups, voters described Democrats as elitist and condescending. When the Democratic firm Navigator Research polled swing districts after the last election, 56 percent of respondents said the party didn’t look out for working people, and a majority said Democrats didn’t share their values. The road to winning back working-class voters looked difficult and uncertain.

Trump, by abandoning all restraint in his kleptocratic smash-and-grab, has made it easier. In a September poll from The New York Times and Siena University, voters identified Republicans as the “elitist” party by 10 points. The Times quoted a 40-year-old who’d voted for Trump two years earlier: “The people that are ‘in with him,’ who look or act a certain way, are the ones that are going to be given an opportunity.”

Few things have laid bare the president’s essential elitism like his alliance with America’s tech oligarchs. Trump ran against Big Tech in 2020, when he saw it as an ally of Democrats, but he was less interested in curbing the industry’s power than co-opting it. Now that he’s done that, tying Silicon Valley’s fortunes to his own, he can’t countenance criticism of it. He’s attempted, absurdly, to rebrand A. I. as “super intelligence,” and said that communities that reject data centers risk becoming “backwards and poor.”

Silicon Valley was once seen as a bastion of liberalism, but a recent Politico poll found that voters across the political spectrum now associate it with the Republican Party. At the same time, Big Tech — and particularly A. I. and data centers — has rarely been more reviled. This summer, a leaked memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee called data centers “a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle” and warned that public fury about them could cost the Republican Jon Husted his Senate seat in Ohio.

Rob Flaherty, former head of digital strategy for Joe Biden, is a founder of Tomorrow Together, a new super PAC that goes after Republicans for their ties to the A. I. industry. He shared polling his group commissioned about A. I. and data centers in several swing districts. In Pennsylvania’s Eighth District, held by a Republican, Rob Bresnahan, 51 percent of respondents feel strongly unfavorably toward data centers. Only 5 percent feel strongly favorably. Voters see A. I., Flaherty told me, as “these guys sitting in a room somewhere cooking up technology that’s going to make your life worse, making you pay for it, and buying off the government to do it.”

Now that Democrats seem likely to retake at least one house of Congress, tech companies are rushing to hire Democratic lobbyists. Given the enormous resources Silicon Valley kingpins wield, some Democrats might be tempted to seek a rapprochement with the industry. “I worry that Democrats are going to say, ‘We need to rebuild our alliances with tech,’ and miss the opportunity that’s in front of their face here,” said Flaherty. That would be a terrible mistake. The opportunity before Democrats is about more than being on the right side of a winning issue. Democrats have a unique chance, after decades of culture wars, to wrest the mantle of populism from Republicans and thus change the terrain on which American elections are fought.

“They are unanimous in their hate for me — and I welcome their hatred,” Franklin Delano Roosevelt said in 1936 about monopolists, speculators and war profiteers. Democrats should remember his words when they retake power. A good enemy is a terrible thing to waste.

The Times is committed to publishing a diversity of letters to the editor. We’d like to hear what you think about this or any of our articles. Here are some tips. And here’s our email: letters@nytimes. com.

Follow the New York Times Opinion section on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Bluesky, WhatsApp and Threads.

Michelle Goldberg has been an Opinion columnist since 2017. She is the author of several books about politics, religion and women’s rights and was part of a team that won a Pulitzer Prize for public service in 2018 for reporting on workplace sexual harassment.
