Martin McDonagh Says Art Can Change the World. Just Not as Much as Murder.

The New York Times October 31, 2026

The Interview

The Interview

Credit... Philip Montgomery for The New York Times

Supported by

By David Marchese

The writer-director Martin McDonagh has carved out a highly esteemed cinematic career as a chronicler of extreme, and often extremely bloody, behavior carried out on a relatively intimate scale. “The Banshees of Inisherin” (2022), to pick one of his films, was about two friends on a remote Irish island descending into a feud. “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri” (2017), to pick another, looked at a mother’s attempt to get justice for her murdered daughter. That those movies, despite their dark setups, are often as vulgarly funny as they are emotionally affecting is evidence of McDonagh’s originality — and his skill too. (McDonagh was an enfant terrible of the British theatrical world before he turned to filmmaking.) The 56-year-old’s films have earned a cumulative 18 Academy Award nominations, and “Six Shooter” (2004) earned him an Oscar for best live-action short.

With the new “Wild Horse Nine,” his fifth feature, which is already earning major awards-season buzz, McDonagh has widened the aperture. The movie, in theaters Nov. 6, follows two C. I. A. agents, played by John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell, who have been deployed to Chile in 1973 to destabilize the country’s nascent democracy after President Allende was elected. That setup, which pivots on a fateful trip to Easter Island, allows McDonagh to explore big ideas about political power and America’s foreign misadventures, in addition to his more typical forays into male friendship, interpersonal ethical dilemmas and gleefully crass humor. As he explained to me when we spoke in New York this fall, those elements all add up to something that for McDonagh — however counterintuitive it may seem — are expressions of hope.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Amazon | iHeart

“Wild Horse Nine” is coming out in the middle of a broader conversation — and argument — over America’s place in the world. That often comes down to a binary: Is America a force for good or bad? How do you see America’s place? Right now, I’m not sure. I guess we’re all a little bewildered about what it stands for. But the film explores a time when, seemingly, America’s place in the world was as the good guy, which is what most kids in the West — not just in the U. S. but in the U. K. and Ireland, Western Europe — are brought up to feel. The C. I. A. are the good guys and the K. G. B. are the bad guys; America is the good guy and Russia is the bad. But the more I read about what the C. I. A. were up to throughout the end of the last century, and particularly in Chile — to destabilize and help overthrow a democratically elected government, which ended up in fascist horrors for 15 years — it makes you think that you’re not being told the truth about the West and its moral outlook.

There’s a line in “Wild Horse Nine”: “Life is sad, everything is sad.” That line struck me as a melancholy iteration of a line from your play “The Pillowman,” which is: “The world’s a pile of [expletive].” There are moments of grace in your work, but is that your view? That’s not me. In both instances, it’s the setup to a joke, in a way. And both of those characters are quite nasty, tough cop characters. So I don’t know if that’s the way I feel about cops. I don’t think so. It’s weird because I guess my stuff comes out dark and sad in a lot of places, but I’m so the opposite. I never thought I’d be in a position to make a film, for instance. I never thought that would be open to me growing up as a working-class kid in London. So no, I definitely don’t feel that way about the world.

I do think of your work as generally pretty dark. Really?

Yeah. How could it be the case that the work doesn’t represent something about your innermost feelings about life? But questioning and disbelieving what you’re told isn’t dark, and making art is always hopeful, even if it’s dark art. I always think of Leonard Cohen and people saying that his stuff is depressing. I find it the total opposite. The tunes are beautiful. It’s poetic. I mean, I’m not disagreeing with people who say my stuff is on the dark side, but in the writing of it, I’m joyful. The performances are so wonderful, and the visual, cinematic parts of it are so wonderful, that darkness honestly doesn’t come into it from my perspective.

You said that making art is a hopeful act. Do you think the art that you make has the ability to change the people who see it? That’s a hard one. But if an audience has come out having laughed a lot and learned some stuff, particularly in this one about Chile, then that is what I’m after, and all of that is hopeful.

I used to agree with you, but now I don’t. I often think of a quote, from the British comedian Peter Cook, about the political efficacy of satire. He said, I’m paraphrasing, something like, Well, the greatest satire in the world was in Weimar Germany, and that stopped Hitler right in his tracks. [Laughs] It’s a very good line. Is hopeful work going to stop stuff? I don’t know. But is anything?

So I think of your work as —— Dark and bleak. [Laughs]

Dark and bleak, but also as the product of someone who likes to provoke a reaction, even if that’s a recoil. Um. …

Am I wrong about that? No, no. “Recoil” I might question. I often think about this. Yeah, it’s all quite provocative. It’s never intentionally offensive. It’s often outrageous. For instance, Malkovich’s character in this movie is outrageous. But I don’t think he, or even the film, or any of my stuff, is offensive. I always feel like my heart is in the right place morally. I have a predilection for being naughty. In this movie, there’s a scene about cheeses, for instance, that is quite naughty. But it never occurs to me to be offensive.

What’s the difference between being outrageous and being offensive? One is deliberately trying to hurt or attack an audience, whereas the other is to almost delight in something you haven’t heard before or you might not have thought of.

Do you want to say the thing about cheeses, or should I? You can go ahead.

So Malkovich’s character has a little disquisition about how what he calls the “gay countries” make the best cheeses. Yeah, Holland, France, the U. K. and Switzerland make great cheeses, and they are some of the “gay countries.” Russia is definitely not a gay country. I’m going to get in so much trouble.

It’s in the movie! It’s true. And Russia doesn’t have good cheese, and there’s a connection between the two, which is then connected to democracy, and democracy leads to gay, leads to good cheeses. Something I’ve thought about often and I think is true.

I’m sure there are people who will find that scene problematic or offensive. But when you’re watching it — and I’ve watched it with a whole lot of audiences, mostly pretty liberal audiences — the biggest laughs in the whole film are in that scene. And I think it’s because it’s outrageous, but there is some kind of weird something to it.

But going back 30 years, there have been people who have said your work is offensive. Do you feel as if the conversation about what causes offense — who can say what, and using what language — has evolved or changed in that time? It’s gotten worse, especially in the last 10 years. Only in the last 10 years have I been asked to change words in plays from 25, 30 years ago because of offense taken by certain words that wasn’t there 25 years ago. Those words were there to be either outrageous or to be truthful. If you’re writing a racist character, they’re going to use racist language. To try and cut those out 25 years later — for what reason? I’m never quite sure. If you don’t like that in a play, you should just not do the play. You shouldn’t try and change the play 25 years later.

Is it the N-word that people ask you to change? No, actually much softer, but words that could be seen as equally racist or offensive.

When I was preparing for this interview, I read a lot of essays about your work, and there were two that stood out to me on the topic of race. There was a piece by Hilton Als about your play “A Behanding in Spokane” where he equated a Black character in it to a Stepin Fetchit type. And my colleague at The Times, Wesley Morris, wrote a piece about “Three Billboards” where he said he thought the characters’ use of the N-word was glib. Those are two Pulitzer Prize-winning critics, both Black men, who saw something troubling in the work. Does that make you think, Maybe there is something I need to look at that I’m doing? Or do you think, No, they just don’t get it? After the play, the one that Hilton had the issue with, I did have a look back on it and wondered about the amount of offensive words. I felt my heart was in the right place when I wrote it, mostly about portraying the stupidity of the main guy who is racist. But you definitely take it on board. If you grew up completely antiracist, and that’s part of what your attempt at art is about, when that doesn’t go across to certain critics, you definitely have a think about it.

What do you think about it? Just to question the language a little bit in the next one, or maybe take a little more care about that subject. Less so about the film. I feel like the film was taken as redemption to a character that I didn’t feel was true. I don’t agree as much with that one.

Your work often generates questions about political correctness or the use of language. But there’s comparatively less writing about the violence. Why do you think one subject gets people agitated and the other — violence — seems to raise no questions for people? It’s weird, right? Well, I’d have to disagree.

You get it for violence, too? Yeah. That it’s gratuitous and always there and doesn’t need to be.

What do you make of that? I don’t think it’s always there, and I never make it gratuitous — never intentionally. Especially with the stage work, I was brought up having to watch English plays, which were, like, people drinking cups of tea for two and a half hours, and I always wanted to shoot them — onstage. [Laughs] So that naturally evolved into the plays I made. I’m being a bit glib, but I did think plays should be as exciting as the best films, and that meant you should be able to do anything onstage that you can do in a film, which led to a little violence now and then, but always with a moral dimension to it. Again, I would never want to be offensive with it. But I think they’ve been getting less and less violent. If you discount all the fingers in “Banshees,” there’s hardly any violence at all. I guess the donkey gets it, but offscreen!

“Wild Horse Nine” is a film, like “Banshees of Inisherin,” about characters who are thinking about their legacy — what they’re leaving behind and what their life will amount to. Is that a question that you think about? Oh, I knew you were going to go there. I think so. With every piece of work, you’re hoping to add to your canon of good stuff, and if you do enough of them or leave behind enough of them, that’s a route to happiness.

Why would leaving behind good work be a route to happiness? Well, you’ve got to have something. When you get a play right, it’s gone forever. It’s beautiful in the moment, but I can’t show you “The Beauty Queen of Leenane” from ’96, or “The Pillowman” from London. You put all your energy into those pieces of hopeful art and they’re gone. I think that’s probably why I’ve stuck with films lately, and why I’m happier artistically: They’re there and I can see them and I know that other people are going to be able to see them. In answer to the legacy bit of the question, it’s a pretty good thing if that’s what your role has been in the artistic world, just leaving some good films behind. I want them to be full of good acting and funny moments, and in this one a bit of truth about history that isn’t spoken about enough, and in “Banshees” a take on male friendship that’s not explored too much.

The new film is also about a male friendship. What ideas were you interested in exploring this time around? “Banshees” was the end of a loving male relationship. “Wild Horse Nine” is in the middle of a love affair, almost. I think of these two guys, Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich, as this old married couple who bicker and drive each other nuts, but there’s a love that’s fundamentally there in every scene. My male friendships are quite deep and sad and open and everything that a female friendship is acknowledged to be and is seen in the culture. I like the gentleness of my male friendships, and to show a bit more of that and not just have a buddy movie is what I was trying to get at with this film.

A lot of the male friends in your work are exploring ethical dilemmas. In your own life, have you and a friend had to work through an ethical problem? I don’t think so. Have you?

Of course. I think the great ethical dilemma of my life is, if it makes sense to say, a post-mortem ethical dilemma. I’m wasting your time talking about this. I’m loving it.

My best friend from growing up died from suicide. I had no idea he was hurting that much. And then trying to think through — this was a few years ago now — What were my ethical responsibilities there? How did I fail? What was I culpable for? And then also how much blame — or not — to apportion to him for what he did. I still think about it. And do you talk about that with your male friends?

Yeah. And do they have a similar feeling?

We have pretty different feelings. One of my good friends says this was an instance of mental illness and my friend had fallen through the care cracks, as it were, and how can you blame someone for that? But probably too harshly I can think, I don’t think he was mentally ill, and my friend who died does have some responsibility for what he did. I don’t think either of us are incontrovertibly right. Yeah, but even that right there is a fascinating discussion you’ve had with your close male friends, and that’s not necessarily something you ever really see in a Hollywood movie. And that, in a very different way, is what I’ve been trying to explore from “In Bruges” (2008) up to now.

I read a collection of academic essays about your work, and at the back of one there’s a biographical timeline. It says, at age 12, “Loses his Catholic faith and begins to listen to punk rock.” What was going on when you were 12? Were those things related? They totally were. I got into the Clash particularly around that age, 12 or 13. They were such a great band to help a kid question everything. I was a working-class kid who had no future apart from a dead-end job, and I left school very young, at 16. Bands like the Clash showed you that there was another way. You didn’t have to have a life that was dictated to you. You didn’t have to work in a factory or an office. There was hope. So, yeah, I grabbed onto that with both hands at the age of 12. And the Catholic thing, I think if you’re starting to question governments and people who force you to do things against your will, which is the punk-rock ethic, naturally the Catholic Church is going to be right in the firing line.

Have you ever regained your faith? No. There are parts of it that never fully go. I’m sure my moral sense is informed by the good stuff I took from the stories of Jesus or whatever. But I’m getting more and more entrenched in some kind of antireligious feeling in general. It is one of the worst things that’s happening in the world, and it seems to be getting worse.

What aspects of your current self would the Clash-loving teenage Martin McDonagh feel most proud of? And what are the aspects that would make him think, Oh, that’s who I turned out to be? Oh, god.

If any. I don’t want to assume you’ve betrayed any youthful ideals. Weirdly, the first time I learned about Chile and Allende and Victor Jara and all the things that this film talks about was from a Clash song called “Washington Bullets” on the album “Sandinista!” And again, I was like 12 or 13 when I first heard it, didn’t know any of these people or any of those situations, and started reading up about it. Joe Strummer was a god to me, and his passion and his morality was always an inspiration, and I always wanted to do something like that. I might have done it in one or two plays, but never in the films have I had a place of anger or wanting to help, I guess. So, for the first time, Joe might be proud of this one.

And what would make the teenage version of you roll your eyes at who you’ve become? That I probably don’t do enough to help in real life. That I have made too much money from it. I don’t have too much guilt about that, because it’s not like I’m killing anyone, I’m just making a film, but that complacency in real life is not what a proper punk rocker should be.

But you can change that now. I can change that this afternoon. What should I do?

Figure out what matters to you and find out how to help. But I think that would be making another film. You can get a viewpoint across to millions of people by making a film. If that’s going to help or not, we don’t know. But I would always come back to that.

So, I think of your dialogue as being stylistically identifiable. Are there things that you know you like to do? I couldn’t put my finger on exactly what it is, but it’s always just slightly overly theatrical and heightened in some way. Pinter and Mamet had a poetic heightening of how people really speak that I thought, This is the way to go.

I can hear Pinter and Mamet in your work — the attention to rhythm, the use of vulgarity, the interplay between a sophisticated wit and low comedy. But I also see your work as coming out of Tarantino — the shocking explosions of violence. [McDonagh bristles]

Was he not an influence early on? Early on. “Pulp Fiction” was around the time I was starting to write the plays. But I don’t really see it anymore. I remember in the early interviews I did, I name-checked him a bit, but I think my stuff has changed since then. That is the only reason I bristled, because I don’t quite see it anymore. And I don’t think our approach to violence is quite the same. The coolness of cinematic violence — I’m trying to walk away from that a little bit. I don’t think Quentin might be in the same place. We talked about gratuitousness, and it’s definitely something I’m trying to stay clear of these days.

You and Phoebe Waller-Bridge have been together for a decade. You’re both private about your relationship, but I read a quote that she gave about being inspired by your play “The Pillowman.” She said: “It was the first play I saw that made me think theater can be really exciting. Sometimes you need to see something like that — a piece of work that wakes you up, that makes you go, ‘Yes, of course that can be done,’ and gives your imagination permission to go 17 million other places.” What of her work has inspired you? “Fleabag” was game-changing and eye-opening and so insightful and funny. I learned so much about that woman, and women and feminism and storytelling. And then Season 2 took it to an even more beautiful place, and I think I learned a lot about love through Season 2.

What about love? Just about how important it is, and how lovely it is when you get there.

I want to return to the punk-rock informed portion of the interview. People are talking about “Wild Horse Nine” as an awards-season contender. You’ve been fortunate enough to be in that position a couple of times in your career. What’s the punk-rock part of Martin McDonagh’s soul that’s like, “I cannot believe I’m here doing this?” What makes you blanch? I knew you were going that way with the question. I knew it! What’s a punk-rock boy like you doing at the Oscars?

No, no. It’s not that. Good for you that you’re at the Oscars. I do ask myself that question.

I’m trying to understand where that part of you manifests in the world. I can see it in the work. It’s a good question. I’m not taking the piss.

You can take the piss. I’ve done it to you. You can do it back to me. That’s true! I think the young me would never give a damn about any kind of awards-y thing because it’s all irrelevant. But once you start getting nominated, I find it fascinating. I’m always googling, “Is John Malkovich still the leading contender?” Who’s coming up? Andrew Scott’s coming up. What can we do to destroy his race? [Laughs] Not really. But because even making films is so far away from anything I’d ever thought I’d be involved in, if you double that and think that an Oscar race is something you never thought you’d be involved in, I just find it fun and enjoy it. The work is the work. I would never change what the work is to get one, or make something Oscar-baity or any of that.

I would really like to see Martin McDonagh’s version of an “Oscar bait” movie. Jesus Christ, what would that be?

“The Orphan of Inisherin.” Who’s going to play it? Timothée Chalamet!

There you go. Hang on, he doesn’t win those, though. I’ve got to get it.

By the time he does your movie, he’ll be due. It’s all about the long game. True.

But earlier when you said you should be doing more to help, you then landed on making art as what you can do. That made me think about a scene in “Wild Horse Nine” where John Malkovich’s character is talking to a young left-wing student about going on a march, and he’s so cynically sarcastic. What do you expect to accomplish going on a march? I could imagine that the Malkovich character is even more cynical about the possibility of art changing the world. In your heart, who do you think is closer to the truth, you or him? [Long pause] I think art has changed things. But I think murder has probably changed a lot more. That’s a terribly bleak answer. But I ain’t going to murder anyone, so I’ve got to keep plowing on.

I was thinking about why I feel so pessimistic about the possibilities of art and I realized that a powerful counterargument to my feelings is already in your film: Victor Jara, the Chilean activist folk singer who was targeted and killed by the Pinochet regime. If the Pinochet regime didn’t think it mattered, they probably would have left him alone. And the Pinochet regime is gone and we still have his songs, so that’s something. But in terms of art changing the world, all of the art we’ve seen or the films we’ve loved or the paintings, they have changed the world, because they’re in it. They might not have changed things politically, but this world’s better because of the poems we love and the books we love and the films that we adore. So it’s not that it’s going to affect Trump or society necessarily, but it is a new piece of beautiful art that’s out there, and I think that is always hopeful.

This interview has been edited and condensed from two conversations. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

Director of photography (video): Tre Cassetta

David Marchese is a writer and co-host of The Interview, a regular series featuring influential people across culture, politics, business, sports and beyond.

Why Haley Stevens Can’t Stop Talking About Abdul El-Sayed

The New York Times October 31, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

House

Governor

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

In a frank interview, she described her disappointment and also said she was considering converting to Judaism. Her fiancé had thoughts, too.

By Reid J. Epstein

Reid J. Epstein had three conversations with Haley Stevens on Friday, including one over lunch at her home and two on the phone.

Representative Haley Stevens of Michigan stood up from her dining table, where the tuna fish and matzo ball soup sat half-eaten, and let loose about the moment she grew disillusioned with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed.

It happened this month, during her state’s first Senate debate between Dr. El-Sayed, who defeated her in a bitter Democratic primary in August, and former Representative Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee. Dr. El-Sayed, an outspoken critic of Israel, was asked if Iran or Israel posed a greater threat to the United States. He dodged the question, calling it a “ridiculous hypothetical.”

This was unacceptable to Ms. Stevens.

“He’s a good speaker,” she said during the lunchtime interview on Friday at her home in Birmingham, Mich., raising her voice and rising from the table. “He’s an orator. He is gifted. Then how does that happen? Come on!”

Since the debate, Ms. Stevens has sat for a procession of cable television interviews that have been increasingly critical of Dr. El-Sayed, her endorsement of him becoming shakier by the day. Their hug at a party unity brunch in August has faded into distant memory.

On Friday, Ms. Stevens announced that she would attend a Sunday church service in Detroit with Dr. El-Sayed, a peace offering brokered by Representatives Debbie Dingell of Michigan and James E. Clyburn of South Carolina. But Ms. Stevens’s statement came with a caveat: a demand that Dr. El-Sayed publicly disavow an ad that one of his allies posted online. She called the ad antisemitic because it blamed U. S. support for Israel for high grocery prices.

On Friday, Dr. El-Sayed pushed back.

In a blistering statement, he offered a reminder that he beat her in August and an assertion that “Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.”

Whether their planned joint appearance on Sunday will go ahead seems up in the air.

Ms. Stevens said late Friday that she was not sure if the church event was still happening, or even if she was still invited. She said that no one from Dr. El-Sayed’s team had called her on Friday. She also said she had not retracted her endorsement of him and did not plan to.

“I haven’t had time to digest this,” she said. She added, “I don’t think this is a melodrama.”

Some other Michigan Democrats have been baffled by Ms. Stevens’s unsupportive media tour in the final days of the campaign, with Dr. El-Sayed serving as a key chess piece in the party’s push to take back the Senate. Polls show Dr. El-Sayed in a close race with Mr. Rogers. To win the chamber, Democrats need to retain Democratic-held Senate seats like Michigan’s and flip at least four states held by Republicans.

“I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing,” Mallory McMorrow, a state senator who also ran for the U. S. Senate in Michigan and dropped out a month before the primary, said on CNN on Friday. “This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes.”

Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign declined to discuss Ms. Stevens’s commentary.

Ms. Stevens’s growing criticism of Dr. El-Sayed serves as a stark sign of just how fiercely resistant some moderate Democrats and Jewish voters remain to his candidacy.

Several times in the interviews, she returned to her anger over the online ad, made by Rebellion PAC, a left-wing group that backed Dr. El-Sayed, and his refusal to publicly disavow it. The El-Sayed campaign has said it did not make and is not responsible for the ad.

“Maybe it’s how you fund-raise, maybe it is what you want people to believe, but the reality is that we are not going to say that the cost of groceries is because of Jews and the Jewish state,” Ms. Stevens said. “We’re not going to say we don’t have health care because of Jews and the Jewish state.”

Ms. Stevens is not Jewish but has always been a pro-Israel Democrat. She attended a Jewish sleep-away camp as a teenager and now represents suburban Oakland County, which is home to a large segment of Michigan’s Jewish population. Tensions over Israel dominated her primary with Dr. El-Sayed, when the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s main super PAC spent at least $30 million backing her campaign.

She also now has a partner who may feel even more strongly about the issue than she does.

Her fiancé, Jason Turkish, a Jewish lawyer who has raised money for both Democrats and Republicans, has gone even further than she has in criticizing Dr. El-Sayed. He publicly endorsed Mr. Rogers and appeared at a campaign event with him on Wednesday.

Ms. Stevens said that in anticipation of her wedding next summer to Mr. Turkish, she had met with a rabbi to discuss the possibility of converting to Judaism.

Over lunch and in two subsequent phone calls, including one with both her and Mr. Turkish, Ms. Stevens said she felt compelled to speak out for Jewish constituents who are scared of the prospect of Dr. El-Sayed in the Senate.

“There’s people who are hurt and worried about a bunch of different things,” she said. “They’re making sacrifices because of affordability. Someone in the Jewish community said, — six months ago, it was during the primary — safety is our affordability issue because of attacks on Jewish elected officials’ homes, attacks to their lives, attacks on the synagogues.”

Ms. Stevens repeated her assertion that she supported all Democrats running, including Dr. El-Sayed, and that she planned to vote for him. But asked if she wanted him to win, she was more circumspect.

“I think he’s going to win,” she replied.

Asked again if she wanted Dr. El-Sayed win, she dodged again.

“I don’t know why you’d ask me that,” she said.

Pressed one more time about her public criticism of Dr. El-Sayed, she offered a little more.

“I ran for a Democratic nomination, intent in understanding that I wanted a Democrat to win,” she said. “We sat down for a long period of time, Abdul and I did, in the first quarter of ’25, before we both decided to run, making that commitment to each other, so of course.”

It was not a ringing endorsement.

But while Mr. Rogers has welcomed Ms. Stevens’s supporters, she said he had not called her.

Then there is the matter of Mr. Turkish.

Even as Ms. Stevens had lunch with a New York Times reporter, Mr. Turkish was sitting for his own interview live with TMZ. He said Ms. Stevens would pull her support from Dr. El-Sayed if he did not soon disavow the grocery prices ad.

“I don’t think she’s going to be supporting Abdul El-Sayed very much longer,” Mr. Turkish told TMZ.

After his comments aired, Ms. Stevens invited the Times reporter to call her back, and this time she had Mr. Turkish on the line.

She said that her fiancé had not caused her to change her positions on Israel or Dr. El-Sayed.

“I think I’ve changed his opinion,” she said. “He goes, ‘You’re more Jewish than me.’”

In the interview, Mr. Turkish said he had expected Dr. El-Sayed to “move to the middle” on Israel after the primary. He called Dr. El-Sayed’s response to the debate question about Iran and Israel “the tipping point for me” and declared that his own safety would be in jeopardy if Dr. El-Sayed were elected to the Senate.

“I think I’d be less safe on this planet if Abdul El-Sayed is the senator, if he is insisting on sticking to the current program,” Mr. Turkish said. “He is so unwelcoming to people who have reasonable anxieties about Jews being scapegoated once again, as they have been for thousands of years, that the idea that he will steer not just U. S. policy, but foreign policy globally, it makes me extremely, extremely anxious.”

Mr. Turkish said he believed Ms. Stevens, 43, still had a bright future in politics.

“I know there’s going to be other opportunities,” he said. “I think she can run for the United States Senate again if she wants to.”

Though he is a veteran fund-raiser and an accomplished lawyer, Mr. Turkish had not been a sought-after political surrogate. His endorsement had never made news before now.

But he said he felt compelled to make a public endorsement for Mr. Rogers and appear with him at a campaign event because he did not want his public image to be a late-night TV sendup of him and Ms. Stevens.

“My friends and family members are asking me what I’m doing,” Mr. Turkish said. “I think they wanted to hear more from me than what they got off of two spoofed appearances on ‘The Tonight Show.’”

Reid J. Epstein is a Times reporter covering campaigns and elections from Washington.

As Midterms Near, Top Law Firms That Capitulated to Trump Are on the Sidelines

The New York Times October 31, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

House

Governor

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

None of the firms that struck deals to avoid crippling executive orders are publicly involved in the major legal efforts to check the Trump administration’s attempts to meddle in the midterm elections, a review by The New York Times shows.

By Michael S. Schmidt and Jim Rutenberg

Whenever Norm Eisen, a leader of the legal resistance against President Trump, wanted to try to hold Mr. Trump accountable over the last decade, one of his first calls was to Brad Karp, the chairman of the white shoe law firm Paul Weiss.

Without hesitation, Mr. Karp would give Mr. Eisen free legal counsel on how to best oppose Mr. Trump, and would then deploy the firm’s vast legal muscle — at no cost — to help.

“He was one of the greatest champions of voting and civil rights — and for democracy — in the country, and to have someone like that advising you, resourcing you and fighting for you was indispensable,” Mr. Eisen said.

Now, as Mr. Eisen prepares to lead a coalition that has vowed to stop Mr. Trump if he tries to interfere in the midterm elections, Paul Weiss, one of nine firms to strike deals with the administration to avoid crippling executive orders, is largely on the sidelines, according to Mr. Eisen and a lawyer with direct knowledge of the matter.

The void left by Paul Weiss is only a sliver of the impact of the deals the nine firms made with Mr. Trump early in his second term. In exchange, they pledged to do nearly a billion dollars in free legal work to causes Mr. Trump champions, casting doubt on whether they would be willing to stand up to the president.

Measuring the consequences of the deals is difficult, but the lead-up to the midterm elections offers new clues. Few of the nine firms are publicly involved in the major legal efforts to check Mr. Trump and his administration’s attempts to meddle, a review of public documents and interviews with democracy advocates, election lawyers and voting rights litigators shows.

The absence of the firms has raised serious worries about whether the legal profession is equipped to respond to the administration, which has already begun to file litigation intended to sow confusion about the outcome of the election. But lawyers like Mr. Eisen say that they are just as prepared and point to a string of recent court victories as evidence of their prowess.

Some of the firms have scrubbed their websites of their storied histories working on voting rights cases. At one firm that made a deal with Mr. Trump, several lawyers are quietly volunteering to help voting rights causes, hoping that their bosses do not find out, according to a lawyer at one of the firms who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The chilling effect, the interviews show, has extended to several of the top 100 firms in the United States that did not cut deals with Mr. Trump. Fearing being targeted, they have also avoided politically sensitive cases, according to interviews.

So many of them — including ones that have made deals with Mr. Trump and those that have not — have declined to help one longtime civil rights group, the Advancement Project, that it has started an internal tracker to stay on top of all the firms declining to team up on cases.

“I’ve been told, ‘We don’t do civil rights work involving the administration anymore,’ and, ‘We don’t do voting rights work anymore,’’’ said John Powers, the legal director at the Advancement Project, which often litigates voting rights cases by joining with better-financed private firms.

Most recently, when the Advancement Project filed suit with the N. A. A. C. P. against aspects of the Justice Department’s election-monitoring plans this fall, it had to set out on its own without a private partner. (On Friday, Mr. Powers said that it had received a new offer of help.)

“It’s been a sea change,” Mr. Powers said.

In some cases, Mr. Powers added, partners at firms working with the Advancement Project pulled back their support, dropped out entirely or agreed only to help on the condition that they not be named publicly.

“All too often we’re having to find workarounds because we don’t have the support,” he said.

Mr. Powers would not name the firms because he was hoping the private support would return in the future, he said.

“The pendulum is going to swing,” he predicted.

Law firms have played a key role since the civil rights movement in checking the federal government, even though suing the government over voting and civil rights cases typically pays far less compared with representing corporations. But the chance to work on those issues pro bono became a persuasive recruiting tool for firms. It served as evidence that incoming associates could not only make a lot of money assisting companies and wealthy people, but also do good.

During elections in recent decades, associates and partners have volunteered to be stationed in swing states where they could quickly initiate legal challenges on Election Day or if there was a contested counting of the results. Firms have pledged to represent poll workers while also bringing complex legal challenges against states encroaching on voting rights.

Paul Weiss repeatedly promoted its role in a landmark 1965 voting rights case. Dozens of articles and news releases on its website laid out its work during the Trump era on voting rights and election law.

“We remain steadfast in our commitment, supporting recent voting rights actions in several courts nationally as counsel of record,” the firm wrote on its website on a page dedicated to its pro bono election rights work.

But some time after Paul Weiss, which donated more money to Democrats in 2024 than any other firm, struck the deal with Mr. Trump in March 2025, the page for voting rights was taken down, along with 30 other pages related to its work on the subject.

A search of the firm’s website for the words “voting” and “voting rights” returns just two results.

Paul Weiss and seven other firms did not respond to questions asking for examples of voting rights cases or other matters the firm is working on in opposing the administration. (One of the firms that made a deal with Mr. Trump — Cadwalader, Wickersham & Taft — merged with another firm.)

Mr. Trump’s norm-breaking use of power during his first term, like child separation at the border, led many firms to use their pro bono hours to oppose the administration. His attempts to interfere with the 2020 election only established more fodder.

But the postures of the firms changed during Mr. Trump’s second term.

During Mr. Trump’s first term, firms deployed their resources to oppose Mr. Trump because they faced no cost for doing so, financially or politically.

But now firms see those cases as liabilities for their profits.

In their place, lawyers like Mr. Eisen have helped establish a network of lawyers across the country. It includes pro-democracy groups, legal nonprofits, public interest law firms and a few of the most high-profile firms, like WilmerHale, that fought back when Mr. Trump targeted them with executive orders.

Mr. Eisen, who leads the Democracy Defenders Fund, said that while the group of lawyers may be different, the quality of the legal work remains. He added that he had more than enough lawyers to counter Mr. Trump in court.

“We have not seen a single time in the past 20 months in which I did not have the resources,” he said. “The muscle is still there.”

Even if Paul Weiss or any of the firms that made deals with Mr. Trump wanted to help, Mr. Eisen said, he and his clients would not trust that they would zealously represent them, given the leverage Mr. Trump continues to hold.

At the same time, Mr. Eisen acknowledged, the attempts to hold Mr. Trump accountable could use Mr. Karp, his expertise and the army of lawyers he used to deploy.

“I miss Brad,” he said.

Aric Toler contributed reporting. Alain Delaquérière and Seamus Hughes contributed research.

Michael S. Schmidt is an investigative reporter for The Times covering Washington. His work focuses on tracking and explaining high-profile federal investigations.

Jim Rutenberg is a writer at large for The Times and The New York Times Magazine and writes most often about media and politics.

When there is A. I. to build, who has time for romance? Techies are going out less and expecting more on each date — including a family health history.

San Francisco’s A. I. boom has drawn a wave of young ambitious people who are now reshaping the city’s dating life. Credit... Kelsey McClellan for The New York Times

Supported by

By Emmy Martin

Reporting from San Francisco

Mehul Agarwal, a co-founder of the artificial intelligence start-up Koyal, has a goal. He wants to find a wife before he gets rich.

The 24-year-old says he wants to be loved before the money comes, so he never has to wonder whether a partner is attracted to him or his success. But he has strict criteria.

A potential girlfriend must be smart, Mr. Agarwal said, adding that “someone who went to Stanford or M. I. T. is great.” She must be beautiful, which he is careful to distinguish from “hot,” a term he considers shallow. She must be kind, and in possession of a personality, “which is very, very hard when in San Francisco,” he said. And finally, she has to like him back.

Mr. Agarwal moved to San Francisco a year ago, when his A. I. filmmaking company, which has raised $3.4 million, joined the start-up accelerator Y Combinator. This year, he has been on a handful of dates. On one, which took two months to schedule, Mr. Agarwal said, he and his date were both exhausted from their jobs — she worked at an A. I. start-up, too — and they were so practiced at professional small talk that the evening felt less like a date than a networking meeting.

“What I’ve told my parents is if I’m 28 and haven’t found someone, then I would love to enter in the arranged marriage circuit,” said Mr. Agarwal, who has never had a girlfriend.

San Francisco’s A. I. boom has drawn a wave of young ambitious people who are now reshaping the city’s dating life. Start-up founders and engineers are dating less because they are working more as they try to build A. I. products and establish their fortunes, many said. So when they date, they bring a high-stakes mind-set to it, which means a first coffee can feel like a final-round interview.

“You don’t need to understand if they have cancer in their family, you don’t need to understand on the first date if they really want three children,” said Sina Hartung, 29, a co-founder of the A. I. health technology company Eureka Health who became exasperated by the dating scene in San Francisco. She lived there for three years before moving to New York in August.

The intensity is showing up in the daters who screen partners against fixed criteria, in those who outsource their messages to chatbots and in the dating coaches who charge thousands of dollars a month to translate romance into the language of a start-up.

Founders “don’t want to waste time, so you only go on a date when you really feel there’s something to explore,” said Mr. Agarwal, who works long hours. Many A. I. start-up workers keep “996” schedules — 9 a. m. to 9 p. m., six days a week — a norm borrowed from China’s tech scene.

Joyce Zhang, 32, a dating coach in San Francisco who charges $5,000 a month, works exclusively with tech founders, she said. A former product manager at the payments company Stripe, she coaches clients using the tech vocabulary they already think in — their “top of funnel” (the raw pool of prospects) and their “conversion rate” of dates that actually happen.

Her clients approach dating as any other problem to be solved with money, Ms. Zhang said. Some have connected their dating-app data to spreadsheets to track their matches; others obsess over gaming the apps’ algorithms.

Clients also run their replies to dates through A. I. chatbots like ChatGPT, she said. Some share their entire dating history with ChatGPT and ask the chatbot to diagnose their patterns. In those cases, Ms. Zhang said, she spends the coaching sessions pushing the techies toward trusting their intuition. Her job, she said, is to help them overcome their “blind spots.”

Amanda Chung, 25, who works at the A. I. start-up Nectar Social, is single and dates casually. Fresh off a long relationship and wanting to keep things low-key, she said most of the men she had met in San Francisco wanted something serious “even if they aren’t ready for it yet.”

One founder she saw for a few weeks would meet only after 10 p. m. because of his work schedule. Another spent an evening quizzing her about her job and her working style, “trying to check off boxes internally,” she said.

The prospects were so uninspiring that she eventually paused her Hinge account. “I was like, oh, wow, is that really it?” Ms. Chung said.

San Francisco has long had a reputation for skewing male and nerdy in the 20-something dating pool, with many female residents popularizing the phrase, “The odds are good but the goods are odd.”

The city has about 106 men to every 100 women, versus roughly 98 men to every 100 women nationally, according to the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey. Dowell Myers, who studies population change at the University of Southern California, said the recent A. I. arrivals might not yet register in census data, which lags by about two years.

In some corners of San Francisco, young singles are getting creative with dating. On a Saturday night at Kilowatt, a bar in the Mission neighborhood, people packed together for an event called “Date My Ex,” where participants on a stage pitch someone they love in five minutes or less, with a slide deck. Attendees wore name tags and waved paper hearts on sticks whenever a pitch landed, like bidders at an auction for other people’s exes.

One presenter rated the friend he had come to pitch on a bar graph against “the average dating experience.” Another slide read: “5’11” (but his hair adds 2” so kinda 6’1”)” and “works in tech (but isn’t happy about it).”

Still another presentation was about Joe Berusch, 27, who keeps “one foot out” of the tech world. He said he was convinced the intense daters who asked about family medical history on a first date were a loud local minority. A. I. has made many of the chores of adult life so frictionless that people expect dating to work the same way, but it’s “fundamentally” different, he said.

The “Date My Ex” event was part of a “Date My Friend” series run by Annalise Wulf, 25, and two friends as a tongue-in-cheek rebuke of San Francisco’s extreme dating requirements and as an alternative to dating apps.

“People in San Francisco, they work really hard, they have crazy long hours, especially in the start-up culture,” Ms. Wulf said. “So to even go on a date with someone, if it doesn’t feel amazing, if the sparks aren’t flying right away — it just takes time to develop those things, and I don’t think a lot of people in San Francisco have the time to do that.”

Mr. Agarwal, meanwhile, is still looking for someone who meets his criteria. His most promising prospect this year did not work out because of his schedule. They had two dates before he left for three weeks to India, where his start-up does much of its business. Then he spent five days in Los Angeles. Then there was more travel.

“I need to be really sure, and I don’t know her well enough to make that kind of bet,” he said.

That gives him three and a half years to find the love of his life before he turns the search over to his parents.

Emmy Martin is a reporter covering the technology industry from San Francisco and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship class.

What to Know About China’s Top-Secret Spaceplane

Wired October 29, 2026

A winged Chinese spacecraft bearing a strong resemblance to the US military’s X-37B spaceplane was photographed in orbit by a passing US-owned commercial satellite in 2024, and we finally have the image.

The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays. In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the US Space Force.

The photo was taken by a commercial imaging satellite owned by a company called Vantor, known as Maxar in 2024. Vantor is one of several companies that provide reconnaissance imagery of locations around the world to the US military and US intelligence agencies. The same Earth-imaging satellites can point their telescopes at objects in space.

Lower-resolution views of a Chinese spaceplane showing the vehicle’s general shape were publicly available before the Defense Intelligence Agency assessment. A US Space Force official revealed Maxar’s observation at a 2024 conference in South Korea, but the Pentagon did not release the full-resolution image to the public until Monday, when it appeared in an unclassified DIA assessment of threats to the United States in space.

The DIA report doesn’t reveal much new about what the Chinese spaceplane does in orbit. China has launched four spaceplane missions since 2020, with durations of up to nine months. The fourth mission is in orbit today after launching in February. It is not publicly known whether China has one or more such spaceplanes in its inventory.

The Space Force has two X-37Bs flying in rotation, with the longest of their eight missions to date running two-and-a-half years from launch until landing. US officials have released photos of the X-37B vehicles, published information about their design and dimensions, and disclosed a handful of experiments they have carried into orbit. Most of the X-37B’s activities in space are classified.

Like the X-37B, China’s spaceplane lifts off inside the payload shroud of a conventional rocket, then operates as a satellite once in orbit. The spaceplane flies like a miniature unpiloted version of NASA’s Space Shuttle and reenters the atmosphere for an autonomous land runway landing at the end of each mission. Ground teams then refurbish it for another flight.

The “enhanced maneuverability” of spaceplanes makes them “more suitable for certain missions than traditional satellites,” the DIA said in its report. So far, the Chinese spaceplane has only flown in low-Earth orbit (LEO) at an altitude of a few hundred miles. One of the Space Force’s X-37B flights soared to an altitude of more than 24,000 miles before using aerobraking to set up for reentry and landing.

Spaceplanes like China’s and the X-37B can also deploy small satellites from their cargo bay. Most recently, China demonstrated an ability to catch an object in orbit, perhaps using a robotic arm. The vehicle now in space released a sub-satellite in June and recaptured it in July, then did the same thing again in August and September, according to an analysis of open source orbital tracking data by Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist who catalogs spaceflight activity.

The official name of the Chinese spaceplane is even a mystery. It is often called Shenlong in Western publications, citing reports from the 2000s about China’s development of a robotic spaceplane. Chinese state media only refer to the vehicle as Chongfu Shiyong Shiyan Hangtian Qi, or CSSHQ, which means reusable experimental spacecraft, according to a fact sheet published by the Secure World Foundation.

The DIA did not disclose the exact circumstances of Maxar’s observation of the Chinese spaceplane, such as its timing, location, or distance, but Earth observations often use cameras to view other objects in space as their orbits intersect, an emerging field known as non-Earth imaging (NEI).

NEI allows commercial operators and government analysts to inspect satellites. This is especially useful for gleaning information about classified or proprietary satellite designs, extending a new avenue for international and corporate espionage to the high frontier.

The capability exhibited by Maxar and other commercial companies in the NEI field is distinct from the recent actions of some military spacecraft, such as Russia’s Kosmos 2612, which deliberately maneuvered to approach a US-registered radar imaging satellite earlier this month. Commercial NEI observations come from chance encounters, often at extremely high speed.

The DIA’s assessment of space threats includes an update on China’s pursuit of anti-satellite technology, or “counterspace” weapons. The intelligence agency reported the Chinese military likely considers directed-energy weapons (DEWs) “ideal counterspace systems” because they can be used to permanently or temporarily disable a satellite. One potential use for lasers in space would be to dazzle a sensor on an adversary’s satellite.

“China has multiple ground-based laser weapons with varying power levels to disrupt, degrade, or damage satellites in LEO,” the DIA said. “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits.”

The DIA noted China’s testing of ground-based anti-satellite missiles and the country’s historic demonstration last year of satellite refueling in geosynchronous orbit, a regime some 22,000 miles (36,000 kilometers) over the equator, something no other country has achieved above LEO. China has also tested a robotic arm that could snag a spacecraft out of orbit, and now operates a growing fleet of satellites called TJS that routinely approach foreign spacecraft.

The US Space Force also has a constellation of inspector satellites in geosynchronous orbit and recently procured more that could be refueled, overcoming maneuverability limitations. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed last month that the Pentagon has fielded weapons in space, making the United States the first nation to acknowledge possession of orbital weapons.

Russia is pursuing its own orbital combat program, which includes an ambition to deploy a nuclear weapon in space, according to US intelligence officials.

A more conventional Russian weapons system, known as Nivelir, is designed to fire projectiles from one satellite to smash into another. The Russian military simulated an attack using the Nivelir system in 2020. In April, Russia launched a fleet of small satellites into an orbit close to a commercial radar remote sensing satellite owned by ICEYE that provides reconnaissance imagery to Ukraine. One of the Russian satellites moved within “tens of meters” of the ICEYE satellite earlier this month before backing away, US officials said.

This story originally appeared on Ars Technica.

Polymarket Halted International Trading After Hackers Drained Accounts

Wired October 29, 2026

Trading has resumed on Polymarket’s flagship international platform after a hack that drained money from the wallets of some traders.

A third-party vendor based in the United Kingdom was breached, not the prediction market’s website itself. Law enforcement in the UK have been notified of the incident, the company said. Trading was initially paused while the company investigated for several hours.

On X, prominent traders complained that they had lost money; blockchain analytics firm Bubblemaps reported that around 700 users appeared to have been affected, with approximately $2.7 million stolen. Polymarket declined to comment when WIRED asked how many traders were impacted by the breach and how much money was lost, but the company said it will refund impacted traders.

The hack did not impact users on Polymarket US, the company’s newer platform for people within the United States. Polymarket runs two separate prediction markets; Polymarket US operates as a federally regulated financial exchange within the country, while the flagship Polymarket is a cryptocurrency-based platform that is banned in the United States and a number of other countries.

This is not the first time that Polymarket traders have experienced security woes. In June 2026, Polymarket experienced another breach, which resulted in over $2 million in losses for impacted traders.

The company has been a lightning rod for controversy since its 2020 launch. In the past few years, it has been the center of several high-profile alleged insider trading incidents resulting in arrests. One case involved a Special Forces soldier accused of wagering on the capture of Venezuela’s former leader; another involved a Google employee who allegedly used confidential information to make millions. In both cases, the suspects have pleaded not guilty.

Polymarket recently raised $1 billion in August 2026, with a fundraising round led by 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. It is now valued at $21 billion.

A Defense Contractor Gave Their Personal AI Agent Access to a Secure Pentagon System

Wired October 29, 2026

Earlier this year, sources tell WIRED, a contractor caused a security incident at the Department of Defense by connecting a secure centralized system used by multiple intelligence agencies to their personal account for Claude Code, Anthropic’s AI coding agent. It appears that the agent used by the contractor, who is employed by the global consulting firm Accenture, then sent information about the DOD system, including login credentials, to a high-risk, third-party website.

The centralized system contains controlled unclassified information (CUI), which is considered sensitive and not to be released to the public without review. CUI can include information about critical infrastructure, nuclear submarine propulsion, and vulnerabilities to chemical and biological terrorism. Additionally, security experts say, access to the system could allow for the exploitation of even more sensitive ones.

“It puts all the data that’s in there at risk,” says a source aware of the incident, who requested anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the press. If the third-party software was compromised, “there could be somebody out there with the ability to log into a secure environment without anyone knowing. It’s 100 percent a national security threat and could cause irreparable harm.”

A DOD spokesperson tells WIRED that “the Department does not comment on the status of its networks or systems.”

“We take all concerns seriously. These allegations were thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit. We fully complied with our legal and contractual obligations,” an Accenture spokesperson tells WIRED. When pressed, Accenture didn’t offer clarification on who conducted the investigation, or dispute that there had been what could be characterized as an incident.

The Accenture employee is alleged to have connected a secure production environment to their personal Claude account so as to allow an AI agent to write and deploy code. Claude is currently barred from being used by DOD staff. (Anthropic directed WIRED to the company’s usage policy, which instructs users not to use its products to “interfere with the operation of military bases and related infrastructure” or to “bypass security controls such as authentication systems, end point protection, or monitoring tools without authorization.”)

The Accenture employee’s AI agent ran on the DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched. Sources indicate that despite the security risks posed by the AI coding agent, Accenture employees did not treat the incident as severe or urgent. DOD employees and federal contractors are required to report any cybersecurity incident within 72 hours of its discovery, but sources indicate Accenture did not initially report the breach to the government at all.

“We are in a conflict with Iran right now,” says the employee, noting that Iran has attempted to hack several federal agencies and parts of US infrastructure. “It’s the worst time to be having this kind of cavalier attitude.”

Accenture currently has more than $3.5 billion in contracts with the federal government, nearly $605 million of which are with the DOD. The company also contracts with other federal agencies, such as the Department of Education, the General Services Administration, and the Department of Energy, among others. Earlier this month, the Federal Bureau of Investigation found that an Accenture contractor failed to patch a vulnerability that led to the hacking group ShinyHunters getting access to the details of thousands of the Bureau’s employees. The FBI removed that contractor in early October.

Matt Triner, founder of Hunter Strategy, a Washington, DC-based IT consulting company, says that the issue exemplifies the conflicting demands government contractors face more broadly. “Organizations are often punished for reporting incidents like this, even though it’s the right and legal thing to do,” says Triner. In many cases, he says, a company could lose government contracts by admitting they’ve had a security breach, though he says that an incident like the one described is “absolutely one that would need to be reported.”

Triner also notes that the increasing pressure on contractors to deliver projects faster and at a lower price point is at odds with prioritizing safety and security. “Unfortunately, everyone is operating in a system where there are competing rules and incentives, and that existed before AI, but now it’s the same problem on speed,” says Triner.

The coding environment accessed by the Accenture contractor is run on the Non-classified Internet Protocol Router Network (NIPRNet), a DOD network used for unclassified information. While it does connect to the internet—contractors and employees can access their emails and web browsers through the network—it is heavily secured.

According to the source, in order to automate the process of writing code and spinning up cloud servers, the contractor gave their login credentials to the Claude agent. This gave the agent administrative access and allowed it to bypass the security controls enforced through the normal login process. The AI agent—which was not only writing code but also committing it or saving the code into the system on behalf of the Accenture employee—needed to connect out to the internet to perform its tasks. In doing so, it appears to have sent the contractor’s login credentials, passwords, and a map of NIPRNet out to a third-party website.

WIRED is declining to name the third-party website so as to protect the system from further vulnerability, but the National Institute of Standards and Technology has previously identified it as high risk because it has a vulnerability that could let hackers inject instructions into an AI coding agent to steal credentials.

The system the AI agent accessed contained CUI. “Information from a CUI environment is not supposed to leave that infrastructure,” says the source. “There is no insight about what happened to the information, including the login credentials, after it was sent to [that service], whether it’s been retained”

Depending on the agency and its work, CUI can include anything from personally identifiable information to proprietary business or contracting information. According to the DOD’s website, CUI can include information on “the securing and safeguarding of explosives, hazardous chemicals, or pipelines,” documentation related to the designs of “military or space equipment or technology,” and “the exact location and quantities of radioactive material.”

Distinct from the actual data, a map of it could be incredibly valuable to a hacker. “Once an attacker understands how those things fit together, even if those things are public information, what is sensitive is how we are putting those things together and turning that into actionable intelligence,” says Triner.

While a map might not get a hacker into a system, he says, it could help an adversary move faster once they do have access and “help an attacker understand where the crown jewels are.”

Jake Williams, a former NSA hacker and faculty at IANS, an intelligence and security consultancy, says that an AI agent running code in NIPRNet presents a “huge problem, and there are huge national security impacts.”

Williams notes that while individual pieces of data or information might be considered CUI, “when that unclassified information is aggregated, that can become classified itself.” For instance, the location of certain hazardous materials might be CUI, as might be information about the vulnerability of the facilities that house them. Combined, however, they could reveal information that would be kept classified.

But this is not the only way classified information may have been put at risk. Frequently, tools and code are tested in NIPRNet before being deployed into more sensitive systems like the Secret Internet Protocol Router Network (SIPRNet), the military’s secured network for classified information, and Joint Worldwide Intelligence Communications System (JWICS), a secure intranet for top secret information. Both SIPRNet and JWICS are air gapped, a security measure that means they are not connected to any outside networks. On a practical level, that means SIPRNet and JWICS would be extremely difficult for a hacker to access remotely.

But with the login credentials exfiltrated by an AI agent, a hacker could access NIPRNet and insert a backdoor or other malicious code into a tool or system. Without proper review, this code could end up deployed in one of the air-gapped systems.

“The code could operate completely normally in NIPR and do something malicious and undisclosed in a SIPR network, that is 100 percent possible,” says Williams. Exfiltrating data out of these networks would be difficult, he adds, but malicious code could be used to attack the systems from the inside. “I think the most likely thing would be some kind of distributed denial of service attack,” he says.

Triner says that even something more subtle, such as slowing down intelligence operations and activities, could cause damage and make users lose trust in a tool, even once the problem is fixed.

As vibe coding, or prompting an AI assistant to write the code for a product described by an engineer, is becoming more common, vetting code is becoming more of a challenge. AI is capable of generating code at a volume that far surpasses human productivity, making it time-consuming and difficult to vet.

“When you’re using an agent, you have no idea of the supply chain or even the inference chain of what has ultimately generated the code,” says Williams. “A lot of the code that these LLMs were trained on is itself vulnerable, and they can regurgitate the same kinds of architecture and architectural issues that we see in other code.”

The government does have a way to identify flawed code in NIPRNet. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) scans code for bugs and flaws before allowing it to run. But Williams notes that a hacker-inserted “backdoor is not a vulnerability, even if we may not want it there,” and therefore would likely fly under the radar of SAST’s detection. SAST also does not usually identify structural issues in the logic chain of how code is created.

There’s no indication that hackers were able to get into a classified or top-secret system. Still, Williams says, the incident should raise significant alarms. “Architecturally, any information about NIPR that you can’t see through open-source intelligence, DOD considers a close hold regardless of whether something touches a classified network,” he says.

This is not the first time the DOD has been made vulnerable because of AI-related issues. Last year, ProPublica revealed that Microsoft was using “digital escorts” on its projects with the federal government, wherein American employees with security clearances would be overseeing code written by outsourced workers in China. Experts who spoke to ProPublica said that the program presented a particular security risk because the American employees were often not able to vet the code themselves, leaving openings for malicious code to be inserted unknowingly into government systems.

The ‘Pain in the Ass’ Math That Could Save Vibe Coding From Itself

Wired October 29, 2026

Stanford researcher Chuyue Sun and her fellow computer scientists developed an AI tool that completed an engineering project in less than half a day for under $500, compared to the five months it took three highly skilled experts to do the same work manually. The dramatic reduction in time and cost, which Sun reported in a recent paper, is among the early results that are awakening an obscure field of coding and mathematics known as formal verification.

For decades, developers have envisioned using math to prove that their software is bug-free. This process is long and laborious, requiring engineers to write precise statements about the goals of their software and convert their code into formulas that can be validated. While companies already run sophisticated tests to identify as many flaws in their software as possible, they rarely shell out for formal verification, which can catch even more erratic behavior.

Now, a wave of startups is betting that generative AI will make formal software verification both practical and essential. Among them is &Truth, which Sun joined in August and which publicly launched on Thursday. Sun’s research demonstrated the technology’s potential by using AI to verify part of the code that encrypts conversations in the messaging app Signal.

“Bridges, buildings, they don’t collapse, because people did math before constructing them,” says Ilya Sergey, &Truth’s chief science officer. “Why don’t we do the same for code? The technology to mathematically reason was all there, just difficult to scale.”

&Truth has raised $70 million from investors and aims to eventually verify any programming language. Rival Harmonic, which was cofounded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev and has received $295 million in funding, announced this week that its math-focused AI agent Aristotle supports verifying software written in C and hardware designs in Verilog. It is evaluating the technology with potential users, including chipmakers Tensordyne and Nvidia, whose venture capital arm is one of the startup’s investors.

And just last week, Anthropic and the verification startup Theorem jointly announced they had used AI to assist in finding bugs in open source software that trillions of tests had failed to detect. They also introduced an add-on for Claude to help other developers with verification. Costs of the initial project were not disclosed.

The big promise is a future where software runs more reliably with fewer security headaches. But whether AI can bring formal verification beyond the most critical systems at organizations like NASA and Apple and into widespread use remains an open question.

The technology is still in the prototyping stage. Though demand is high, it’s unclear how much customers are willing to pay and how they prefer to adopt the technology. Formal verification relies on making assumptions about how computers and people interact with software, and some experts are skeptical about its ability to catch bugs stemming from user error and hardware breakdowns.

Will Wilson, who runs the bug-hunting AI software startup Antithesis, calls formal verification “a trap” for math nerds like himself. Antithesis spent millions of dollars to formally verify some of its cybersecurity defenses, a process Wilson describes as a “pain in the ass.” Yet the startup still uncovered additional errors using its own tool, and Antithesis has also found bugs in software that several of its customers had formally verified. “It can give you some assurance, but only robust exhaustive testing can prove your assurance is true,” Wilson says.

Or as Vitalik Buterin, the engineer known for creating the Ethereum cryptocurrency, put it in a blog post earlier this year, “formal verification is not a panacea.” But he and other proponents of the approach still believe it will be an important defense against AI systems launching cyberattacks and wreaking havoc.

Boeing planes, Amazon servers, and more than 2.5 billion active Apple devices contain at least some formally verified software, according to company disclosures. The code in question is typically security-related, and vulnerabilities in it could cause serious harm if exploited.

Byron Cook, a distinguished scientist and vice president at Amazon Web Services, says formal verification has eased customer concerns about cloud security and helped internal teams move faster by squashing big bugs early on.

But several midsized tech companies tell WIRED they have typically verified only one key feature of their products, if any at all. They cite a lack of verification engineers, costs that outweigh the potential risks, and, perhaps most importantly, concerns that waiting weeks for code to be formally verified could slow innovation.

Earlier this year, Apple’s security team said that some of the issues formal verification uncovered in its “corecrypto” library, which is used for encryption, could not have been found any other way. But the company added that it has to be “conservative” when adding new code to corecrypto to ensure it can keep pace with reviewing it.

Two cybersecurity executives at major companies that haven’t formally verified any code say they aren’t sure whether automation will make it worthwhile. But the executives, who weren’t authorized to speak publicly, say they could imagine paying major AI labs for “verified” AI-generated code.

Developers of open source software projects, which are the bedrock of many apps, are increasingly experimenting with AI-aided verification. The nonprofit Beneficial AI Foundation used a grant from Anthropic to validate the same encryption code this year as Sun did at Stanford. Michael Rosenberg, a maintainer of the library known as curve25519-dalek, hopes sustainable funding emerges for ongoing verification efforts. “I have no ideas as to how that’s going to happen, though, and we certainly shouldn’t rely on the goodwill of the AI companies,” he says.

Some of the startups eager to expand verification also aren’t sure whether to deploy their tools directly to customers or through intermediaries like Anthropic. Their general plan is to use AI to automate much of the work involved in defining how a program is supposed to behave. For example, specifications for a data table might require that it contain the same items before and after sorting, just in a different order. Further automation efforts, which may not involve AI, would translate that code into a format that math tools like Lean, Rocq, and Isabelle can use to check whether the code works as intended.

Another recent entrant to the formal verification field is Madan Musuvathi, who left Microsoft Research after more than 20 years to found the startup Truidic. After incidents like the OpenAI hack of Hugging Face, he felt there was an urgent need to commercialize his studies. “AI in the hands of attackers can be extremely powerful,” Musuvathi says, but verification can “make AI safe and secure for everyone, everywhere.”

Proofcraft, one of the few companies that has long offered traditional verification, says growing excitement about the process is translating into a flood of inquiries from potential customers. June Andronick, the company’s CEO, and Gerwin Klein, its chief scientist, say interest easily outpaces what they and their competition can provide.

But both worry that AI-generated specifications could inspire “unjustified trust” in the results. Verifiers are also eager to preserve the joy their work brings them. Klein calls it “pretty addictive, like a puzzle game.” If all goes well, he’ll be doing more solving than ever.

Mistral Says Its AI Model ‘Le Chonk’ Has Leapfrogged China in the Open-Weight Race

Wired October 29, 2026

A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now says Le Chonk is the “world’s best” open-weight model for automated coding and cybersecurity.

The advances, Mistral says, were made possible by feeding the model increasingly difficult cybersecurity and coding problems, which allowed the trillion-parameter Le Chonk to match or surpass models from leading Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Z. ai.

“It’s a pivotal moment in the global AI leadership race,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at Mistral, told reporters during a press briefing. “It offers frontier capabilities for enterprises and governments to defend against an increasing threat level in cyber.”

The finalized version of Le Chonk is now freely available for anybody to access. After a flurry of AI-related cybersecurity incidents, Mistral claims that it’s important for the West to have its own advanced open-weight models. “You have no guarantee that [Chinese models] won’t behave maliciously. They can be threat vectors,” Stock said.

The most high-profile episode occurred when one of OpenAI’s models broke loose from a testing sandbox and hacked into multiple companies over the summer. It sparked panic over the idea that AI could escape human oversight and be abused by threat actors to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. (One of the affected companies, Hugging Face, used an open-weight model from China to assess and defend against the attack.)

Since then, AI has unearthed security vulnerabilities in ubiquitous software, too. In October, a raft of websites were taken offline after an AI tool discovered serious flaws in a foundational piece of web technology.

Mistral pitches its open-weight models, like Le Chonk, as part of the solution. If AI is destined to become a central feature of both cyber offense and defense, the argument goes, businesses and governments will need to be equipped with models that are freely available and cannot be switched off remotely, unlike proprietary models from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

“AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor can cut off electricity from one day to another,” Stock said. “Once you open source the weights, they’re all over the internet. It’s impossible to cut off access.”

The trade-off, however, is that freely available models can also be downloaded and customized by threat actors.

“It’s clearly a dual-use technology,” Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “Anything that’s available to download and circulate unfettered has the ability to be abused as well as used for productive purposes.”

According to Pilling, though it’s possible a Chinese model with internet access could siphon away data, all advanced models are capable of going rogue without careful supervision—no matter their country of origin.

“The technical realities and the narrative—which often has a nationalistic leaning—are two different things,” he says.“It’s about having the right monitoring and controls in place to be confident that, even if the model was trying to be deceptive or nefarious, you might have some way of detecting it.”
